summary: Vision-language models such as CLIP enable zero-shot classification from arbitrary class names, but under test-time corruptions, their visual encoder projects distorted features onto incorrect textual anchors with high confidence: a phenomenon we term modality bias. Standard entropy minimization reinforces these overconfident errors, which creates a confirmation-bias loop and collapses the predicted label distribution. We propose an online test-time adaptation (TTA) method that breaks this loop at three levels. At the representation level, a frozen self-supervised backbone (e.g., DINO v2) is combined with CLIP through a cross-covariance logit ensemble. CLIP text prototypes are projected into the feature space of this text-free backbone, so the self-supervised branch classifies native image features and is less affected by the text bias of CLIP. At the optimization level, a gated test-time information-maximization objective pairs per-sample sharpening with batch-level diversity, while an adaptive gate excludes unreliable samples from the gradient. At the prediction level, an online logit adjustment corrects the residual class-distribution skew. CDIM outperforms the compared CLIP-based online TTA baselines on ImageNet-C, CIFAR10-C, and CIFAR100-C, and remains competitive in continual and mixed-domain TTA. Extensive analyses and ablation studies verify the contribution of each of its components. Our code is available at this https URL

AI.tldr: The paper proposes CDIM, an online test-time adaptation method for CLIP that combines CLIP with a frozen DINOv2 backbone through a cross-covariance logit ensemble, a gated information-maximization objective and online logit adjustment, to counter modality bias under corruptions.
AI.motivation: Under test-time corruptions CLIP's visual encoder projects distorted features onto wrong text anchors with high confidence, and standard entropy minimization reinforces these errors, causing a confirmation-bias loop and collapse of the predicted label distribution.
AI.method: At the representation level, CLIP text prototypes are projected into the feature space of a frozen self-supervised DINOv2 backbone, combined with CLIP through a cross-covariance logit ensemble. At the optimization level, a gated information-maximization objective pairs per-sample sharpening with batch-level diversity, and an adaptive gate excludes unreliable samples from the gradient. At the prediction level, online logit adjustment corrects residual class skew.
AI.result: CDIM outperforms compared CLIP-based online TTA baselines on ImageNet-C, CIFAR10-C and CIFAR100-C and remains competitive in continual and mixed-domain TTA. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Breaking the confirmation-bias loop at representation, optimization and prediction levels makes online test-time adaptation of CLIP more robust to corruptions.

title: Polarimetric Scattering-Structure Contrastive Learning for Few-Shot HRRP Recognition
summary: Few-shot high-resolution range profile (HRRP) recognition is challenged by strong aspect-dependent variation and sparse novel-class support. We propose polarimetric scattering-structure contrastive learning (PSS-CL), which supplies an episodic HRRP encoder with a structured physical training view. Dominant local responses are represented by their soft affinities to canonical polarimetric mechanisms, normalized range locations, and energy contributions. A symmetric cross-view objective transfers this scattering structure to the learned HRRP representation, while episodic prototype learning supports novel-class inference without the physical branch. We conduct Random-aspect and Cross-aspect experiments on a six-class measured dataset. In Cross-aspect 1-, 3-, and 5-shot recognition, PSS-CL achieves 81.73%, 86.92%, and 90.98% mean class accuracy (MCA), respectively, outperforming the best competing results by 5.62%, 3.09%, and 3.56%.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes PSS-CL, a contrastive learning method that gives an episodic HRRP encoder a physics-based training view of polarimetric scattering structure, improving few-shot radar target recognition on a six-class measured dataset.
AI.motivation: Few-shot high-resolution range profile recognition faces strong aspect-dependent variation and very few support samples for novel classes.
AI.method: Dominant local responses are described by soft affinities to canonical polarimetric scattering mechanisms, normalized range locations and energy contributions. A symmetric cross-view contrastive objective transfers this scattering structure to the learned representation, while episodic prototype learning supports novel-class inference without the physical branch.
AI.result: In Cross-aspect experiments on a six-class measured dataset, PSS-CL reaches 81.73%, 86.92% and 90.98% mean class accuracy for 1-, 3- and 5-shot recognition, outperforming the best competing results by 5.62, 3.09 and 3.56 points.
AI.conclusion: Injecting polarimetric scattering structure as a training-time view improves few-shot HRRP recognition under aspect changes without needing the physical branch at inference.

title: SPA-Q: Structure-Preserving Adaptive Post-Training Quantization for Monocular Depth Estimation
summary: Monocular depth estimation (MDE) has advanced rapidly with the emergence of foundation models such as Depth Anything. Their transformer-based architectures provide strong generalization across diverse scenes and domains, but also incur high computational and memory cost, making efficient deployment challenging. Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) provides an efficient and practical solution for model compression, yet low-bit PTQ remains challenging for MDE models. When applying PTQ to Depth Anything, we identify two key challenges: (i) independently minimizing the quantization error of the query and key projections fails to preserve the attention maps induced by their interaction, and (ii) quantization errors accumulate across layers, resulting in intermediate feature distribution shifts. To address these issues, we propose SPA-Q, a Structure-Preserving Adaptive PTQ framework for MDE, consisting of two main components. First, Attention-Preserving Calibration (APC) determines query and key quantization parameters by matching the full-precision attention distribution. Second, Channel-Wise Distribution Alignment (CWDA) learns channel-wise affine transformations to mitigate quantization-induced distribution shifts, and the learned parameters are absorbed into the weights after training. Experimental results show that SPA-Q consistently outperforms existing PTQ methods under 4-bit quantization, achieving an average 25.9% reduction in AbsRel and a 17.3% improvement in $\delta_1$ across NYUv2 and KITTI datasets.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes SPA-Q, a post-training quantization framework for Depth Anything-style monocular depth estimators that preserves attention maps and corrects channel-wise distribution shifts, outperforming existing PTQ methods at 4-bit on NYUv2 and KITTI.
AI.motivation: Transformer-based monocular depth foundation models are expensive to deploy, and low-bit post-training quantization degrades them because independently minimizing query and key quantization error does not preserve their attention interaction, and errors accumulate across layers.
AI.method: Attention-Preserving Calibration (APC) sets query and key quantization parameters by matching the full-precision attention distribution. Channel-Wise Distribution Alignment (CWDA) learns channel-wise affine transformations to mitigate distribution shifts, and these are absorbed into the weights after training.
AI.result: At 4-bit quantization SPA-Q consistently outperforms existing PTQ methods, with an average 25.9% reduction in AbsRel and a 17.3% improvement in delta-1 across NYUv2 and KITTI.
AI.conclusion: Structure-preserving calibration of attention and channel distributions makes low-bit quantization of monocular depth models substantially more accurate.

title: 3DGS-VBench+ and 3DGSV-Assessor: A Multi-Dimensional Subjective Benchmark and a Reference-Flexible Objective Model for 3D Gaussian Splatting Video Quality Assessment
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables real-time novel view synthesis (NVS), but its heavy storage makes compression essential, and both training and compression introduce representation-specific distortions. Since generative compression in many methods treats geometric and color attributes via different parameters, it can induce dimension-specific distortions, motivating multi-dimensional assessment. Moreover, real-world captures generally lack an aligned ground-truth video for a synthesized, continuous camera trajectory, leaving only sparse captured views as references. To enable multi-dimensional quality assessment of 3DGS videos with scarce aligned references, we first present 3DGS-VBench+, a large-scale subjective video quality assessment (VQA) benchmark comprising 3{,}036 3DGS reconstructions, each paired with a rendered video, across 11 real-world and 22 synthetic scenes, generated by 6 representative compression algorithms at systematically designed levels and annotated with 9{,}108 MOSs covering overall, geometry, and color quality. Based on 3DGS-VBench+, we propose 3DGSV-Assessor, a reference-flexible, large multimodal framework that scores all three dimensions in one generation pass and fuses a ranking-based reference cue into the frozen regressor through a bounded gate, supporting both reduced-reference (RR) and no-reference (NR) assessment. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art correlation with human perception on 3DGS-VBench+ and strong zero-shot generalization to other NVS benchmarks. The dataset and code will be released at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces 3DGS-VBench+, a subjective benchmark of 3,036 compressed 3D Gaussian Splatting videos with 9,108 MOS annotations, and 3DGSV-Assessor, a reference-flexible large multimodal model that scores overall, geometry and color quality.
AI.motivation: Compressed 3DGS videos can have dimension-specific distortions in geometry and color, and real captures lack aligned ground-truth videos for synthesized camera trajectories, so only sparse captured views are available as references.
AI.method: The benchmark pairs 3,036 3DGS reconstructions across 11 real-world and 22 synthetic scenes, compressed by 6 algorithms at designed levels, with MOS annotations covering overall, geometry and color quality. 3DGSV-Assessor scores all three dimensions in one generation pass and fuses a ranking-based reference cue into a frozen regressor through a bounded gate, supporting reduced-reference and no-reference assessment.
AI.result: 3DGSV-Assessor achieves state-of-the-art correlation with human perception on 3DGS-VBench+ and strong zero-shot generalization to other novel view synthesis benchmarks. No specific numbers are given in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: A multi-dimensional benchmark and a reference-flexible model enable quality assessment of 3DGS videos when aligned references are scarce.

title: E2I-Flow: EEG-to-Image Reconstruction via Wavelet-Temporal Cross-Attention and Conditional Flow Matching
summary: Electroencephalography (EEG)-based visual decoding and reconstruction aims to recover visual information from non-invasive brain signals. But there are challenges due to the complex temporal-frequency characteristics of EEG signals and the difficulty of discrete denoising framework in mapping neural activity to meaningful visual representations. Here, we propose E2I-Flow, an EEG-to-image decoding and reconstruction framework that combines a novel EEG encoder for time-frequency representation learning from EEG features, and conditional flow matching for visual decoding. A stationary-wavelet frequency branch and a temporal-mixing branch are integrated through bidirectional cross-attention and adaptive fusion, with the resulting EEG representations aligned to ground-truth image embeddings using contrastive and mean-squared-error loss supervisions. The aligned EEG representation is then used as a condition for a Transformer-based flow-matching model to predict the corresponding visual embedding for image synthesis. Experimental results show strong zero-shot EEG-to-image retrieval and improved visual reconstruction performance, outperforming several state-of-the-art baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes E2I-Flow, an EEG-to-image framework that encodes time-frequency EEG features with a stationary-wavelet branch and a temporal-mixing branch, then uses conditional flow matching to predict image embeddings for reconstruction.
AI.motivation: EEG-based visual decoding is challenged by the complex temporal-frequency structure of EEG signals and by the difficulty of mapping neural activity to visual representations with discrete denoising frameworks.
AI.method: A stationary-wavelet frequency branch and a temporal-mixing branch are joined by bidirectional cross-attention and adaptive fusion. The EEG representation is aligned to ground-truth image embeddings with contrastive and mean-squared-error losses, then used as the condition for a Transformer-based conditional flow-matching model that predicts the visual embedding for image synthesis.
AI.result: The framework shows strong zero-shot EEG-to-image retrieval and improved visual reconstruction, outperforming several state-of-the-art baselines. No specific numbers are given in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Combining wavelet-temporal EEG encoding with flow matching improves EEG-based visual decoding and reconstruction.

title: Learning to Falsify: Hierarchical Multiple Instance Learning for High Resolution AI-Generated Image Detection
summary: Recent advances in generative models have made synthetic images increasingly photorealistic, posing growing challenges to reliable and generalizable detection of AI-generated images. Existing methods typically rely on holistic image-level classification, which may overlook local artifacts, especially in high-resolution images. To address this limitation, we formulate this task as a falsification-driven multiple instance learning problem, where a single fake patch can falsify the whole image, while a real image requires all patches to be authentic. Based on this formulation, we propose \textit{Learning to Falsify (LTF)}, a hierarchical multiple instance learning framework that models an image as multiple bags of instances across different spatial levels and aggregates their predictions under the falsification-inspired principle. We further introduce Cross-Shuffle during training to encourage the model to learn local artifact evidence rather than image-level shortcuts. Furthermore, we propose the \textit{Falsification-driven Test-time Aggregation Strategy (FATAS)}, a plug-and-play module that extends the same falsification-inspired principle to existing detectors by aggregating patch-level predictions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LTF achieves strong generalization and robustness across multiple benchmarks, while FATAS substantially improves representative detectors in high-resolution scenarios without retraining. Code is available at this https URL

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Learning to Falsify (LTF), a hierarchical multiple instance learning framework for high-resolution AI-generated image detection, plus FATAS, a plug-and-play test-time aggregation that lets existing detectors use the same falsification principle without retraining.
AI.motivation: Image-level classifiers for AI-generated images may overlook local artifacts in high-resolution images, and a single fake patch should be enough to flag a whole image while a real image needs all patches to be authentic.
AI.method: The image is modelled as multiple bags of instances across several spatial levels, and their predictions are aggregated under the falsification principle. Cross-Shuffle during training encourages learning local artifact evidence rather than image-level shortcuts. FATAS aggregates patch-level predictions of existing detectors.
AI.result: LTF achieves strong generalization and robustness across multiple benchmarks, and FATAS substantially improves representative detectors on high-resolution images without retraining. No specific numbers are given in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Falsification-driven multiple instance aggregation improves the detection of high-resolution AI-generated images, both as a trained model and as a test-time module.

title: A Universal Raw-IQ Radar Encoder for Cross-Sensor Human Sensing
comment: Accepted at the 2027 IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision (WACV)
summary: Radar-based human sensing typically relies on end-to-end task-specific models trained on hand-chosen signal projections, which generalize poorly across unseen users, tasks, and hardware. We argue that the dominant signal processing choice, the micro-Doppler spectrogram, is a poor starting point for transfer because it keeps the Doppler axis, which carrier frequency rescales, and discards the angular axis, which carrier frequency leaves unchanged. We instead pretrain a convolutional beta-VAE without labels on clutter-removed raw radar measurements from four platforms spanning 60 and 77 GHz and 4 to 12 virtual antennas, aligned by a unified spectral interpolation grid. For every downstream benchmark the encoder stays frozen, and only a small supervised temporal classifier is trained on its embeddings. We compare against supervised models trained end to end on each benchmark and a pretrained radar foundation model across ten settings covering activity, gesture, sign-language, and gait recognition. When the test users and the radar are seen during training, our encoder is best on all five benchmarks. For users never seen in training, it leads on three of four benchmarks, by 4.8 to 23.2 points. On subject-disjoint gait recognition, it is best for each of the four held-out subjects and 8.3 points above the strongest baseline on average, even though its pretraining excluded every recording of this radar. Excluding the test radar from pretraining costs at most 5.3 points on any benchmark. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a universal raw-IQ radar encoder, a convolutional beta-VAE pretrained without labels on clutter-removed raw radar measurements from four platforms, which is frozen and paired with a small temporal classifier for human sensing across users, tasks and hardware.
AI.motivation: Radar human-sensing models trained end to end generalize poorly to unseen users, tasks and hardware, and the micro-Doppler spectrogram discards the angular axis and keeps a Doppler axis that carrier frequency rescales, making it a poor starting point for transfer.
AI.method: A convolutional beta-VAE is pretrained without labels on clutter-removed raw radar measurements from platforms at 60 and 77 GHz with 4 to 12 virtual antennas, aligned by a unified spectral interpolation grid. The encoder stays frozen and only a small supervised temporal classifier is trained per downstream benchmark.
AI.result: Across ten settings covering activity, gesture, sign-language and gait recognition, the encoder is best on all five benchmarks when test users and radar are seen in training. For unseen users it leads on three of four benchmarks, by 4.8 to 23.2 points. On subject-disjoint gait recognition it is best for each held-out subject and 8.3 points above the strongest baseline on average, and excluding the test radar from pretraining costs at most 5.3 points.
AI.conclusion: A label-free, frozen raw-IQ encoder transfers across users, radars and tasks better than end-to-end supervised models and a pretrained radar foundation model.

title: Predicting Void Points in Self-Occluding Forest Volumes
summary: Synthetic Aperture Imaging (SAI) enables drones to observe forest canopies by warping and averaging multiple displaced views at a common depth. However, occlusion is suppressed rather than eliminated, causing poorly observed regions to appear occupied and leading to systematic biomass overestimation. The Deep Forest project cannot distinguish reconstruction artifacts from real vegetation because its training data relies on measured reflectance points, excluding empty space and preventing the network from learning explicit occupancy boundaries. This thesis addresses the problem by modifying training labels rather than the imaging process. Each simulated scene is rendered twice: as a 9x9 grid of top-down captures for focal-stack generation and as 550 depth-clipped slabs derived from scene geometry to provide occupancy labels, explicitly representing void space as a negative class. A Gazebo pipeline generates procedural forest stands containing 80-200 trees across three species. A pretrained Pix2Pix model translates rendered RGB images into a synthetic near-infrared band, and Light Field Rendering produces aligned focal stacks of 550 planes across three channels. Four architectures were evaluated on a held-out scene. The plain 2D U-Net achieved an IoU of 0.6290, outperforming the volumetric 3D U-Net (0.5707). Established reconstruction methods performed substantially worse: COLMAP achieved 0.3446 and DepthAnything3 0.2959, both after their respective optimal dilation sweeps. An RGB-input variant of the volumetric architecture achieved the highest IoU of 0.6514 without dilation or per-scene calibration. These results highlight the limitations of conventional reconstruction methods, which recover visible surfaces but struggle to infer occupancy within closed canopies.

AI.tldr: The thesis proposes relabelling forest-canopy training data with explicit void (empty space) occupancy labels from scene geometry, so that networks learn occupancy boundaries in self-occluding forest volumes captured by synthetic aperture imaging, with a plain 2D U-Net scoring best.
AI.motivation: Synthetic aperture imaging suppresses occlusion rather than removing it, so poorly observed regions look occupied and bias biomass estimates upward, and the Deep Forest training labels cover only measured reflectance points, so the network never learns empty space.
AI.method: Each simulated Gazebo forest scene (80 to 200 trees, three species) is rendered as a 9x9 grid of top-down captures for focal stacks and as 550 depth-clipped slabs providing occupancy labels with void as a negative class. A pretrained Pix2Pix translates RGB to a synthetic near-infrared band, and Light Field Rendering produces 550-plane focal stacks. Four architectures are compared on a held-out scene.
AI.result: The plain 2D U-Net reaches IoU 0.6290, above the volumetric 3D U-Net at 0.5707. COLMAP reaches 0.3446 and DepthAnything3 0.2959 after their optimal dilation sweeps. An RGB-input volumetric variant reaches the highest IoU, 0.6514, without dilation or per-scene calibration.
AI.conclusion: Changing the training labels to represent void space is more effective for forest occupancy than conventional reconstruction methods, which recover visible surfaces but struggle to infer occupancy within closed canopies.

title: SEEK-VAU: Towards Evidence-Faithful Video Anomaly Understanding via Agentic Search
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (main conference track). 27 pages, 5 figures
summary: Most video anomaly understanding (VAU) systems still infer anomaly judgments from evidence collected in a feed-forward way under predefined rules, typically sampled frames, or events clustered from such frames. This protocol fails when the collected evidence is incomplete under imperfect predefined rules, because once reasoning begins the model can no longer search for the missing evidence. We address this limitation with SEEK-VAU, which reframes VAU as an agentic search-and-verify interaction protocol under a bounded search budget: instead of passively reasoning over pre-collected evidence, the policy actively gathers evidence across the three stages of an anomaly event chain (precursor, trigger, and aftermath) and verifies its sufficiency before finalization, turning event-chain completeness into an explicit design rather than an outcome of predefined rules. A bounded budget caps the cost of this search, but does not by itself teach the policy where to look or when to stop. To make this behavior learnable, we introduce evidence-faithful counterfactual verification (EFCV), which rewards selected evidence that remains supportive, compact, and necessary under counterfactual verification. We further introduce SEEK-Bench, featuring video-level episodes with temporal interval annotations, semantic QA and event-chain stage labels. Together, SEEK-VAU and SEEK-Bench establish a strong foundation for evidence-faithful and actively verifiable VAU.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes SEEK-VAU, which reframes video anomaly understanding as a bounded agentic search-and-verify process over the precursor, trigger and aftermath stages of an anomaly, trained with evidence-faithful counterfactual verification and evaluated on the new SEEK-Bench.
AI.motivation: Feed-forward video anomaly understanding relies on predefined rules and pre-collected frames or events, so when the evidence is incomplete the model cannot search for what is missing.
AI.method: The policy actively gathers evidence across the three stages of an anomaly event chain under a bounded search budget and verifies sufficiency before finalizing. Evidence-faithful counterfactual verification (EFCV) rewards selected evidence that remains supportive, compact and necessary under counterfactual verification. SEEK-Bench provides video-level episodes with temporal interval annotations, semantic QA and event-chain stage labels.
AI.result: The abstract reports no quantitative results.
AI.conclusion: SEEK-VAU and SEEK-Bench are presented as a foundation for evidence-faithful and actively verifiable video anomaly understanding.

title: Multi-Path Mamba Diffusion for 3D Point Cloud Semantic Scene Completion
summary: 3D semantic scene completion plays a critical role in enabling various downstream tasks within autonomous systems by estimating both missing geometric structures and semantic information in scene data. In this work, we introduce a unique neural framework that integrates state space modeling with diffusion-based generative approaches to enhance 3D point cloud semantic scene completion. We propose \textit{MPath Mamba} diffusion network, leveraging a skip-triple Mamba structure, dimensional decomposition residuals, and multi-directional dilations within multi-path data to efficiently process long-sequence data for feature extraction. The proposed method operates in the conditioned latent space of a variational autoencoder, enhanced by a state-space mechanism to improve 3D point cloud representation and reconstruction. Extensive experiments conducted on the SemanticKITTI benchmark demonstrate that our approach achieves highly competitive performance for 3D point cloud semantic scene completion.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes MPath Mamba diffusion, a network that combines Mamba state-space blocks with diffusion in the latent space of a VAE to perform 3D point cloud semantic scene completion, evaluated on SemanticKITTI.
AI.motivation: Semantic scene completion for autonomous systems requires estimating missing geometry and semantics efficiently for long point-cloud sequences.
AI.method: The network uses a skip-triple Mamba structure, dimensional decomposition residuals and multi-directional dilations across multi-path data, and operates in the conditioned latent space of a variational autoencoder.
AI.result: Experiments on the SemanticKITTI benchmark show highly competitive performance for 3D point cloud semantic scene completion. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: State-space modelling combined with latent diffusion is a competitive approach to 3D semantic scene completion.

title: SparseGraph-I2P: Consistency-Guided Hypothesis Selection for Efficient Image-to-Point-Cloud Registration
summary: Coarse-to-fine image-to-point-cloud (I2P) registration risks discarding correct but ambiguous patch pairs, while retaining more candidates repeats fine matching over overlapping patches. SparseGraph-I2P aims to improve registration recall by increasing the inlier ratio at the pose solver, using sensor or monocular depth. A Coarse Hypothesis Graph combines appearance with depth-derived first- and second-order compatibility to select a fixed budget of patch pairs. Sparse Fine Matching decodes each queried pixel once and skips pixel--point comparisons covered by an ancestor patch paired with the same point-cloud region. With sensor depth, depth-aware filtering ranks correspondences by SC2 spectral support for a single EPnP solve. With monocular depth, depth or inverse depth is calibrated from correspondence geometry before filtering. SparseGraph-I2P achieves the highest registration recall and lowest latency among the compared methods on RGB-D Scenes V2 and 7-Scenes with sensor depth. With predicted depth, it retains the highest recall on RGB-D Scenes V2 at an additional calibration cost. Code will be released.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes SparseGraph-I2P, an image-to-point-cloud registration method that selects patch pairs with a consistency-guided coarse hypothesis graph and performs sparse fine matching, reaching the highest recall and lowest latency on RGB-D Scenes V2 and 7-Scenes with sensor depth.
AI.motivation: Coarse-to-fine image-to-point-cloud registration either discards correct but ambiguous patch pairs or repeats costly fine matching over overlapping patches when more candidates are kept.
AI.method: A Coarse Hypothesis Graph combines appearance with depth-derived first- and second-order compatibility to select a fixed budget of patch pairs. Sparse Fine Matching decodes each queried pixel once and skips comparisons covered by an ancestor patch. With sensor depth, depth-aware filtering ranks correspondences by SC2 spectral support for a single EPnP solve; with monocular depth, depth is calibrated from correspondence geometry before filtering.
AI.result: With sensor depth SparseGraph-I2P achieves the highest registration recall and lowest latency on RGB-D Scenes V2 and 7-Scenes. With predicted depth it keeps the highest recall on RGB-D Scenes V2 at an additional calibration cost. No specific numbers are given in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Increasing the inlier ratio at the pose solver through graph-based hypothesis selection improves recall and speed for image-to-point-cloud registration; code is to be released.

title: Gradient-Guided Orientation Learning for Weakly Supervised Oriented Object Detection
comment: Accepted to WACV 2027. 10 pages, 4 figures, 7 tables
summary: Weakly supervised oriented object detection (WS-OOD) aims to reduce the annotation cost of rotated bounding boxes by leveraging cheaper annotations such as horizontal boxes or points. However, these weak annotations provide no explicit orientation information, forcing existing methods to infer object angles through indirect geometric consistency or equivariant constraints. Such indirect supervision often becomes ambiguous and unstable under real-world appearance variations, including illumination changes, color shifts, shadows, and background clutter. In this paper, we present a simple yet effective gradient-guided orientation learning strategy for WS-OOD. Motivated by the observation that the input image itself contains useful orientation priors, our method extracts dominant gradient-based orientation cues from object regions and converts them into pseudo-angle labels for auxiliary supervision, enabling the detector to learn orientation-aware representations without requiring rotated bounding box annotations or extra learnable parameters. Furthermore, since AP can mask substantial angular errors when spatial IoU remains high, we introduce an orientation-aware evaluation metric that incorporates angular discrepancies into the standard AP protocol. Extensive experiments on weakly supervised oriented detection benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed pseudo-angle supervision improves both detection performance and orientation estimation quality, while the proposed metric provides a more faithful assessment of angle prediction than conventional AP alone.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a gradient-guided orientation learning strategy for weakly supervised oriented object detection, which derives pseudo-angle labels from dominant image gradients, and an orientation-aware AP metric that penalizes angular errors.
AI.motivation: Weak annotations such as horizontal boxes or points give no explicit orientation, so existing methods infer angles indirectly through geometric consistency or equivariance, which is ambiguous under illumination, colour, shadow and clutter changes.
AI.method: Dominant gradient-based orientation cues are extracted from object regions and converted into pseudo-angle labels for auxiliary supervision, requiring no rotated-box annotations or extra learnable parameters. An orientation-aware evaluation metric incorporates angular discrepancies into the standard AP protocol.
AI.result: The pseudo-angle supervision improves both detection performance and orientation estimation quality on weakly supervised oriented detection benchmarks, and the new metric gives a more faithful assessment of angle prediction than conventional AP. No specific numbers are given in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Image-derived gradient orientation priors provide simple and effective supervision for weakly supervised oriented detection, and standard AP can mask angular errors.

title: MambaHand: Local Identity and Behavioral Sequence Learning with Mamba for Dynamic Hand Gesture Authentication
summary: Dynamic hand gesture authentication (DHGA) is an emerging biometric technique that contains both physiological and behavioral identity characteristics. However, existing methods primarily rely on convolutional networks or manually designed motion representations, making it difficult to jointly capture fine-grained local identity differences and long-range behavioral dependencies during hand gesture execution. To address these challenges, we propose a two-stream identity representation learning framework, MambaHand Net, to combine CNNs with Mamba for DHGA. The proposed framework consists of a Local Identity Stream (LIS) and a Behavioral Sequential Stream (BSS). The LIS extracts frame-wise local identity cues with a convolutional network, while the BSS preserves spatial tokens from intermediate visual features and constructs first-order and second-order temporal difference sequences to model multi-order behavioral variations. Moreover, the bidirectional Mamba is incorporated into the BSS to model semantic motion across different spatial locations, enabling efficient long-range modeling of hand gesture execution habits. Finally, attention-guided spatial token aggregation and a two-stream fusion strategy are used to integrate local identity cues and multi-order behavioral patterns into a discriminative identity representation. Our method achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) average performance on the SCUT-DHGA benchmark dataset, demonstrating that combining CNNs with Mamba is an effective new solution for DHGA.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes MambaHand Net, a two-stream dynamic hand gesture authentication model that combines a CNN local identity stream with a bidirectional Mamba behavioural stream over first- and second-order temporal differences, reaching state-of-the-art average performance on SCUT-DHGA.
AI.motivation: Dynamic hand gesture authentication needs both fine-grained local identity cues and long-range behavioural dependencies, which CNN-based methods and hand-designed motion representations capture poorly.
AI.method: The Local Identity Stream extracts frame-wise identity cues with a CNN. The Behavioral Sequential Stream keeps spatial tokens from intermediate features, builds first- and second-order temporal difference sequences, and applies bidirectional Mamba to model motion across spatial locations. Attention-guided spatial token aggregation and two-stream fusion produce the final identity representation.
AI.result: MambaHand Net achieves state-of-the-art average performance on the SCUT-DHGA benchmark. No specific numbers are given in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Combining CNNs with Mamba is an effective approach to dynamic hand gesture authentication.

title: ReXMo: End-to-End Video Character Replacement with Expression and Motion Preservation
summary: Video character replacement aims to replace actors while preserving facial expressions, motions, and scene dynamics. Existing methods typically rely on masked generation with pose guidance, limiting fine-grained expression and motion preservation in complex scenes. We propose ReXMo, an end-to-end framework that supports single-, multi-, and selective character replacement scenarios. ReXMo introduces paired triplet supervision, where synthesized driving videos and original videos share identical performances but different identities, enabling scalable training through synthetic data generation. An In-Context Diffusion Transformer learns identity transformation by jointly conditioning on driving videos, reference identities, and text prompts, while an Expression Enhancement Adapter improves facial expression preservation in multi-person scenes. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ReXMo outperforms existing methods in identity fidelity, motion consistency, expression preservation, and visual quality. Our dataset and code will be publicly released.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes ReXMo, an end-to-end video character replacement framework that preserves expressions and motion using paired triplet supervision from synthetic data, an In-Context Diffusion Transformer and an Expression Enhancement Adapter for multi-person scenes.
AI.motivation: Existing video character replacement methods rely on masked generation with pose guidance, which limits fine-grained expression and motion preservation in complex scenes.
AI.method: Paired triplet supervision uses synthesized driving videos and original videos that share a performance but differ in identity, enabling scalable training with synthetic data. An In-Context Diffusion Transformer learns identity transformation from driving videos, reference identities and text prompts, and an Expression Enhancement Adapter improves expression preservation in multi-person scenes. The framework supports single, multi and selective replacement.
AI.result: ReXMo outperforms existing methods in identity fidelity, motion consistency, expression preservation and visual quality, according to the abstract. No specific numbers are given.
AI.conclusion: Triplet-supervised in-context diffusion can replace characters in videos while keeping expressions and motion intact; the dataset and code are to be released.

title: BhopalMLS: A LiDAR Dataset for Semantic Scene Understanding in Heterogeneous Urban Environments
comment: Accepted at WACV 2027 (Evaluations and Datasets Track). 37 pages: main paper, references and supplementary material. Project page: this https URL
summary: We introduce BhopalMLS, a large-scale Mobile Laser Scanning (MLS) dataset from a dense, heterogeneous urban environment in Bhopal, India, with mixed traffic, informal structures, and narrow unplanned streets. It spans approximately 10 km of road corridors with over 1.2 billion points and 19,518 annotated instances across 62 fine-grained static categories, grouped into 12-class and 21-class benchmark taxonomies; 6 optional moving-class subclasses support dynamic-object analysis. Existing 3D datasets, collected in well-planned cities, are structurally more uniform than such unplanned settings, and lack their subtype diversity. On semantic and instance segmentation at both granularities, fine-tuned foundation models surpass supervised baselines: Utonia(L) reaches 71.28% mIoU (vs. PTv3's 68.04% from scratch) and 44.07% mAP50 on the 12-class benchmark. Cross-region experiments against four established datasets (Ke-MLS, Toronto-3D, Paris-Lille-3D, SemanticKITTI) reveal a consistent asymmetric transferability: models trained on BhopalMLS transfer better than the reverse on every pair, for both Utonia(L) and Concerto(L) (mean 21.5, up to 36 mIoU points), holding even when the target is denser. Factor-controlled retraining at a fixed label budget, repeated on both models, attributes this to the coverage of BhopalMLS's subtype inventory rather than to dataset size or corridor geometry: collapsing each class to a single subtype costs 13.0 and 13.3 mIoU points for Utonia(L) and Concerto(L). BhopalMLS therefore offers a testbed for 3D perception beyond well-planned cities. Data and an interactive viewer are at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces BhopalMLS, a mobile laser scanning LiDAR dataset from Bhopal, India, with over 1.2 billion points and 19,518 annotated instances across 62 static categories, and shows that fine-tuned foundation models outperform supervised baselines and transfer asymmetrically across datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing 3D urban datasets are collected in well-planned cities and are structurally more uniform than dense, heterogeneous cities with mixed traffic and informal structures, and they lack subtype diversity.
AI.method: The dataset covers about 10 km of road corridors with 62 fine-grained static categories grouped into 12-class and 21-class taxonomies, plus 6 optional moving-class subclasses. Utonia(L) and Concerto(L) foundation models are fine-tuned and compared with PTv3 trained from scratch, and cross-region transfer is tested against Ke-MLS, Toronto-3D, Paris-Lille-3D and SemanticKITTI, with factor-controlled retraining at a fixed label budget.
AI.result: Utonia(L) reaches 71.28% mIoU and 44.07% mAP50 on the 12-class benchmark, versus 68.04% mIoU for PTv3 from scratch. Models trained on BhopalMLS transfer better than the reverse on every pair, with a mean gain of 21.5 and up to 36 mIoU points. Collapsing each class to one subtype costs 13.0 and 13.3 mIoU points for Utonia(L) and Concerto(L).
AI.conclusion: Subtype coverage in the training data, rather than dataset size or corridor geometry, explains the transfer advantage, and BhopalMLS provides a testbed for 3D perception beyond well-planned cities.

title: Phase-DGS: Phase-guided Dynamic Gaussian Splatting from Unsynchronized Multi-view Video
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026. Project page: this https URL
summary: Spatiotemporal scene reconstruction with Dynamic Gaussian Splatting (DGS) fundamentally depends on perfect temporal synchronization across all cameras, an assumption rarely achievable in practice. Industry-standard synchronization requires expensive specialized hardware and complex setup, while data-driven alternatives including audio-based alignment, geometry matching, and pose tracking remain limited by restrictive environmental or scene-specific assumptions. To overcome these limitations, we propose Phase-DGS, a framework that replaces conventional timestamps with a semantic phase representing each frame's inherent state within the underlying motion cycle. Frames capturing the same motion state share the same phase regardless of which camera records them or when, naturally establishing spatiotemporal correspondence across unsynchronized cameras. We validate Phase-DGS under temporal offsets, frame drops, and camera freezes, achieving up to +8.5 dB PSNR improvement over baselines while enabling seamless integration with existing DGS backbones including RealTime-4DGS and FreeTimeGS.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Phase-DGS, a dynamic Gaussian Splatting framework that replaces timestamps with a semantic motion-cycle phase so that frames from unsynchronized multi-view cameras can be aligned without hardware synchronization.
AI.motivation: Dynamic Gaussian Splatting assumes perfect synchronization across cameras, which needs expensive hardware or is limited by audio, geometry or pose-based alignment methods that rely on restrictive assumptions.
AI.method: Each frame is assigned a semantic phase representing its state within the underlying motion cycle. Frames showing the same motion state share a phase regardless of camera or capture time, which establishes spatiotemporal correspondence across unsynchronized cameras, and the phase is used with existing DGS backbones such as RealTime-4DGS and FreeTimeGS.
AI.result: Phase-DGS is validated under temporal offsets, frame drops and camera freezes, with up to +8.5 dB PSNR improvement over baselines. The abstract gives no other specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Phase-based correspondence lets dynamic Gaussian Splatting work from unsynchronized multi-view video and integrates with existing backbones.

title: Learning from Unlabeled Photographs for General Oral Image Analysis
summary: Oral photographs contain rich clinical information and hold significant potential for artificial intelligence applications; however, most models are trained for individual tasks and rely on costly expert annotations. We hypothesized that self-supervised training on unlabeled oral photographs could produce transferable visual representations for heterogeneous vision tasks. To test this hypothesis, we developed DOVE (Dental Optical Visual Encoder) by domain-adaptive self-supervised pretraining on approximately 530,000 unlabeled oral photographs collected from publicly accessible sources. DOVE was benchmarked against 3 established baselines across 5 classification datasets and 4 segmentation datasets, covering both frozen backbone evaluation and end-to-end finetuning. DOVE achieved the strongest overall performance, ranking best in few-shot transfer and label efficiency on most benchmarks. Under the 20-shot frozen-backbone protocol, DOVE outperformed the second best DINOv3 by 4.37 percentage points in mean macro-F1 across classification datasets and by 4.49 percentage points in mean macro-Dice across segmentation tasks. Under end-to-end finetuning, DOVE achieved at least 80% of the strongest full-data baseline's performance across most evaluation datasets using only 10% of the labeled training data. Qualitative retrieval and feature analyses further indicated better organization of image-level and spatial representations. These findings support DOVE as a generalizable and label-efficient backbone for oral vision research.

AI.tldr: The paper presents DOVE, a self-supervised oral-photograph encoder pretrained on about 530,000 unlabeled images, which gives stronger few-shot and label-efficient transfer than three baselines including DINOv3 across 5 classification and 4 segmentation datasets.
AI.motivation: Oral photographs carry rich clinical information, but most models are trained for individual tasks and depend on costly expert annotations, so a transferable visual representation learned without labels is needed.
AI.method: Domain-adaptive self-supervised pretraining on about 530,000 unlabeled oral photographs from publicly accessible sources yields DOVE, which is benchmarked against three established baselines under frozen-backbone evaluation and end-to-end fine-tuning.
AI.result: Under the 20-shot frozen-backbone protocol DOVE outperforms the second best, DINOv3, by 4.37 points in mean macro-F1 across classification datasets and by 4.49 points in mean macro-Dice across segmentation tasks. With end-to-end fine-tuning on 10% of the labels it reaches at least 80% of the strongest full-data baseline on most datasets. Retrieval and feature analyses show better organization of image-level and spatial representations.
AI.conclusion: DOVE is a generalizable and label-efficient backbone for oral vision research.

title: VISAGE: Vertex-based Intrinsic Surface Appearance GEneration via Dual-Stream Diffusion for Arbitrary 3D Heads
summary: Recovering identity-faithful, physically based surface appearance for 3D human heads from sparse images remains challenging. Existing methods often rely on UV-based pipelines, introducing seam artefacts, or operate in image space, limiting surface consistency. We present VISAGE, Vertex-based Intrinsic Surface Appearance GEneration, a surface-based conditional diffusion framework that synthesises per-vertex albedo and roughness directly on arbitrary mesh topologies, without requiring consistent UV parameterisation at training time. VISAGE combines global spectral processing with local geodesic K-Nearest-Neighbour refinement, enforcing structural coherence while restoring detail beyond the truncated spectral basis. Multi-view RGB images condition the network via visibility-aware cross-attention, enabling occlusion-robust synthesis across the full head surface. Region-specific modules specialise in semantically demanding and distinct areas (eyes, mouth, skin and hair), while a tangent-space output projection recovers fine iris detail. We further introduce a scalable procedural augmentation pipeline that enriches raw geometry scans with physically plausible albedo, roughness and normal maps for training. The predicted attributes render directly as a single RGBA vertex-colour channel. VISAGE reduces FID by 42.7% on NPHM and 22.5% and 4.4% on zero-shot FaceVerse and i3DMM, respectively, relative to the strongest baseline, with a 7.2M-parameter core network.

AI.tldr: VISAGE is a conditional diffusion model that generates per-vertex albedo and roughness directly on arbitrary 3D head meshes, without UV parameterisation. It reduces FID against the strongest baseline by 42.7% on NPHM and by 22.5% and 4.4% on zero-shot FaceVerse and i3DMM.
AI.motivation: UV-based pipelines for physically based head appearance introduce seam artefacts, and image-space methods limit surface consistency. Existing methods do not produce identity-faithful, consistent surface appearance from sparse images on arbitrary topologies.
AI.method: A surface-based conditional diffusion framework that combines global spectral processing with local geodesic K-nearest-neighbour refinement, conditioned on multi-view RGB images through visibility-aware cross-attention. It adds region-specific modules for eyes, mouth, skin and hair, a tangent-space output projection for iris detail, and a procedural augmentation pipeline that enriches raw scans with albedo, roughness and normal maps. The core network has 7.2M parameters.
AI.result: On NPHM, FID drops by 42.7% relative to the strongest baseline. On zero-shot FaceVerse and i3DMM, FID drops by 22.5% and 4.4% respectively. The predicted attributes render directly as a single RGBA vertex-colour channel.
AI.conclusion: Vertex-based diffusion removes the need for consistent UV parameterisation at training time and improves surface appearance generation for arbitrary 3D heads, including on unseen datasets.

title: SPOD: Recovering Suppressed Temporal Evidence in Video-LLMs via Single-Pass Orthogonal Decomposition
comment: 10 pages, 4 figures, 1 table. Accepted to ACM Multimedia 2026 (MM '26)
summary: Video Large Language Models (Video-LLMs) have achieved strong performance on many video understanding tasks, yet remain vulnerable to temporal hallucination in time-sensitive reasoning scenarios such as scene transition understanding and event ordering. Existing solutions either require costly retraining or introduce inefficient multi-pass inference and external supervision at test time. In this work, we show that temporal evidence is already encoded in Video-LLM hidden representations but is not fully exploited during standard inference. Motivated by this observation, we propose Single-Pass Orthogonal Decomposition (SPOD), a training-free framework that recovers suppressed temporal evidence through analytical hidden-state manipulation in a single forward pass. SPOD consists of two components: Frame Distinctiveness Analysis (FDA), which identifies salient frames from middle-layer hidden-state geometry, and Temporal Delta Subspace (TDS), which constructs orthogonal temporal and prior subspaces from weighted inter-frame hidden-state differences. By decomposing final hidden states into temporal, prior, and residual components and rescaling them independently, SPOD enhances dynamic information, suppresses static appearance bias, and preserves complementary information. Experiments on VidHalluc, EventHallusion, and VideoMMMU show that SPOD consistently outperforms strong inference-time baselines across temporal reasoning tasks and model architectures while retaining near-vanilla inference efficiency. These results suggest that improving temporal reasoning in Video-LLMs may depend not only on additional supervision, but also on recovering temporal evidence already present in their internal representations. Our code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: SPOD is a training-free method that improves temporal reasoning in Video-LLMs by rescaling hidden-state components in a single forward pass. It recovers temporal evidence already present in the model's representations and outperforms inference-time baselines on VidHalluc, EventHallusion and VideoMMMU.
AI.motivation: Video-LLMs remain prone to temporal hallucination in time-sensitive reasoning. Existing fixes either need costly retraining or add multi-pass inference and external supervision at test time.
AI.method: Single-Pass Orthogonal Decomposition has two components: Frame Distinctiveness Analysis, which picks salient frames from middle-layer hidden-state geometry, and Temporal Delta Subspace, which builds orthogonal temporal and prior subspaces from weighted inter-frame hidden-state differences. The final hidden states are decomposed into temporal, prior and residual components, and each is rescaled independently.
AI.result: SPOD consistently outperforms strong inference-time baselines on VidHalluc, EventHallusion and VideoMMMU across temporal reasoning tasks and model architectures. Its inference cost stays close to vanilla inference.
AI.conclusion: Better temporal reasoning in Video-LLMs may depend on recovering temporal evidence already encoded in hidden states, not only on additional supervision.

title: TEXMET: A Deep Learning Benchmark for Archaeological Textile Reconstruction
comment: 26 pages, 14 figures, 14 tables. Accepted version of the article published in ACM Journal on Computing and Cultural Heritage (2026). Dataset: this https URL
summary: The reconstruction of fragmented historical textiles presents a significant challenge in computational archaeology. The Oseberg ship burial, dating to 834 CE, yielded hundreds of degraded textile fragments that have resisted systematic computational analysis. While deep learning has revolutionized image-based puzzle solving, progress on archaeological textiles has been limited by the lack of domain-specific datasets and systematic evaluation of modern architectures. To address this gap, we present TEXMET, a curated dataset of 18,644 historical textile images from the Metropolitan Museum of Art's Open Access collection, representing the first textile-specific benchmark for puzzle-solving research. Using TEXMET, we conduct a systematic evaluation of three state-of-the-art puzzle-solving models: JPDVT, FCViT, and DiffAssemble. Our experiments reveal that the transformer-based models pre-trained on standard datasets fail to generalize to textiles, but domain-specific fine-tuning proves highly effective. The graph-based DiffAssemble model, when fine-tuned on TEXMET, achieves 85.89% puzzle accuracy on textile data. Most significantly, applying this fine-tuned model to 45 highly degraded Oseberg fragments yields a performance increase from 26.67% to 64.44% puzzle accuracy. These results establish TEXMET as a new benchmark for textile reconstruction and demonstrate that domain adaptation is essential for applying puzzle-solving methods to imagery of real archaeological materials.

AI.tldr: TEXMET is a benchmark of 18,644 historical textile images from the Metropolitan Museum of Art for puzzle-solving research on archaeological textiles. Fine-tuning DiffAssemble on it raises puzzle accuracy on 45 degraded Oseberg fragments from 26.67% to 64.44%.
AI.motivation: Reconstructing fragmented archaeological textiles, such as the Oseberg ship burial fragments, has resisted computational analysis. Progress has been limited by the lack of domain-specific datasets and systematic evaluation of modern puzzle-solving architectures.
AI.method: The authors build TEXMET, a curated dataset from the Met Open Access collection, and evaluate three puzzle-solving models (JPDVT, FCViT and DiffAssemble) on it. They fine-tune the graph-based DiffAssemble model on textile data and apply it to the Oseberg fragments.
AI.result: Transformer-based models pre-trained on standard datasets fail to generalise to textiles, while domain-specific fine-tuning is highly effective. Fine-tuned DiffAssemble reaches 85.89% puzzle accuracy on TEXMET, and on 45 degraded Oseberg fragments accuracy rises from 26.67% to 64.44%.
AI.conclusion: TEXMET is established as a benchmark for textile reconstruction, and domain adaptation is essential for applying puzzle-solving methods to real archaeological material.

title: Bounded AUKS: A Novel Evaluation Metric for Anomaly Detection via Bounded Area Under the Kolmogorov--Smirnov Curve
summary: Recent literature widely used global metrics such as AUROC and AUPRO to quantify the detection performance. AUROC and AUPRO scores are approaching 100% in some public datasets such as MVTec AD dataset and VisA dataset, which misleadingly suggests that the pixel-level anomaly detection task has already been solved. Threshold-independent metrics represented by AUROC inherently ignore the threshold selection process, which is inevitable in practical applications. Although AUPRO restricts the False Positive rates (FPRs) to an acceptable range, extremely low FPRs can lead to increased false negative rates (FNRs). We argue that there is a lack of metrics capable of quantifying the separation between the anomaly score distributions of normal and anomalous samples, which hinders advancements in anomaly detection. In response, we propose the Bounded Area Under the Kolmogorov--Smirnov curve (Bounded AUKS), a partial integral metric that integrates the difference between TPR and FPR within a data-driven bounded range. Specifically, we introduce AUKS from KS integral as a direct measure of separability between the anomaly score distributions. The bounded range is determined only by score distributions of normal test samples. Lower bound excludes the uninformative high-FPR region. Upper bound avoids evaluation in extreme regions that aggressively push FPR towards zero, which result in a very low recall. Our experiments on 9 models across MVTec AD and VisA datasets show that Bounded AUKS can address the limitations of existing metrics and has a better performance in evaluating unsupervised anomaly detection models.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Bounded AUKS, a threshold-independent metric for anomaly detection that integrates the TPR-FPR separation over a data-driven bounded range of the Kolmogorov-Smirnov curve. It is evaluated on nine models across MVTec AD and VisA.
AI.motivation: AUROC and AUPRO approach 100% on MVTec AD and VisA, which suggests pixel-level anomaly detection is solved. AUROC ignores threshold selection, and AUPRO can push FPR so low that FNR rises. No existing metric directly measures separation between normal and anomalous score distributions.
AI.method: Bounded AUKS is the area under the Kolmogorov-Smirnov curve, integrated between a lower bound that excludes the uninformative high-FPR region and an upper bound that avoids extremely low-FPR regions. Both bounds are determined only by the score distribution of normal test samples.
AI.result: Across nine models on MVTec AD and VisA, Bounded AUKS is reported to address the limitations of existing metrics and to discriminate better among unsupervised anomaly detection models.
AI.conclusion: Bounded AUKS offers a more informative way to evaluate unsupervised anomaly detection than saturated global metrics such as AUROC and AUPRO.

title: iMED: A Multi-Endoscope Dataset for Surgical 3D Perception
comment: Published at ECCV 2026. 25 pages, including supplementary material. Code and dataset: this https URL
summary: We introduce iMED, the first synchronized multi-endoscope dataset for robot-assisted minimally invasive surgery (RAMIS), designed to address a fundamental limitation in surgical vision benchmarking: the absence of independent held-out viewpoints. Existing surgical datasets capture single-trajectory sequences from a single endoscope, making it impossible to distinguish geometric generalization from photometric interpolation along a narrow forward-facing path. iMED provides 340 sequences ~170K synchronized timepoints with 4 views per timepoint) recorded simultaneously from two independent stereo endoscopes across ex vivo, postmortem, and live surgical settings, spanning 14 specimens with diverse anatomical regions and motion regimes. The dataset includes calibrated camera intrinsics, ArUco-based frame-wise pose estimates with uncertainty quantification, instrument segmentation masks, and rich clinical metadata. Using a train-on-one-endoscope, test-on-another evaluation protocol, we benchmark 23 state-of-the-art methods across rigid and deformable novel view synthesis, pose estimation, feature matching, and monocular depth estimation. Our experiments show that methods relying primarily on photometric supervision degrade substantially under this held-out-endoscope setting, while methods with explicit geometric regularization are more robust across views in our benchmark. Notably, large-scale foundation models transfer surprisingly well to surgical imagery, often outperforming domain-specific models, suggesting pitfalls in current fine-tuning protocols. iMED establishes a new evaluation protocol for geometric generalization in surgical vision.

AI.tldr: iMED is a multi-endoscope dataset for surgical 3D perception, with 340 synchronised sequences from two stereo endoscopes. Benchmarking 23 methods under a train-on-one-endoscope, test-on-another protocol shows that photometric methods degrade while geometric regularisation and foundation models hold up.
AI.motivation: Existing surgical datasets come from a single endoscope on a narrow forward path, so geometric generalisation cannot be separated from photometric interpolation. Independent held-out viewpoints are missing from surgical vision benchmarks.
AI.method: The dataset records about 170K synchronised timepoints with four views each from two independent stereo endoscopes, across ex vivo, postmortem and live surgery, with 14 specimens. It provides calibrated intrinsics, ArUco-based pose estimates with uncertainty, instrument masks and clinical metadata. The evaluation protocol trains on one endoscope and tests on the other.
AI.result: Methods relying mainly on photometric supervision degrade substantially under held-out-endoscope evaluation. Methods with explicit geometric regularisation are more robust across views. Large-scale foundation models transfer surprisingly well and often outperform domain-specific models.
AI.conclusion: iMED establishes a new protocol for geometric generalisation in surgical vision, and the results suggest pitfalls in current fine-tuning practice.

title: Point interpolation and distributional universality in flow-based generative models
summary: Motivated by the expressive power of neural ordinary differential equations in flow-based generative modeling, we study the approximation of probability measures by pushforwards generated by parameterized families of Lipschitz vector fields. For Wasserstein distances, we establish a quantitative relationship between finite-sample point interpolation and distributional approximation, and derive universality criteria based on $L^p$-approximation of transport maps. In particular, affine-invariant families containing a non-affine vector field are universal from compactly supported absolutely continuous base measures. For total variation, we show that coordinate-wise dynamics are insufficient in dimensions $d\geq 2$ and establish sufficient conditions based on one-dimensional Sobolev approximation and shear-type mixing. We further examine the role of point interpolation, establishing when different regimes relate to one another and when approximate interpolation can be made exact.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how well flow-based generative models built from Lipschitz vector fields approximate probability measures. It gives Wasserstein universality criteria based on point interpolation and L^p approximation of transport maps, and shows that coordinate-wise dynamics are insufficient for total variation in dimension d of at least 2.
AI.motivation: Neural ODEs motivate flow-based generation, but the approximation theory of pushforward families of Lipschitz vector fields, and how it relates to finite-sample interpolation, is not settled.
AI.method: The authors derive a quantitative link between finite-sample point interpolation and distributional approximation in Wasserstein distance, and state universality criteria via L^p approximation of transport maps. For total variation, they give sufficient conditions based on one-dimensional Sobolev approximation and shear-type mixing.
AI.result: Affine-invariant families that contain one non-affine vector field are universal from compactly supported absolutely continuous base measures in Wasserstein distance. For total variation in dimension at least 2, coordinate-wise dynamics are insufficient.
AI.conclusion: The results clarify which vector-field families are expressive enough for flow-based generative modelling, and when approximate point interpolation can be made exact.

title: Two-Layer Random ReLU Networks Can Separate Disjoint Classes
summary: Set separation by continuous linear functionals is fundamental in functional analysis and convex optimization and underlies binary classification in machine learning. Support vector machines provide maximum-margin affine separators for linearly separable data, while kernel methods represent nonlinear decision rules through linear separation in a reproducing-kernel Hilbert space. We study when two classes, not necessarily convex or linearly separable in the input space, can be separated with positive margin by finite ReLU networks and by random ReLU features. At the deterministic level, we prove that positive-margin separation by a finite ReLU network is equivalent to the existence of finite closed convex covers whose opposite-label members have positive pairwise distances, and exactly two hidden layers suffice. For random separation, suppose each class is represented as a finite union of nonempty closed convex cells, possibly unbounded. If every opposite-label cell pair has positive distance and its closed difference cone is pointed, then two independent random ReLU layers yield a common positive-margin affine separator with high probability. The first layer separates the feature image of each negative cell from the feature image of the positive class by a hyperplane through the origin. It also controls all cross-class distances uniformly. The second layer combines cellwise scores through Chebyshev polynomials and realizes the resulting polynomial using Gaussian Hermite features, followed by a uniform finite-width approximation. With the remaining geometric, bias, and confidence parameters fixed, each sufficient width is quadratic in the largest Gaussian width of a spherical difference-cone section, hence at most linear in its span dimension. An example shows that this squared Gaussian-width dependence is sharp for both layers.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that two classes, not necessarily convex or linearly separable, can be separated with positive margin by a finite ReLU network with exactly two hidden layers, and by two random ReLU layers with high probability. Each sufficient width is quadratic in the largest Gaussian width of a spherical difference-cone section.
AI.motivation: Set separation by continuous linear functionals underlies classification, but when nonlinear ReLU networks and random ReLU features can separate classes with positive margin is not characterised for general, possibly unbounded, convex-cell class representations.
AI.method: The deterministic result equates positive-margin separability by a finite ReLU network with the existence of finite closed convex covers whose opposite-label members have positive pairwise distances. The random result uses two independent ReLU layers: the first separates each negative cell from the positive class through the origin, and the second combines cellwise scores with Chebyshev polynomials, realised by Gaussian Hermite features and a uniform finite-width approximation.
AI.result: Exactly two hidden layers suffice for deterministic positive-margin separation. Under pointed closed difference cones and positive cell distances, two random layers give a common positive-margin affine separator with high probability. The width dependence is quadratic in the largest Gaussian width and at most linear in the span dimension, and an example shows the squared Gaussian-width dependence is sharp.
AI.conclusion: The paper gives a geometric characterisation of ReLU separability and a width bound for random ReLU features, with the dependence shown to be tight for both layers.

title: How Risky Is Your Data-Driven Policy?
summary: Data-driven algorithms are ubiquitous across industries, and there is an extensive literature on analyzing their \emph{average} performance. The risk profile of such algorithms, while critical, is much less understood. This paper quantifies the risk of data-driven policies and isolates its sources. We evaluate a policy through the conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) of its loss over the training sample, any policy randomization, and the future outcome, at a fixed unknown distribution. Regret against an oracle that knows the distribution decomposes into expected post-sample regret (PS), the average outcome-only CVaR gap of the selected action, and a sample-risk premium (SR), the additional tail risk omitted by averaging those evaluations. The analogous premium vanishes under expected loss. We characterize when the premium vanishes and how large it is relative to post-sample regret. For losses with a continuous density near the tail cutoff, we identify conditions under which both components decay at the same rate, yet the limiting ratio of the premium to post-sample regret can reach the thousands. When a probability mass at the cutoff moves with the action, the premium can decay more slowly and dominate post-sample regret. We establish conditions under which sample average approximation learns the oracle action at rate $n^{-1/2}$ in both settings, but its combined-risk regret is of order $n^{-1}$ in the first and $n^{-1/2}$ in the second. In finite-sample numerical examples of SAA in both settings, the premium accounts for approximately $74\%$--$97\%$ of regret.

AI.tldr: The paper decomposes the regret of data-driven policies against a distribution-aware oracle into post-sample regret and a sample-risk premium arising from CVaR-based risk. The premium can dominate regret, and SAA's combined-risk regret is order n^(-1) or n^(-1/2) depending on the setting.
AI.motivation: Data-driven algorithms are analysed mainly by their average performance, while their risk profile is much less understood. The sources of the risk gap between a learned policy and an oracle are not isolated.
AI.method: Each policy is evaluated by the CVaR of its loss over the training sample, any policy randomisation, and the future outcome. Regret decomposes into expected post-sample regret, the average outcome-only CVaR gap of the chosen action, and a sample-risk premium, the extra tail risk that averaging omits. The authors characterise when the premium vanishes and compare its rate with post-sample regret, for continuous-density losses and for losses with probability mass at the cutoff that moves with the action.
AI.result: For continuous-density losses both components can decay at the same rate, yet the limiting ratio of premium to post-sample regret can reach the thousands. With mass at a moving cutoff, the premium can dominate. Sample average approximation learns the oracle action at rate n^(-1/2) in both settings, with combined-risk regret of order n^(-1) in the first and n^(-1/2) in the second. In finite-sample SAA examples, the premium accounts for about 74% to 97% of regret.
AI.conclusion: The sample-risk premium is a central, not secondary, source of regret when decisions are judged by tail risk, and it should be analysed separately from post-sample regret.

title: Nearly Linear-Time Follow-the-Perturbed-Leader for Weakly Observable Graph Bandits
summary: We study online learning with directed weakly observable feedback graphs and propose a Follow-the-Perturbed-Leader (FTPL) policy that achieves best-of-both-worlds guarantee with nearly linear expected time complexity. To preserve the simple structure of FTPL, we develop a novel graph-based loss estimator that combines forced exploration, conditional geometric resampling and adaptive learning rates with surrogate probabilities. Our policy achieves $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\delta_*^{1/3} T^{2/3})$ regret for adversarial regimes as well as $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\delta_* \log T / \Delta_{\min}^2)$ regret for stochastic regimes, where $\delta_*$ and $\Delta$, respectively, denote the fractional weak domination number and the suboptimality gap. These results show that refined guarantees for problems with minimax regret of $\Theta(T^{2/3})$ can be obtained through appropriately designed adaptive learning rates and loss estimators without sacrificing the simplicity of FTPL.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Follow-the-Perturbed-Leader policy for online learning with directed weakly observable feedback graphs that runs in nearly linear expected time and achieves best-of-both-worlds regret bounds. The bounds are refined by the fractional weak domination number and the suboptimality gap.
AI.motivation: Prior graph-bandit methods with minimax regret of order T^(2/3) do not give a simple, efficient FTPL policy with data-dependent guarantees for weakly observable feedback graphs.
AI.method: The policy uses a graph-based loss estimator that combines forced exploration, conditional geometric resampling and adaptive learning rates with surrogate probabilities. The structure of FTPL is kept.
AI.result: The policy achieves O~(delta_*^(1/3) T^(2/3)) regret in adversarial regimes and O~(delta_* log T / Delta_min^2) regret in stochastic regimes, where delta_* is the fractional weak domination number and Delta_min is the suboptimality gap.
AI.conclusion: Refined, instance-dependent guarantees are achievable for graph bandits through adaptive learning rates and loss estimators without sacrificing the simplicity of FTPL.

title: Conditional independence and graphical models for rankings
summary: Ranking models define probability distributions over rankings and are fundamental in applications such as preference learning and decision-making. Without structural assumptions, these models are intractable due to their factorial complexity. Although independence assumptions are key to reducing complexity and enabling interpretability, standard notions of conditional independence must account for the mutual exclusivity constraints inherent to rankings. We introduce relative rank models, a probabilistic framework based on structured coarsenings of the ranking space that relax these constraints while preserving relative order information. This representation enables a well-defined notion of conditional independence for rankings and allows rankings to be modeled using Bayesian networks. As a result, standard methods for learning and probabilistic inference can be applied to rankings, with interpretable representations based on conditional independence. We further show that two prominent ranking models based on independence assumptions tailored to rankings arise as special cases, providing a unifying framework for independence in ranking models.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces relative rank models, which use structured coarsenings of the ranking space to define a well-behaved notion of conditional independence for rankings. This lets rankings be modelled with Bayesian networks, and two known independence-based ranking models appear as special cases.
AI.motivation: Ranking models are intractable without structural assumptions because of factorial complexity. Standard conditional independence does not respect the mutual exclusivity constraints inherent in rankings.
AI.method: The authors define relative rank models, a probabilistic framework over structured coarsenings of the ranking space that relax mutual exclusivity while preserving relative order information. Conditional independence is defined within this framework, and Bayesian network factorisations are used for ranking.
AI.result: The framework enables standard learning and probabilistic inference methods to be applied to rankings. Two prominent ranking models based on independence assumptions are shown to be special cases.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a unifying framework for independence in ranking models with interpretable conditional-independence representations.

title: One-shot Distributed Learning via Weighted Averaging with Server-side Information
comment: 16 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables. Includes appendices with proofs and numerical experiment details
summary: Distributed learning has drawn considerable attention due to its capability of learning from distributed data without aggregating raw observations. However, frequent exchange of model updates can become the main bottleneck of communication. Therefore, one-shot approaches where each worker fits a local model and sends it to the server to aggregate emerge. It is known that averaging can achieve the so-called pooled-data mean squared error (MSE) order of a hypothetical node that has access to data from the server and all the workers, and performs empirical risk minimization (ERM) on it. However, when the number of workers increases too fast compared to the local sample size, nonzero local estimation bias prevents averaging from achieving this order. In this paper, we study whether independent server data can overcome this limitation. We consider $m$ workers with $n$ observations each and a server with $p$ observations, all i.i.d., giving $N=mn+p$ observations in total. Under certain regularity conditions, a pooled-data ERM achieves MSE of order $\mathcal O(N^{-1})$. We analyze deterministic nonnegative averaging of convex-loss M-estimators, with equal worker weights and the server's own estimator included. Under our assumptions, including nonzero local bias of order $n^{-\alpha}$, $\alpha\geq1$, sample-size weighted averaging achieves the pooled-data MSE order whenever $m=\mathcal O(n^{2\alpha-1})$. Above this worker scale, it does so if and only if $p=\Omega(nm\cdot m/n^{2\alpha-1})$. Hence, server-only estimation, whose MSE is of order $\mathcal{O}(p^{-1})$, can achieve pooled-data order while sample-size weighting fails. Analytical examples and synthetic experiments illustrate when averaging matches the pooled-data MSE order, complemented by CIFAR-10 experiments comparing aggregation strategies with linear and nonlinear classifiers.

AI.tldr: The paper studies one-shot distributed learning in which m workers send local estimators to a server that also holds p i.i.d. samples.
