AI.motivation: Small students degrade on long reasoning-model solutions, and recent work shortens these by interpolating the teacher with a short-answer model. What the student weights retain when the teacher stops thinking is unknown.
AI.method: LoRA adapters from three students and three teacher pairs are compared at each interpolation ratio. The authors locate where the update subspace shifts most and identify a shared adapter subspace linked to thinking-like behaviour, then test by removing it and by grafting it into a short-answer student at twice its weight.
AI.result: The shared subspace keeps about half its effect after the point where the teacher stops thinking in one pair, and largely empties after thinking stops. Removing it largely turns the behaviour off for every pair, student and benchmark. Only in one pair and one other student does it leave clearly fewer markers than removing the top update components, and random directions often nearly match it elsewhere. Grafted at twice its weight, it turns early markers on, but the student rarely finishes.
AI.conclusion: A weight subspace tied to distilled thinking-like behaviour can be identified, although its specificity compared with random directions varies across settings.

title: AdSteer: Native Advertising in Large Language Model Generation
summary: Large language model (LLM) services face rapidly rising serving costs. To sustain free or affordable access for a broad user base, alternative monetization mechanisms are needed. Native advertising offers a promising approach, as it creates economic value by aligning user intent with merchant offerings. Yet how to integrate sponsored content naturally into LLM responses remains largely underexplored. Existing approaches primarily rely on prompt-level injection, multi-pass rewriting, or fine-tuning, which can compromise response quality or introduce additional computational costs. We propose AdSteer, a lightweight decoding-time advertising framework that adaptively adjusts token probabilities to integrate contextually appropriate advertisement into responses. AdSteer calibrates the strength and duration of advertising influence, making sponsored content a natural part of the response. Experiments on GEM-Bench across three application scenarios show that AdSteer achieves an average improvement of 14.1% in overall score over the strongest baselines and 22.5% fewer total tokens on average than rewrite-based methods. These results demonstrate that AdSteer provides an effective and practical solution for native advertising in LLMs.

AI.tldr: AdSteer is a lightweight decoding-time method that integrates sponsored content into LLM responses by adjusting token probabilities. On GEM-Bench across three scenarios it improves overall score by 14.1% over the strongest baselines and uses 22.5% fewer tokens than rewrite-based methods.
AI.motivation: LLM serving costs are rising, and native advertising could fund free access, but existing approaches use prompt injection, multi-pass rewriting or fine-tuning, which can hurt quality or add computation.
AI.method: AdSteer adaptively adjusts token probabilities during decoding, calibrating the strength and duration of advertising influence so that sponsored content fits the response context.
AI.result: On GEM-Bench across three application scenarios, AdSteer gives an average 14.1% gain in overall score over the strongest baselines, and uses 22.5% fewer total tokens on average than rewrite-based methods.
AI.conclusion: Decoding-time steering is presented as an effective and practical route to native advertising in LLM responses.

title: PACT: Certifying What Is Written in Parallel Decoding of Diffusion Language Models
comment: 17 pages, 10 figures. Code: this https URL
summary: Parallel decoding speeds up masked diffusion language models by writing several tokens per forward pass. Published commit rules choose these tokens by testing the predicted distributions. Under sampling the written tokens are drawn, and these tests do not see them. We find that answer quality follows the reliability of the tokens actually written. An answer's log probability splits into this reliability and the dependence within each step. We propose PACT, a training-free commit rule that draws the tokens first, certifies the set it will write and spaces the positions of each step apart. This certificate holds at every temperature, and we show that no rule with the same guarantee commits more positions. Experiments use four models of the LLaDA and Dream families and HumanEval, MBPP, GSM8K, MATH500 and IFEval benchmarks. PACT reaches the quality of published commit rules with fewer forward passes. Spacing removes positions from each step, yet it usually lowers the total cost because later steps then write more tokens. At the same speed, published decoders also write a word twice in a row far more often than PACT. These results suggest that commit rules should certify the tokens they write. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: PACT is a training-free commit rule for parallel decoding in masked diffusion language models. It draws tokens first, certifies the set it will write and spaces positions within each step, and reaches the quality of published rules with fewer forward passes.
AI.motivation: Published commit rules test predicted distributions, but under sampling the tokens actually written are drawn after the test and are not checked. Answer quality follows the reliability of the tokens actually written.
AI.method: PACT draws the tokens, certifies the set to be written and spaces the positions of each step apart. The certificate holds at every temperature, and the authors show no rule with the same guarantee commits more positions. Experiments use four LLaDA and Dream models on HumanEval, MBPP, GSM8K, MATH500 and IFEval.
AI.result: PACT reaches the quality of published commit rules with fewer forward passes. Spacing removes positions from each step but usually lowers total cost, since later steps write more tokens. Published decoders repeat a word twice in a row far more often than PACT.
AI.conclusion: Commit rules should certify the tokens they actually write, which improves quality and efficiency in parallel diffusion decoding.

title: Tokenizer Myths and Where To Find Them
summary: Tokenization is a fundamental component of modern language models: before a model sees data, its tokenizer has already determined how the data appears. We identify and challenge three myths in the tokenization research literature. Myth #1: Bits-Per-Byte (BPB) is agnostic to the tokenizer and/or the vocabulary size: BPB is tokens per byte times bits per token, and the two factors do not cancel; using untrained models, we show that BPB prefers some tokenizers over others: the model has learned nothing, but the tokenizer--model pair has. Myth #2: lower BPB means a better model: On untrained models, BPB strongly prefers some vocabulary sizes, even though accuracy remains at chance, and on real models trained on the same data, BPB correlates weakly with downstream performance. Myth #3: different "tokenizer-agnostic" metrics yield consistent results: The "unigram-normalized loss" is not tokenizer-agnostic; its reported correlation of 0.989 with BPB comes from a confounder and falls to 0.057 once fixed; from the same data the two metrics select different vocabularies at each model size. We present a tokenizer trilemma: no metric can score only the true distribution best, give the same predictions the same score, and tie all untrained models, so choosing a metric is choosing a research question. We conclude with a caution for reading the tokenization literature and a conjecture for future work.

AI.tldr: The paper challenges three myths in tokenization research: that bits-per-byte (BPB) is tokenizer-agnostic, that lower BPB means a better model, and that "tokenizer-agnostic" metrics agree with each other.
AI.motivation: Tokenizer choice shapes what models see, yet the literature relies on metrics whose tokenizer dependence is not well understood, so comparisons may be misleading.
AI.method: Experiments with untrained models show BPB favors some tokenizers and vocabulary sizes even at chance accuracy; trained models are compared on downstream performance; the unigram-normalized loss is re-examined for a confounder; a tokenizer trilemma formalizes the limits of any metric.
AI.result: On untrained models BPB strongly prefers some vocabulary sizes while accuracy stays at chance; on trained models BPB correlates weakly with downstream performance; the reported 0.989 correlation between unigram-normalized loss and BPB falls to 0.057 once the confounder is fixed, and the two metrics select different vocabularies at each model size.
AI.conclusion: Choosing a tokenizer-comparison metric amounts to choosing a research question, and the authors give cautions for reading the tokenization literature.

title: Shared Context Candidate Scoring with Jointly Adapted Readout Networks
comment: 11 pages, 3 figures, 6 tables. Jingyang Du and Yiben Fu contributed equally to this work and share first authorship. Corresponding author: Yang Shen
summary: Repeated decisions over a shared document create two distinct opportunities: reusing document computation and adapting how question representations score candidate answers. We present Q64, a candidate-scoring system that preserves a frozen 64-layer Qwen3.8-27B text backbone, reuses its hybrid prefix state and intermediate document representations, and jointly trains a residual adapter with a four-layer decoder and candidate-conditioned readout. We used ZiYor, a self-evolving AI system, to explore and refine the Q64 design. We specified the scoring method, implemented the system, and evaluated its accuracy and latency. The final adaptation stage updates 88.66 million parameters using 8,192 selected training views. On a fixed 5,112-item evaluation combining ARC-Challenge, ANLI-R3, and stratified subsets of MMLU-Pro and CMMLU, joint adaptation improves four-benchmark macro accuracy from 66.46% to 74.32%. It remains below the native 27B baseline at 75.68% and AnyJev Qwen3-32B L0 at 76.68%. On a separate synthetic workload with 4,096 document tokens and 50 questions, median cold-request latency is 2.237 seconds, compared with 5.383 seconds for the native baseline and 56.872 seconds for the measured batched AnyJev configuration. Short single-question requests do not share this advantage. The evidence supports an accuracy-latency tradeoff in the evaluated systems, rather than a backbone reduction or an isolated component advantage. Public benchmarks informed earlier development, and real-document multi-question validation remains open.

AI.tldr: Q64 is a candidate-scoring system that reuses the document computation of a frozen 27B Qwen3-based backbone and jointly trains a residual adapter and a candidate-conditioned readout, trading some accuracy for lower latency on shared-document workloads.
AI.motivation: Repeated decisions over a shared document allow reuse of document computation and adaptation of how questions score candidate answers, which existing setups do not exploit together.
AI.method: The system keeps a frozen 64-layer Qwen3.8-27B text backbone, reuses its hybrid prefix state and intermediate document representations, and jointly trains a residual adapter with a four-layer decoder and candidate-conditioned readout; the design was explored and refined by ZiYor, a self-evolving AI system.
AI.result: On a fixed 5,112-item evaluation (ARC-Challenge, ANLI-R3, and stratified MMLU-Pro and CMMLU subsets) joint adaptation raises four-benchmark macro accuracy from 66.46% to 74.32%, below the native 27B baseline at 75.68% and AnyJev Qwen3-32B L0 at 76.68%; on a synthetic workload with 4,096 document tokens and 50 questions, median cold-request latency is 2.237 s versus 5.383 s for the native baseline and 56.872 s for batched AnyJev; single-question requests gain nothing.
AI.conclusion: The evidence supports an accuracy-latency tradeoff in the evaluated systems rather than a backbone reduction or an isolated component advantage, and real-document multi-question validation remains open.

title: COMPREHEND: Ultra-Fine-Grained Benchmark Understanding by Entailment Hierarchy
summary: Understanding what kind of prompts users typically ask and how well an LLM performs on these prompt categories is crucial for LLM practitioners. The existing methods satisfy the demand by hierarchically clustering the user prompts and synthesizing the cluster names using an LLM to build a taxonomy. However, the cluster names from these methods are usually too general for humans to understand the detailed prompt distributions and identify the exact strengths and weaknesses of LLMs. In this study, we propose COMPREHEND, which automatically constructs an ultra-fine-grained entailment hierarchy for the prompts. The entailment hierarchy replaces the cluster names in the taxonomy with sentences to provide more precise cluster descriptions for more fine-grained categorization. Compared with EvalTree, a state-of-the-art taxonomy construction method, COMPREHEND improves an entailment/faithfulness metric from 22.6 to 41.7 and an informative metric from 16.3 to 39.1 in WildBench. Our experiments also show that the weakness report generated based on our entailment hierarchy is much more informative than EvalTree in terms of predicting the response scores in the benchmark. All the code is released in this https URL.

AI.tldr: COMPREHEND builds an ultra-fine-grained entailment hierarchy over user prompts, replacing short cluster names with descriptive sentences, to give more precise descriptions of where an LLM is strong or weak.
AI.motivation: Existing taxonomy methods cluster prompts and name clusters with an LLM, but the names are often too general to reveal detailed prompt distributions and specific model weaknesses.
AI.method: COMPREHEND automatically constructs an entailment hierarchy for the prompts in which each cluster is described by a sentence, enabling finer categorization, and uses it to generate weakness reports.
AI.result: Compared with EvalTree, a state-of-the-art taxonomy construction method, COMPREHEND raises an entailment/faithfulness metric from 22.6 to 41.7 and an informative metric from 16.3 to 39.1 on WildBench; its weakness reports are more informative for predicting benchmark response scores than EvalTree's.
AI.conclusion: Sentence-level entailment hierarchies give more precise and more useful descriptions of LLM capability distributions than general cluster names.

title: Sparse Internal Control of Language Models
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 45 pages, 5 figures. Code and experimental records: this https URL
summary: Language models are increasingly used in text generation, decision support, and automated interaction, creating a need for localized, reversible, and selective control of their behavior. Activation steering demonstrates that internal interventions can alter the behavior of frozen models, but how to select and evaluate compact, multi-site control interfaces remains an open question. I introduce sparse internal control, a framework for steering target behavior by applying inference-time interventions to a small set of internal model nodes. A local target-controllability formulation characterizes candidate site--direction pairs by their behavioral effects and specifies constraints on target recovery, off-target preservation, and intervention energy. Two complementary selectors instantiate this formulation: Driver-OMP selects nodes for sparse reconstruction of a desired behavioral displacement, while Coverage-Driver favors stable coverage across prompts. I propose a six-axis control-evaluation protocol measuring reachability, signed reversal, dose response, feedback controllability, off-target preservation, and held-out reuse. Exploratory experiments on indirect object identification, MMLU multiple-choice question answering, sentiment steering, and refusal steering provide evidence for the feasibility of steering task-defined behavior through sparse internal interventions. The six-axis evaluation characterizes these interventions beyond target movement, revealing distinct control properties that depend on the task and available direction information. Together, the formulation, reference algorithms, and evaluation protocol provide a foundation for the systematic study and development of internal control methods for language models.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces sparse internal control, which steers a frozen language model's behavior by applying inference-time interventions to a small set of internal nodes, with a six-axis evaluation protocol for such control interfaces.
AI.motivation: Activation steering can change frozen model behavior, but how to select and evaluate compact, multi-site control interfaces was an open question.
AI.method: A local target-controllability formulation scores site-direction pairs by behavioral effect under constraints on target recovery, off-target preservation, and intervention energy; two selectors instantiate it, Driver-OMP (sparse reconstruction of a desired behavioral displacement) and Coverage-Driver (stable coverage across prompts); a six-axis protocol measures reachability, signed reversal, dose response, feedback controllability, off-target preservation, and held-out reuse.
AI.result: Exploratory experiments on indirect object identification, MMLU multiple-choice question answering, sentiment steering, and refusal steering provide evidence that task-defined behavior can be steered through sparse internal interventions, with control properties that depend on the task and the available direction information.
AI.conclusion: The formulation, reference algorithms and evaluation protocol are offered as a foundation for systematic study of internal control methods for language models.

title: Do Multi-Turn Conversational Capabilities Carry Over from Text to Speech? A Parallel Multilingual Benchmark
summary: Successful multi-turn voice interaction requires models to retain information from earlier turns, follow persistent instructions, and track revisions to conversational state. These abilities are usually evaluated from transcripts, leaving open whether successes demonstrated from text carry over when the same turns are spoken, and whether this transfer is consistent across languages. We introduce Omnilingua-AudioMC, a strictly parallel multilingual extension of Audio MultiChallenge, to study this question. The benchmark contains 354 conversations and 1,404 rubric items across ten languages, with content, turn structure, cross-turn dependencies, and evaluation criteria aligned across transcript and speech conditions. Across six speech-language models, the shift from reference transcripts to direct speech input is strongly model- and language-dependent: models with similar transcript performance can diverge substantially under speech, and their relative strengths across languages can change. Paired rubric-level analysis shows that aggregate transcript-speech gaps can obscure which conversational requirements are preserved, because losses of transcript-demonstrated successes can be offset by gains on other items. Replacing preceding user turns, the current turn, or both with model-generated transcripts localizes recoverable degradation: for the two models with the largest gaps, history substitution yields a larger macro-level improvement than current-turn substitution in all ten languages, while the strongest direct-speech model gains little from either. These results show that transcript performance is an unreliable proxy for multilingual spoken conversational ability and identify the representation of preceding spoken context as an important source of recoverable degradation. Our code is publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Omnilingua-AudioMC is a parallel multilingual spoken multi-turn benchmark across ten languages showing that transcript performance is an unreliable proxy for conversational ability under direct speech input.
AI.motivation: Multi-turn voice interaction is usually evaluated from transcripts, leaving open whether abilities shown in text carry over when the same turns are spoken and whether this holds across languages.
AI.method: The authors build a strictly parallel multilingual extension of Audio MultiChallenge with 354 conversations and 1,404 rubric items in ten languages, aligned across transcript and speech conditions, and evaluate six speech-language models; they run paired rubric-level analysis and substitute preceding user turns, the current turn, or both with model-generated transcripts.
AI.result: The transcript-to-speech shift is strongly model- and language-dependent, and models with similar transcript scores can diverge under speech; aggregate gaps can hide preserved and lost requirements; for the two models with the largest gaps, history substitution gives a larger macro-level gain than current-turn substitution in all ten languages, while the strongest direct-speech model gains little from either.
AI.conclusion: Transcript performance is an unreliable proxy for multilingual spoken conversational ability, and the representation of preceding spoken context is an important source of recoverable degradation.

title: The Min-Max theory of language behavior
summary: The "Min-Max" theory of language behavior proposes that humans engage simultaneously in minimization of processing effort and maximization of information content, and that this is a primary driver in language evolution (Ring, 2025). This claim seeks to unify observations from language processing (Mahowald et al., 2013; Futrell et al., 2015; Yadav et al., 2020; Hawkins, 2014), interaction (Hörberg and Sjons, 2023; Tucker et al., 2025; Jaeger and Tily, 2011; Smith and Culbertson, 2025), and corpora (Levshina and Moran, 2021; Levshina, 2023; Newmeyer, 2017), which suggest that considerations of processing efficiency and information content are both implicated in human communication. The interaction between these two processes provides an explanation for human linguistic behavior at various levels (Linders and Louwerse, 2023) and predicts historical developments in language, i.e. related to word order (Ring, 2025). Given that the original formulation of the Min-Max theory is based on observational data, the current paper seeks to validate the theory mathematically. Through a series of experiments that use computational models to investigate the theory's predictions, pretrained and iterated learning models are queried with synthetic data. The experiments show that manipulating the variables of token length and the weight of information content in a tabula rasa model results in word order change, as predicted by the theory. The experiments also identify important differences between computational models and observations of human language data, suggesting that current transformer-based language models may not accurately represent psycholinguistic processes. The overall findings indicate that evolutionary trajectories in language are highly susceptible to minimization of processing and maximization of information content.

AI.tldr: The paper tests the Min-Max theory of language behavior, which holds that minimizing processing effort and maximizing information content drive language evolution, by querying pretrained and iterated-learning language models with synthetic data.
AI.motivation: The Min-Max theory was formulated from observational data, so the authors aim to validate its predictions mathematically using computational models.
AI.method: Pretrained and iterated learning models are queried with synthetic data while token length and the weight of information content are manipulated in a tabula rasa model.
AI.result: Manipulating token length and the information-content weight produces word order change in the tabula rasa model, as the theory predicts; the experiments also reveal differences between the computational models and human language data.
AI.conclusion: Evolutionary trajectories in language appear highly sensitive to processing minimization and information maximization, while current transformer-based language models may not faithfully represent psycholinguistic processes.

title: Typological Feature Induction as a Benchmark for Inductive Metalinguistic Reasoning
summary: Existing metalinguistic reasoning benchmarks require both inference of rules and their application, making failures hard to diagnose. We introduce typological feature induction (TFI) which targets the former step. Given sentences in an unnamed language paired with translations in a known pivot language, models must predict a typological feature of the unnamed language. From Grambank and multi-parallel corpora, we automatically build evaluation questions over 195 languages. We find that LLMs identify 59--80% of these languages from only 16 sentence pairs; and misaligning the translations barely affects their accuracy, suggesting reliance on prior knowledge of the language. Enciphering text to prevent recognition increases the corpus' utility, but mainly for features where target and pivot languages agree. On languages which models cannot identify, neither open model outperforms a majority-value baseline. Since induction from raw text aligns with field linguists' use-case, this work indicates the models tested are not yet ready for this role. TFI offers a scalable path to track progress in this direction.

AI.tldr: Typological feature induction (TFI) is a benchmark that tests whether LLMs can infer a typological feature of an unnamed language from sentence pairs with a known pivot language, isolating the rule-induction step of metalinguistic reasoning.
AI.motivation: Existing metalinguistic benchmarks mix rule inference with rule application, so failures are hard to diagnose.
AI.method: From Grambank and multi-parallel corpora, the authors automatically build evaluation questions over 195 languages in which models must predict a typological feature of an unnamed language given sentences paired with translations in a pivot language; they test misaligned translations and enciphered text.
AI.result: LLMs identify 59-80% of the languages from only 16 sentence pairs; misaligning translations barely changes accuracy, suggesting reliance on prior knowledge; enciphering text helps mainly for features where target and pivot languages agree; on languages the models cannot identify, neither open model beats a majority-value baseline.
AI.conclusion: The tested models are not yet ready for inductive reasoning from raw text as field linguists need, and TFI offers a scalable way to track progress.

title: ReListen: Training-Free Evidence Localization in Hour-Long Audio with Frozen Audio Language Models
summary: Audio language models are meant to answer questions from the audio itself, but an hour-long recording rarely fits in their context, and the answer often depends on a few seconds of it. Transcribing the recording first makes it fit but discards sounds and voices, while systems that return to the audio must be trained for this behavior. We propose ReListen, a training-free method in which a frozen audio language model finds its own evidence before answering. In a Jev-style scan, the model scores each 20-second window by the probability that it helps answer the question, and it then answers from the highest-scoring minute. This minute overlaps the annotated evidence far more often than transcript retrieval, for 88.5% of VoiceGiraffe questions. Without any change, the same scan also grounds events on LAT-Bench as well as a model trained for temporal grounding. Answering from it matches or exceeds hearing the whole recording with a small fraction of the audio, and on VoiceGiraffe it exceeds a transcript of the whole recording by 9.2 points. The selected evidence is also worth hearing rather than reading. Given the same excerpts, reading their transcript matches listening on speech content, but listening is clearly more accurate on questions about sounds and voices. Moreover, ReListen answers faster than every transcript-based system, and its memory stays constant even for recordings too long to hear whole on one GPU. Therefore, a frozen audio language model can search hour-long recordings by itself, without a transcript or additional training.

AI.tldr: ReListen lets a frozen audio language model locate evidence in hour-long recordings by itself, scoring 20-second windows and answering from the highest-scoring minute, without transcripts or training.
AI.motivation: Audio language models cannot fit hour-long recordings in context, while transcription discards sounds and voices and systems that revisit audio need training.
AI.method: In a Jev-style scan, the model scores each 20-second window by the probability that it helps answer the question, then answers from the highest-scoring minute; the method is compared with transcript retrieval and with a model trained for temporal grounding on LAT-Bench.
AI.result: The selected minute overlaps annotated evidence for 88.5% of VoiceGiraffe questions, more often than transcript retrieval; answering from it matches or exceeds hearing the whole recording using a small fraction of the audio and exceeds a whole-recording transcript by 9.2 points on VoiceGiraffe; listening beats reading on questions about sounds and voices; memory stays constant for recordings too long to hear whole on one GPU.
AI.conclusion: A frozen audio language model can search hour-long recordings by itself, without a transcript or additional training.

title: TEMPO: Time Series Understanding via Discrete Tokenization
comment: 9 pages, 2 figures. Presented at the 2nd ICML Workshop on Foundation Models for Structured Data (FMSD), 2026
summary: Time-series interpretation often requires both numerical observations and textual context. Integrating these inputs into a pretrained language model raises a representation question: how should a signal enter the model's token sequence? We present TEMPO, which extends an LLM's vocabulary with discrete codes from a context-aware Transformer tokenizer using finite scalar quantization. A frozen tokenizer maps four-step patches to a 625-code vocabulary; signal tokens, scale statistics, and text are then processed by the LLM's existing self-attention layers. Adaptation updates the new token embeddings and DoRA adapters. With a Qwen3-4B backbone and task-specific fine-tuning, TEMPO achieves macro-F1 scores of 89.0% on activity recognition, 85.0% on sleep staging, and 86.0% on bearing-fault diagnosis. Time-series question answering and qualitative bearing-diagnosis examples further illustrate how this interface combines signal representations with textual context. Together, these results demonstrate the utility of discrete vocabulary extension for time-series understanding.

AI.tldr: TEMPO extends an LLM's vocabulary with discrete codes from a context-aware Transformer tokenizer using finite scalar quantization, letting a Qwen3-4B model read time series alongside text.
AI.motivation: Integrating numerical time-series observations into a pretrained language model raises the question of how a signal should enter the token sequence.
AI.method: A frozen tokenizer maps four-step patches to a 625-code vocabulary; signal tokens, scale statistics and text are processed by the LLM's existing self-attention layers; adaptation updates the new token embeddings and DoRA adapters with task-specific fine-tuning.
AI.result: Macro-F1 reaches 89.0% on activity recognition, 85.0% on sleep staging and 86.0% on bearing-fault diagnosis; time-series question answering and qualitative bearing-diagnosis examples are also shown.
AI.conclusion: Discrete vocabulary extension is a useful interface for combining time-series signal representations with textual context.

title: Evaluating LLMs as Judges of Counterspeech Quality Against Online Hate Speech
summary: Prolonged exposure to hate speech on social media can cause lasting psychological distress among users. Counterspeech has emerged as an effective, non-censorial mitigation strategy, but its deployment requires rigorous quality assessment. Manual assessment is unscalable due to the large volume of content on the Web and imposes severe emotional strain on human annotators. Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a scalable alternative, yet concerns remain regarding their reliability. In this paper, we investigate the extent to which LLMs can effectively perform this task. We test 12 open-weight LLMs of different sizes and families under zero-shot, few-shot, and chain-of-thought prompting, to approximate pointwise and pairwise human expert assessment of counterspeech quality across four dimensions: relevance, coherence, aggressiveness, and suitableness. We find that (i) LLMs show low agreement and moderate rank correlations with human experts: our best configuration, Qwen 2.5 72B on coherence, achieves up to a linear-weighted Cohen's $\kappa_l = 0.19$ and Spearman's $\rho = 0.42$ in pointwise evaluation and an unweighted Cohen's $\kappa = 0.25$ in pairwise evaluation. (ii) Converting pointwise scores into pairwise labels substantially improves human--LLM agreement for selected configurations. For same-instance coherence, Qwen 2.5 72B under zero-shot prompting achieves $\kappa = 0.35$ with converted labels, compared with $\kappa = 0.25$ when judging pairs directly, and Mixtral 8$\times$7B under few-shot prompting improves from $\kappa = 0.07$ to $\kappa = 0.34$. (iii) LLMs agree more with one another than with human experts, particularly in pairwise evaluation, where the strongest model pair, OLMo 2 32B and Llama 3.3 70B on coherence, reaches substantial agreement with $\kappa = 0.76$, whereas their agreement with the experts in the same configuration does not exceed $\kappa = 0.21$.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether 12 open-weight LLMs can judge counterspeech quality against online hate speech, finding low agreement with human experts but higher agreement among the LLMs themselves.
AI.motivation: Manual assessment of counterspeech is unscalable and emotionally costly for annotators, so LLMs are a possible alternative whose reliability is uncertain.
AI.method: Twelve open-weight LLMs of different sizes and families are tested under zero-shot, few-shot and chain-of-thought prompting, approximating pointwise and pairwise expert judgments on relevance, coherence, aggressiveness and suitableness; pointwise scores are also converted into pairwise labels.
AI.result: Agreement with experts is low: the best pointwise configuration (Qwen 2.5 72B on coherence) reaches linear-weighted kappa 0.19 and Spearman rho 0.42, and pairwise unweighted kappa reaches 0.25; converting pointwise scores to pairwise labels improves agreement for some configurations (kappa 0.35 for Qwen 2.5 72B zero-shot on same-instance coherence; Mixtral 8x7B few-shot rises from 0.07 to 0.34); OLMo 2 32B and Llama 3.3 70B agree with each other at kappa 0.76 on coherence but at most 0.21 with experts.
AI.conclusion: LLMs agree more with one another than with human experts, so they cannot yet be relied on as substitutes for expert counterspeech assessment.

title: MIMIC-Note-Extract: A Large-Scale Structured Dataset Extracted from MIMIC-IV-Note Discharge Summaries
comment: Accepted at ML4H 2026, Proceedings Track. Dataset: this https URL
summary: MIMIC is one of the most widely used public hospital datasets for machine learning on electronic health records, yet clinically important information, such as past medical history, allergies, and diagnostic findings, remains confined to free-text discharge summaries. Studies requiring this information must therefore build their own extraction pipelines, duplicating substantial effort across projects. We release MIMIC-Note-Extract (MNE), a large-scale dataset that uses a hybrid extraction pipeline combining deterministic parsing with schema-guided large language model generation to transform 16 sections from 300,720 discharge summaries into structured tables. MNE adds information that has no structured MIMIC counterpart and enriches related tables with broader coverage and greater clinical detail, including 10 times more patient-history entries and medication histories for more than twice as many admissions. Validation by medical doctors confirms extraction accuracy above 92% across sections. Using MNE, we construct a clinical decision-making benchmark for LLM agents, demonstrating how reusable structured representations of clinical narratives reduce data curation effort.

AI.tldr: MIMIC-Note-Extract (MNE) is a structured dataset extracted from 300,720 MIMIC-IV-Note discharge summaries using a hybrid of deterministic parsing and schema-guided LLM generation, with physician-validated accuracy above 92%.
AI.motivation: Clinically important information such as past medical history, allergies and diagnostic findings remains in free-text discharge summaries, so each study must build its own extraction pipeline.
AI.method: A hybrid pipeline combines deterministic parsing with schema-guided LLM generation to turn 16 sections into structured tables, and the authors use the result to construct a clinical decision-making benchmark for LLM agents.
AI.result: MNE adds information with no structured MIMIC counterpart and enriches related tables, including 10 times more patient-history entries and medication histories for more than twice as many admissions; medical doctors validated extraction accuracy above 92% across sections.
AI.conclusion: Reusable structured representations of clinical narratives reduce data curation effort for MIMIC-based research.

title: CardioVascBench:Prioritized Diagnosis Generation from Real-World Chinese Cardiovascular Records
summary: Identifying the primary diagnosis alone does not fully characterize a model's diagnosis-generation performance. We introduce CardioVascBench, a retrospective benchmark for prioritized diagnosis generation from real-world Chinese cardiovascular inpatient records. It contains 3,262 de-identified cases, with 2,174 for training and 1,088 for evaluation, linking clinical narratives and textual ECG reports to expert-verified, ordered discharge diagnoses standardized to ICD-10. An English translation of the evaluation set supports aligned cross-lingual comparison. Our evaluation protocol combines terminology normalization and rank-aware scoring to separately assess primary-diagnosis identification, reference-diagnosis coverage, and list precision. Evaluation across 36 systems shows that higher primary-diagnosis accuracy does not necessarily imply higher list precision against discharge references. We also provide CardioKG-Agent, a knowledge-enhanced baseline combining entity normalization, constrained graph retrieval, and guideline evidence. In a staged comparison of three baseline models, supervised fine-tuning plus the agent achieves a 73.5% higher mean composite score than fine-tuning alone, representing a system-level gain. These results measure retrospective agreement with recorded diagnoses; agreement between metric rankings and physician judgments remains to be validated. CardioVascBench supports research on diagnosis prioritization and knowledge-enhanced generation.

AI.tldr: CardioVascBench is a retrospective benchmark of 3,262 de-identified Chinese cardiovascular inpatient cases for prioritized diagnosis generation, scored with rank-aware metrics that separate primary-diagnosis accuracy from list precision.
AI.motivation: Primary-diagnosis accuracy alone does not characterize how well a model generates a full diagnosis list, and suitable Chinese clinical benchmarks are lacking.
AI.method: Clinical narratives and textual ECG reports are linked to expert-verified, ordered discharge diagnoses standardized to ICD-10; the protocol combines terminology normalization with rank-aware scoring; the authors also provide CardioKG-Agent, a baseline using entity normalization, constrained graph retrieval and guideline evidence.
AI.result: Across 36 systems, higher primary-diagnosis accuracy does not necessarily mean higher list precision; supervised fine-tuning plus the agent gives a 73.5% higher mean composite score than fine-tuning alone in a staged comparison of three baseline models.
AI.conclusion: The results measure agreement with recorded diagnoses only, and agreement between metric rankings and physician judgments remains to be validated; the benchmark supports research on diagnosis prioritization and knowledge-enhanced generation.

title: TraceRouter++: Causal Semantic Routing Realignment via Optimal Transport
summary: Despite their remarkable capabilities, large foundation models (LFMs) remain susceptible to adversarial manipulation. Current safety intervention methods primarily rely on the \textit{locality hypothesis}, rigidly suppressing isolated neurons or features. However, harmful semantics manifest as distributed, cross-layer circuits, rendering localized ablations both brittle against complex jailbreaks and detrimental to general utility. To bridge this gap, we propose TraceRouter++, a routing-level safety intervention framework that explicitly traces safety-relevant causal routing pathways activated under harmful inputs and realigns their unsafe activation states. Our framework operates in a \textit{Discover-Trace-Realign} paradigm: it first pinpoints a sensitive onset layer via attention divergence and disentangles dense activations into interpretable routing features using sparse autoencoders (SAEs). Subsequently, it maps these features to downstream causal circuits via feature influence scores (FIS). Crucially, departing from rigid suppression paradigms, TraceRouter++ introduces a constrained optimal transport (OT)-based soft routing realignment. By formulating safety intervention as a tractable coordinate-wise marginal optimal transport approximation, our method redirects unsafe activation marginals toward safe-reference marginals within causally identified routing subspaces while preserving non-selected coordinates at the intervention point. This mechanism safely redirects malicious semantic flows while leaving orthogonal computational routes intact. Extensive experiments across representative large language models (LLMs), multimodal large language models (MLLMs), and diffusion models (DMs) show that TraceRouter++ outperforms evaluated baselines, improving adversarial robustness while maintaining a favorable safety-utility trade-off. WARNING: This paper contains unsafe model responses.

AI.tldr: TraceRouter++ is a safety intervention that traces causal routing pathways activated by harmful inputs and realigns unsafe activations toward safe references via constrained optimal transport, aiming to improve adversarial robustness without a rigid suppression of neurons.
AI.motivation: Locality-based safety methods that suppress isolated neurons or features are brittle against complex jailbreaks and harm general utility, because harmful semantics are distributed across layers.
AI.method: The Discover-Trace-Realign framework finds a sensitive onset layer via attention divergence, disentangles activations into routing features with sparse autoencoders, maps them to downstream circuits via feature influence scores, and applies a constrained optimal transport soft realignment approximated coordinate-wise within causally identified subspaces.
AI.result: The authors report that TraceRouter++ outperforms evaluated baselines across LLMs, multimodal LLMs and diffusion models, improving adversarial robustness while keeping a favorable safety-utility trade-off.
AI.conclusion: Routing-level realignment is presented as a safer alternative to rigid suppression, redirecting malicious semantic flows while leaving other computation intact.

title: PROSE: Preservation-Constrained Selective Editing for Guilty Bias in Legal Judgment Prediction
summary: Legal judgment prediction models may retain a guilty verdict after a legally decisive condition has been altered such that the specified charge is no longer established. We study this guilty bias via selective repair over matched charge-established and charge-not-established cases, where the unsupported verdict should change while its supported counterpart remains stable. We construct CAIL-MC, a legally reviewed dataset of 11,478 matched pairs covering 261 Chinese criminal charges. Held-out activation interventions show that contrasts learned from correctly resolved pairs transfer to false-guilty cases, but target-reaching interventions can also damage matched supported-guilty decisions. Motivated by this observation, we introduce PROSE, which reconstructs case-specific targets from a training-derived residual geometry, aligns them with a local margin-descent signal, attenuates supported-guilty-sensitive components, and realizes bounded targets through a preservation-regularized low-rank parameter update. Across Qwen3-8B and GLM4-9B, PROSE achieves stronger pairwise safe repair and evidence sensitivity, while preserving standard single-pass inference.

AI.tldr: PROSE is a preservation-constrained selective editing method that repairs guilty bias in legal judgment prediction by changing unsupported guilty verdicts while keeping supported ones stable.
AI.motivation: Legal judgment models may keep a guilty verdict after the legally decisive condition for the charge has been removed, and target-reaching interventions can also damage correct guilty decisions.
AI.method: The authors build CAIL-MC, a legally reviewed set of 11,478 matched charge-established and charge-not-established pairs covering 261 Chinese criminal charges; PROSE reconstructs case-specific targets from training-derived residual geometry, aligns them with a local margin-descent signal, attenuates supported-guilty-sensitive components, and applies a preservation-regularized low-rank update.
AI.result: Across Qwen3-8B and GLM4-9B, PROSE achieves stronger pairwise safe repair and evidence sensitivity while preserving standard single-pass inference.
AI.conclusion: Selective, preservation-constrained editing offers a way to reduce guilty bias without changing normal inference.

title: Residual Attribute Leakage Is an Interface: Auditing Privacy Evaluation After Text De-identification
summary: A privacy evaluation of de-identified text asks a language model (the adversary) to guess a person's protected attribute. We introduce a prior-normalised clipped leakage score of its confidence gain on the true value and audit the conclusions drawn from it. Each verdict depends on an evaluation interface (the queried person, answer options, prior, adversary model and scoring rule), which we vary on fixed releases of three corpora. In a stress test, an editor that writes the opposite-sex form at the same spans a redaction editor would redact misleads the adversary about most people, yet ranks first among editors scored on the same MedQA entries under this score, as under attack accuracy and proper scoring rules read as privacy. A relabelling-invariant reading of AUC ranks that editor sixth of eight, and a rule-aware adversary recovers the attribute from the same text. On ordinary releases most verdict changes are gains or losses of separability; of six choices varied over all pairs, only the adversary reverses comparisons (5 of its 124 changes), and the query can target the wrong person. SACC, a traceable editor we build as the instrument, lets us ablate two editing principles and show where its advantage does not hold.

AI.tldr: The paper audits privacy evaluations of de-identified text, showing that conclusions about attribute leakage depend on the evaluation interface, and introduces SACC as a traceable editor for ablation.
AI.motivation: Privacy evaluations ask an adversary LLM to guess protected attributes, but the verdicts may depend on arbitrary choices in the evaluation interface rather than on the release itself.
AI.method: The authors propose a prior-normalised clipped leakage score based on confidence gain on the true value, vary the queried person, answer options, prior, adversary model and scoring rule on fixed releases of three corpora, and build SACC as an instrument to ablate two editing principles.
AI.result: An editor that writes the opposite-sex form misleads the adversary about most people yet ranks first under this score, attack accuracy and proper scoring rules; a relabelling-invariant reading of AUC ranks it sixth of eight; a rule-aware adversary recovers the attribute from the same text; among six varied choices only the adversary reverses comparisons (5 of 124 changes), and the query can target the wrong person.
AI.conclusion: Privacy verdicts for de-identified text are sensitive to the evaluation interface, so the interface must be audited before conclusions are drawn.

title: HERIT: Enabling Global Access to Hanja-to-English Historical Translation by Mitigating Temporal Bias
comment: Accepted to Findings of EMNLP 2026. 17 pages, 10 figures, 11 tables
summary: Historical archives are invaluable for multidisciplinary research but remain inaccessible globally due to severe language barriers. While manual translation is prohibitively expensive and time-consuming, simply applying existing machine translation models is inadequate due to unique linguistic nuances and the temporal bias inherent in scarce human-labeled corpora. To address these challenges, we propose HERIT, a systematic domain-adaptation pipeline that leverages retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to generate high-quality pseudo-labeled data from abundant Hanja-Korean corpora. This approach substantially expands the training dataset, mitigating both data scarcity and temporal overfitting across different historical periods. Extensive automated and human evaluations demonstrate that HERIT consistently outperforms baselines. Finally, we translate previously untranslated portions of the archives using our model, thereby enabling global access to these resources for researchers.

AI.tldr: HERIT is a domain-adaptation pipeline for Hanja-to-English historical translation that uses retrieval-augmented generation to produce pseudo-labeled training data from Hanja-Korean corpora, reducing temporal bias.
AI.motivation: Historical archives are hard to access for non-specialists, and off-the-shelf machine translation fails on archaic linguistic features and on temporal bias in scarce human-labeled corpora.
AI.method: A RAG-based pipeline generates pseudo-labeled data from abundant Hanja-Korean corpora to expand training data and mitigate data scarcity and temporal overfitting across historical periods.
AI.result: Automated and human evaluations show HERIT consistently outperforms baselines; the authors use it to translate previously untranslated portions of the archives.
AI.conclusion: The pipeline gives researchers broader access to historical archives, with temporal coverage improved by synthetic data expansion.

title: Whose Effect Is It? How Objectives Inflate Learned Subspace Interventions
summary: Interpretability often locates concepts by copying part of a language model's state from one input into another (activation patching). A larger output change counts as stronger evidence that this part carries the concept. Methods that learn which part to copy often change the output more than the whole state does. By that reading, learned parts isolate the concept more cleanly. Yet the whole contains the part. So whose effect is this excess, the network's or the method's? Copying the whole state learns nothing, so it shows what the network produces. We prove that, to first order, the effects of orthogonal parts add up to that of the whole. A part therefore exceeds the whole exactly when the rest moves the output back, which does not require isolating the concept more cleanly. Objectives that reward a larger effect select such parts. Distributed alignment search with cross-entropy, for example, exceeds the whole-state copy just before the output on almost all tasks, and inside the network at most sites. In both, changing only its objective to target what the network produces removes most of the excess. It therefore comes largely from the objective, so a larger learned effect alone is not stronger evidence.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that learned subspace interventions in activation patching look stronger partly because of their objectives, since a part's effect exceeds the whole state only when the rest of the network moves the output back.
AI.motivation: Methods that learn which part of a model's state to copy often produce larger output changes than whole-state copying, and it is unclear whether this excess reflects the network or the method.
AI.method: The authors prove that, to first order, the effects of orthogonal parts add up to the effect of the whole, and compare distributed alignment search with cross-entropy against whole-state copies at several sites and tasks, including with an objective that targets what the network produces.
AI.result: Distributed alignment search with cross-entropy exceeds the whole-state copy just before the output on almost all tasks and at most sites inside the network; changing only the objective to target the network's output removes most of the excess.
AI.conclusion: Much of the excess comes from the objective, so a larger learned effect alone is not stronger evidence that a part carries a concept.

title: ToolSpace: Scaling Tool-Centric Environment Synthesis for Long-Horizon Agents
summary: Large language models are deployed as long-horizon agents that compose diverse tools across MCP services into executable workflows. Existing MCP environment-scaling methods are data-centric: they first synthesize a database and scenario, then derive tools and tasks from them. As a result, tool interfaces may not match real ones, tool compositions are not grounded in execution, and tasks rarely span more than one environment. We propose ToolSpace, a tool-centric framework that reverses this order. ToolSpace mines data, state, and retry dependencies from adjacent calls in execution traces of real MCP services and open agent corpora, using deterministic rules rather than LLM judgment, and clusters the resulting weighted tool-composition graph into environments. Databases are synthesized only for state-mutating environments, while query and stateless tools replay recorded returns. ToolSpace then performs state-aware random walks with rollback and decompiles each chain into a natural-language task with assertion-based checks, keeping only samples that replay successfully from the initial state. Applied to AutomationBench and tau3-Bench Banking, the pipeline produces harder Pro versions on which 7 frontier models drop by up to 38.2 points. Across seven long-horizon tool-use benchmarks, ToolSpace raises Qwen3.6-35B-A3B from 23.0 to 41.0 average score (43.2 with RL) and GLM-5.2 from 44.6 to 56.6, on par with Claude Opus 5. Ablations show that execution-witnessed edges clearly outperform LLM-judged ones, and performance keeps improving with data and environment scale.

AI.tldr: ToolSpace is a tool-centric framework that synthesizes long-horizon agent environments by mining deterministic dependencies from real MCP service execution traces, then generating verified tool-use tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing MCP environment-scaling methods synthesize data first and derive tools from it, so tool interfaces may not match real ones, compositions are not execution-grounded, and tasks rarely span multiple environments.
AI.method: ToolSpace mines data, state and retry dependencies from adjacent calls in traces using deterministic rules, clusters a weighted tool-composition graph into environments, synthesizes databases only for state-mutating environments, performs state-aware random walks with rollback, and decompiles chains into natural-language tasks with assertion-based checks that must replay from the initial state.
AI.result: Applied to AutomationBench and tau3-Bench Banking, the pipeline yields harder Pro versions on which seven frontier models drop by up to 38.2 points; across seven long-horizon tool-use benchmarks, ToolSpace raises Qwen3.6-35B-A3B from 23.0 to 41.0 average score (43.2 with RL) and GLM-5.2 from 44.6 to 56.6, on par with Claude Opus 5; execution-witnessed edges outperform LLM-judged ones.
AI.conclusion: Tool-centric, execution-grounded environment synthesis improves long-horizon agents, and performance keeps improving with data and environment scale.

title: GM League Arena: An Interactive Long-Horizon Task Benchmark Based on Professional Sports League Management
summary: Long-horizon decision-making under sustained competition requires large language models (LLMs) to balance immediate investment with future resource needs. However, local success in multi-step interactions can not adequately capture cumulative decision effects or demonstrate long-term goal achievement under resource constraints and sustained competition. To address this gap, we introduce GM Bench, a benchmark for managing professional sports teams across seasons under resource constraints and competition among teams. We build the environment simulators for four sports and add financial constraints, player demands, and market mechanisms to establish a unified task across sports. Diverse rosters of comparable strength are constructed from real-world player data, and each LLM is evaluated as a team general manager to assess its long-term management capabilities. We evaluate competitive performance, cash reserves, and cross-season improvement across four sports. Over five NBA seasons, Claude Opus 5.5 ranks first among 29 LLMs, while GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol combine strong performance with larger cash reserves.

AI.tldr: GM Bench is a long-horizon benchmark in which LLMs act as sports team general managers across seasons under resource constraints and competition, spanning four sports.
AI.motivation: Local success in multi-step interactions does not capture cumulative decision effects or long-term goal achievement under resource constraints and sustained competition.
AI.method: The authors build environment simulators for four sports with financial constraints, player demands and market mechanisms, construct comparable-strength rosters from real player data, and evaluate each LLM as a team general manager on competitive performance, cash reserves and cross-season improvement.
AI.result: Over five NBA seasons, Claude Opus 5.5 ranks first among 29 LLMs, while GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol combine strong performance with larger cash reserves.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark offers a unified way to assess long-term management capability of LLMs under resource constraints and competition.

title: When Self-Verification Hurts: Calibrated Answer Repair for Financial Question Answering
summary: Financial question answering can fail even when a model extracts a plausible number from the supplied evidence: the answer may attach it to the wrong entity, period, unit, or accounting concept. Asking the model to verify and revise its draft can help, but open-ended revision may alter content that was already correct or inspect the wrong relation and reinforce the original error. We formulate repair as a decision that balances the information it may recover against the correct content it may damage. Based on this trade-off, we introduce Calibrated Answer Repair (CAR), which first estimates whether a draft is likely to benefit from repair, then selects a targeted check, localizes the relevant evidence or draft span, and limits the permitted edit. Across FinRank, Fin-RATE, and FinQA with three open-weight models, CAR outperforms generic verification in all dataset-model settings. At the system level, it recovers 14.6% of initially missed answer requirements while damaging 2.1% of initially correct ones. Its post-draft token cost is over 30 percent lower than the iterative revision alternatives. Ablations on two dataset-model settings show that evidence localization and bounded editing are the main contributors to CAR's gains.

AI.tldr: Calibrated Answer Repair (CAR) decides whether a draft financial answer is worth repairing, then applies a targeted check and a bounded edit, improving over generic verification while limiting damage to correct answers.
AI.motivation: Financial QA fails when a plausible number is attached to the wrong entity, period, unit or concept, and open-ended self-verification can damage correct content or reinforce the original error.
AI.method: CAR first estimates whether a draft is likely to benefit from repair, then selects a targeted check, localizes the relevant evidence or draft span, and limits the permitted edit.
AI.result: Across FinRank, Fin-RATE and FinQA with three open-weight models, CAR outperforms generic verification in all dataset-model settings; it recovers 14.6% of initially missed answer requirements while damaging 2.1% of initially correct ones, with post-draft token cost more than 30% lower than iterative revision.
AI.conclusion: Evidence localization and bounded editing are the main sources of CAR's gains, so repair should be treated as a calibrated decision rather than open-ended revision.

title: ARLoop: Fully-Open Pre-trained Looped Transformers with Attention Residuals
summary: Looped transformers increase effective depth by repeatedly applying a shared set of transformer layers, offering a parameter-efficient way to scale computation. However, standard residual connections aggregate information across recurrent depth into a single stream, providing limited control over which intermediate representations from preceding layers should be reused. In this paper, we introduce ARLoop, a looped transformer architecture based on attention residuals, where the input of each layer is selectively aggregated through attention over model depth. Distinct from standard transformers, we find that looped transformers do not require access to the full residual history: sliding-window depth attention matches or outperforms full-history attention at larger recurrent depths. Across controlled experiments with multiple parameter scales (140M and 370M) and recurrent depths (R = 1 to 5), ARLoop consistently outperforms prior residual designs for looped transformers. More importantly, we further scale ARLoop to 0.6B and 1.2B parameters under a realistic LLM pretraining recipe, demonstrating that the gains transfer to realistic pretraining, with particularly strong improvements on math and coding tasks. Our 1.2B model, pretrained on only 0.5T tokens with three recurrences, outperforms Huginn-3.5B (the only fully-open looped LLM as of our release date) across all evaluated tasks and is competitive with similar-sized non-looped models such as Qwen3.5-2B despite being trained on substantially less data.

AI.tldr: ARLoop is a fully open looped transformer that uses attention residuals with sliding-window depth attention, and its 1.2B model trained on 0.5T tokens outperforms Huginn-3.5B across evaluated tasks.
AI.motivation: Standard residual connections combine recurrent depth into one stream, giving limited control over which intermediate representations a looped transformer reuses.
AI.method: Each layer's input is selectively aggregated by attention over model depth; the authors find that sliding-window depth attention matches or beats full-history attention at larger recurrent depths, test 140M and 370M models at recurrent depths 1 to 5, and scale to 0.6B and 1.2B parameters under an LLM pretraining recipe.
AI.result: ARLoop consistently outperforms prior residual designs for looped transformers, with strong gains on math and coding; the 1.2B model, pretrained on 0.5T tokens with three recurrences, outperforms Huginn-3.5B on all evaluated tasks and is competitive with Qwen3.5-2B despite less training data.
AI.conclusion: The gains transfer from controlled experiments to a realistic pretraining setting, and sliding-window depth attention is sufficient for looped transformers.

title: MDSKILL: Learning to Internalize Skill Memory through Multi-View Distillation for Efficient Dynamic Agent Self-Evolution
summary: Skill memories encode past experiences as textual prompts to improve reinforcement learning (RL) for self-evolving agents. Complementing RL, On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) provides dense, fine-grained supervision to internalize knowledge from skill-guided trajectories and accelerate policy learning. However, self-generated memories often contain noisy supervision and functionally entangled, redundant, or conflicting knowledge, making direct distillation difficult. Under limited training budgets, these issues can hinder knowledge internalization and even degrade performance. To address this problem, we propose MDSKILL, a multi-view distillation approach for skill memory internalization. MDSKILL organizes skill memories into three complementary functional views (state grounding, action planning, and execution control) and selects high-quality skills using dynamic metrics to construct view-specific and integrated reasoning branches. OPSD then transfers and consolidates complementary experiential knowledge across these branches into a shared policy, enabling efficient skill internalization and continuous agent self-evolution. We evaluate MDSKILL on three agent benchmarks against RL, skill-augmented, and self-distillation baselines that do not rely on stronger external teacher models. Without additional computational overhead, MDSKILL improves upon SOTA performance by up to 7.1% and 8.1% on ALFWorld and WebShop. Extensive ablations and evolution analyses further validate its effectiveness in knowledge internalization and policy improvement. The code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: MDSKILL distills agent skill memories through three complementary functional views and on-policy self-distillation, improving self-evolving agents on ALFWorld and WebShop without stronger external teachers.
AI.motivation: Self-generated skill memories are noisy and entangled, with redundant or conflicting knowledge, which makes direct on-policy self-distillation hard under limited training budgets and can degrade performance.
AI.method: MDSKILL organizes skill memories into state grounding, action planning and execution control views, selects high-quality skills with dynamic metrics to build view-specific and integrated reasoning branches, and transfers their knowledge into a shared policy via on-policy self-distillation.
AI.result: Without additional computational overhead, MDSKILL improves on state-of-the-art performance by up to 7.1% on ALFWorld and 8.1% on WebShop, compared with RL, skill-augmented and self-distillation baselines.
AI.conclusion: Multi-view distillation makes skill memory internalization more efficient and supports continued agent self-evolution.

title: A Circuit for In-Context Learning
comment: 38 pages, 22 figures. Code and an interactive walkthrough at this https URL
summary: In-context learning (ICL) lets a pretrained language model perform a task specified by demonstrations in its prompt, with no parameter updates. With arbitrary labels the model must acquire a mapping it cannot have memorized, so the learning happens within a single forward pass. Prior work found candidate parts but not how they compose. We give the composition for few-shot sentence classification with arbitrary labels in three 3-4B-parameter transformers. The model implements a key-value memory over label-token positions: each label token's residual stream encodes the label's identity, and middle-layer attention heads write into it the class of the preceding demonstration as its key. At the query, upper-layer heads match the query's class against the stored keys and copy out the matching labels. An early-layer signal encoding whether any label has repeated gates this readout; in its absence the readers attend to the start of the prompt and no label is favored. A separate set of heads suppresses the most recently seen label. Each step is established causally by activation patching, head ablations against random-head baselines, and steering with the model's own signals. A softmax model of the readout with two constants per head, fit on one prompt distribution, predicts another. The computation is conserved across the three models, the named heads alone reproduce the behaviour, and a transformer trained from scratch grows the same parts. The circuit transfers to semantic concepts and to labels with meaning, and the same parts, with a causal gate, appear from 0.6B to 8B in one family and survive instruction tuning. ICL in this setting is a gated associative lookup built from a few identifiable component types, traced causally from demonstrations to prediction.

AI.tldr: The paper gives a circuit-level account of in-context learning with arbitrary labels in three 3-4B transformers, describing a gated key-value memory over label-token positions that is built from a few component types.
AI.motivation: Prior work identified candidate parts of in-context learning but not how they compose, especially when labels are arbitrary and cannot be memorized.
AI.method: Activation patching, head ablations against random-head baselines, steering with the model's own signals, and a softmax readout model with two constants per head fit on one prompt distribution and tested on another are used to establish each step causally; the circuit is also checked on semantic concepts, meaningful labels, a trained-from-scratch transformer, and a model family from 0.6B to 8B.
AI.result: Middle-layer heads write the class of the preceding demonstration as a key into label-token positions, upper-layer heads match the query's class and copy the matching label, an early-layer repetition signal gates the readout, and a separate set of heads suppresses the most recently seen label; the named heads alone reproduce the behavior, and the same parts appear across scales and survive instruction tuning.
AI.conclusion: In-context learning in this setting is a gated associative lookup built from identifiable component types, traced causally from demonstrations to prediction.

title: Mixture of Wide Experts: Sparse Routing for Interpretable Native Coordinates
comment: 47 pages, 14 figures. Code: this https URL. Models: this https URL
summary: Language models often spread a concept across many internal dimensions, making their features difficult to interpret. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) recover clearer features after training. We ask whether models can instead learn interpretable output coordinates directly. We introduce Mixture of Wide Experts (MoWE), a sparse feed-forward layer in which selected experts read the full representation but write to fixed, disjoint output coordinates. On a controlled task with known hidden causes, this design preserves predictive performance while localizing causes more clearly than dense and standard mixture-of-experts (MoE) models. At approximately matched compute, we train two 19-layer runs of each architecture for 10 billion tokens. MoWE achieves evaluation cross-entropy 2.417 versus 2.452 for dense, while standard MoE reaches 2.22. We measure native-coordinate readability by asking a language-model judge to describe each coordinate from passages where it is strongly active and test that description on new passages. Correcting for descriptions that also fit other coordinates gives a specificity score of 0.523 for MoWE, 0.375 for dense, and 0.268 for standard MoE. TopK SAEs trained on the same FFN updates score 0.489 for dense and 0.556 for MoWE, making native MoWE comparable to the dense SAE. In the first case study, we identify a four-coordinate causal path supporting the model's prediction of degrees after the prompt A right angle is 90. We then copy seven angle-related coordinate values into the model as it processes A rectangle has four, changing its next-token prediction from sides to degrees. In the second, one fixed coordinate set detects hazardous requests and another steers the next token toward refusal. These examples show that MoWE combines sparse conditional computation with coordinates that can be identified and reused directly.

AI.tldr: Mixture of Wide Experts (MoWE) is a sparse feed-forward layer whose selected experts read the full representation but write to fixed, disjoint output coordinates, aiming for model coordinates that are directly interpretable without a sparse autoencoder.
AI.motivation: Language model concepts are spread across many internal dimensions, and sparse autoencoders recover interpretable features only after training; the authors ask whether models can learn interpretable output coordinates directly.
AI.method: Experts in MoWE read the full representation but write to fixed, disjoint output coordinates; the authors compare two 19-layer runs of each architecture trained for 10 billion tokens at approximately matched compute, and measure native-coordinate readability with a language-model judge describing each coordinate and testing the description on new passages.
AI.result: MoWE reaches evaluation cross-entropy 2.417 versus 2.452 for dense and 2.22 for standard MoE; its specificity score is 0.523, versus 0.375 for dense and 0.268 for standard MoE, and comparable to a TopK SAE on dense FFN updates (0.489 dense, 0.556 MoWE); case studies identify a four-coordinate causal path for predicting degrees after a right angle and a fixed set detecting hazardous requests.
AI.conclusion: MoWE combines sparse conditional computation with coordinates that can be identified and reused directly, though the cross-entropy comparison is reported at approximately matched compute rather than exact parity.

title: EpiLoRA: Fusing Many LoRA Adapters into Low-Precision GEMMs for Serving and RL
summary: Low-rank adapters (LoRA) let one base model serve many fine-tuned variants: multi-tenant engines keep a single copy of the base and batch the requests of many tenants, each with its own adapter. As base models move to 8-bit (FP8) and 4-bit formats, their general matrix multiplications (GEMMs) become cheaper, but the adapters do not: engines run them as separate small GPU kernels beside the GEMM, whose latency takes a growing share of every decoding step. An adapter projects its input down to a low rank and back up, and our key observation is that the GEMM needs the down-projection only in its epilogue, the final stage in which it writes its output. EpiLoRA, a plugin for the vLLM engine, therefore launches the down-projection first and the low-precision GEMM as a dependent kernel that streams its weights meanwhile and adds every tenant's up-projection in its epilogue. On NVIDIA Hopper GPUs, EpiLoRA decodes for a single adapter with up to 24% lower time per token than vLLM's fastest configuration, and faster than SGLang and TensorRT-LLM; with many tenants, its adapter kernels deliver more throughput than vLLM's on most GPU-model pairs we tested. The same low-precision base also trains: a LoRA reinforcement-learning trainer that computes on the engine's FP8 weights needs no 16-bit copy, so a 27B model trains on one 48 GB GPU, and an engine that then keeps activations in 16 bits removes most of the remaining mismatch between the model generating training data and the one trained.

AI.tldr: EpiLoRA is a vLLM plugin that fuses the LoRA down-projection into the epilogue of a low-precision GEMM, cutting adapter overhead for multi-tenant serving and enabling LoRA reinforcement learning on FP8 base weights.
AI.motivation: As base models move to FP8 and 4-bit formats, their GEMMs get cheaper but separate small LoRA adapter kernels do not, and these kernels take a growing share of each decoding step.
AI.method: The down-projection is launched first and the low-precision GEMM runs as a dependent kernel that streams its weights and adds every tenant's up-projection in its epilogue; a LoRA RL trainer computes on the engine's FP8 weights without a 16-bit copy.
AI.result: On NVIDIA Hopper GPUs, single-adapter decoding has up to 24% lower time per token than vLLM's fastest configuration and is faster than SGLang and TensorRT-LLM; with many tenants, adapter kernels deliver more throughput than vLLM's on most GPU-model pairs tested; a 27B model trains on one 48 GB GPU.
AI.conclusion: Fusing the adapter into the low-precision base GEMM reduces serving overhead and memory needs, and keeping activations in 16 bits removes most of the training-generation mismatch.

title: When Strong Reasoners Join the Pool: Small Union Premiums and Costly Runaway Generations in LLM Routing
comment: Technical report. 10 pages, 7 figures, 14 tables. Companion to arXiv:2607.03436. Data and code: this https URL
summary: Routing benchmarks often judge a router against a hindsight oracle that counts a query as solved whenever any model's recorded answer is correct, but under stochastic decoding that oracle mixes two different objects: the clairvoyant ceiling of committing to one model per query and the premium of calling several models and keeping any correct answer. A companion study measured this premium at 3.5 percentage points (pp) for 11 small open models on MATH-500; how large it is once current reasoning models enter the pool was unknown. We measure it with a fixed-protocol, pre-committed generation on a single NVIDIA B300: all 500 MATH-500 problems, 30 seeded samples per problem, Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and NVIDIA's Nemotron Nano 9B v2 and Nemotron Super 49B v1.5 (a NAS derivative of the same 70B) under vendor sampling, a 65,536-token cap, a pinned Math-Verify scorer, and an append-only attempt ledger, for 45,000 scored responses. The two reasoning models both reach 96.1% accuracy against 76.2% for the 70B baseline. The empirical product-coupling premium is 0.215-0.588 pp across all two- and three-model pools; the empirical plug-in selection headroom over always calling Nano is 1.27 pp; and resampling Nano three times gives practically the same empirical any-correct rate as calling all three models once. Only 31 responses reached the cap, 25 of them with exactly periodic tails, yet the capped responses account for up to 60.2% of a model's output-length-squared proxy, and long generations made a fourth planned model, Llama-3.1-8B, too slow to finish. The premium is far below the companion's 3.5 pp, but models, pool size and protocol changed together; an oracle gap should therefore be reported with the pool, the protocol, the samples per cell and the decoding budget that produced it.

AI.tldr: The paper measures the union premium of calling several LLMs for routing on MATH-500 with two current reasoning models in the pool, finding the premium far below the 3.5 pp reported by a companion study for small open models.
AI.motivation: Routing benchmarks use a hindsight oracle that mixes the clairvoyant ceiling of one model per query with the premium of calling several models, and the size of that premium with current reasoning models was unknown.
AI.method: A pre-committed generation protocol on a single NVIDIA B300 uses all 500 MATH-500 problems, 30 seeded samples per problem, Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, Nemotron Nano 9B v2 and Nemotron Super 49B v1.5 under vendor sampling, a 65,536-token cap, a pinned Math-Verify scorer and an append-only attempt ledger, for 45,000 scored responses.
