AI.result: The two reasoning models reach 96.1% accuracy against 76.2% for the 70B baseline; the empirical product-coupling premium is 0.215-0.588 pp across two- and three-model pools; plug-in selection headroom over always calling Nano is 1.27 pp; resampling Nano three times gives about the same any-correct rate as calling all three models once; 31 responses hit the cap, and these account for up to 60.2% of a model's output-length-squared proxy.
AI.conclusion: The oracle gap should be reported together with the pool, protocol, samples per cell and decoding budget that produced it, because models, pool size and protocol changed together relative to the companion study.

title: LoopKV: Loop-Aware KV Cache Compression for Serving Looped Transformers
summary: Looped transformers apply a shared block several times per token to improve accuracy without adding parameters. For models such as Ouro that keep a separate key-value (KV) cache per loop, cache memory limits the batch size that amortizes repeated weight reads. Uniform-bit quantization and fixed rules per loop do not allocate precision according to each layer's sensitivity in each loop. Measurements on Ouro show that quantization sensitivity varies across (loop, layer) cells, and the sum of individual cell damages approximates the overall output damage. Sharing damage also varies by cell, with later loops generally tolerating sharing better. Skipping low-attention values to save reads produces errors that compound across loops. LoopKV uses a one-time offline profile to choose 4-bit storage, 2-bit storage or reuse of the final loop's KV for each cell. The planner minimizes reads under budgets for predicted damage and storage. During decoding, each loop reads the high 2 bits of each 4-bit value and fetches the low bits only where its own attention weights require 4-bit precision. A single fused kernel in vLLM executes the plan. Serving Ouro-1.4B on one RTX PRO 6000, the memory-optimized LoopKV-M plan stores 35% less KV than uniform 4-bit quantization (KIVI-4) on the same fused kernel and CUDA graph. It sustains 1.7-2.2x KIVI-4's goodput under a latency service-level objective with a 16K-token maximum length. None of its averages on six public benchmarks falls significantly below BF16's.

AI.tldr: LoopKV compresses the per-loop KV cache of looped transformers by choosing 4-bit, 2-bit or reuse of the final loop's KV for each (loop, layer) cell from an offline sensitivity profile, serving Ouro-1.4B with less memory and higher goodput.
AI.motivation: Looped transformers such as Ouro keep a separate KV cache per loop, so cache memory limits the batch size that amortizes weight reads, and uniform quantization or fixed per-loop rules ignore per-cell sensitivity.
AI.method: A one-time offline profile selects a storage option for each cell; the planner minimizes reads under predicted-damage and storage budgets; during decoding each loop reads the high 2 bits of 4-bit values and fetches the low bits only where attention requires them; a fused kernel in vLLM executes the plan.
AI.result: On one RTX PRO 6000, the memory-optimized LoopKV-M plan stores 35% less KV than uniform 4-bit quantization (KIVI-4) on the same kernel and CUDA graph, sustains 1.7-2.2 times KIVI-4's goodput under a latency SLO with a 16K-token maximum length, and its averages on six public benchmarks do not fall significantly below BF16.
AI.conclusion: Loop-aware, sensitivity-driven KV cache compression can cut memory and raise serving throughput for looped transformers without a significant accuracy loss on the evaluated benchmarks.

title: Text-to-SQL Models Make Choices Without Saying So
summary: A text-to-SQL answer can run, return a plausible number and still compute something other than what the analyst meant. This can happen when the request leaves a calculation choice open, such as whether to count rows or distinct entities, and the model settles it without saying so. Standard benchmarks cannot detect this, because they score each question against a single reference interpretation. We introduce SpecBridge, which tests such a choice by varying it alone: it poses three otherwise identical requests, one leaving the choice open and one per interpretation, and scores each answer by running it. The databases are real, and the choices are ones that made models fail on existing benchmarks. On 204 hand-validated tests, four language models usually compute each interpretation when asked for it, yet for the open request return both in only 15-58% of the tests where they can, often without mentioning the choice. The gap lies in reporting, not in computing. Benchmarks even penalize the alternative: on BIRD questions where such a choice changes the answer, over two in five of the answers marked wrong are right under the other interpretation. Because the gap lies in reporting, a system can narrow it without a stronger model: it first decides whether a request leaves a choice open, then answers each interpretation in its own call. On our tests and on AMBROSIA, an existing benchmark of ambiguous questions, this approach raises the share of open requests that get every interpretation by 29-63 points over the single answer that production assistants give, without lowering precision on clear requests. It also needs fewer user turns than asking a clarifying question.

AI.tldr: SpecBridge tests text-to-SQL models on unstated calculation choices by comparing open requests with per-interpretation requests, finding that models compute each interpretation but often fail to report the alternatives.
AI.motivation: Text-to-SQL answers can run and look plausible while computing something other than the analyst meant when the request leaves a calculation choice open, and standard benchmarks score against a single reference interpretation.
AI.method: SpecBridge poses three otherwise identical requests, one open and one per interpretation, and scores each answer by executing it on real databases; a proposed approach first decides whether a request leaves a choice open and then answers each interpretation in its own call.
AI.result: On 204 hand-validated tests, four language models usually compute each interpretation when asked, but for open requests return both only in 15-58% of the tests where they can, often without mentioning the choice; on BIRD questions where such a choice changes the answer, over two in five answers marked wrong are right under the other interpretation; the approach raises the share of open requests that receive every interpretation by 29-63 points over the single answer of production assistants, without lowering precision on clear requests, and needs fewer user turns than a clarifying question.
AI.conclusion: The gap lies in reporting rather than computation, so a system can narrow it without a stronger model.

title: Sketchpad: certified exact arithmetic with a small vision-language model
comment: 25 pages, 7 figures (6 + 1 Extended Data), 6 Extended Data tables. Demo: this https URL ; code (Apache 2.0): this https URL ; model: this https URL
summary: Language models are accurate on most long-arithmetic problems, but their accuracy is estimated on samples and carries no guarantee for an unseen input; tool use is exact but moves the computation outside the network. We show that exactness at all input lengths becomes a finite, checkable property of a network when each of its steps reads only a bounded view of an external working memory. In Sketchpad, Qwen3.5-0.8B with a low-rank adapter executes arithmetic procedures on a rendered sheet. Each forward pass reads a three-cell view and emits one step: a digit, a carry or borrow, and the next operation. A fixed runtime moves the view and writes no digit of a result. We prove in Lean that the model is then exact on all inputs of any length if and only if it is exact on the finite set of views the runtime presents, that no finite test suffices when steps also read earlier steps, and that the guarantee tolerates bounded numerical perturbation and extends to compositions of procedures. All 2,446 views pass on the deployment device, a laptop GPU running the model in a web browser. The certified model performs signed addition and subtraction, long multiplication and division, square roots and greatest common divisors at arbitrary length. It solved 200 of 200 pre-registered problems in the browser, and 220 of 220 sums of up to 1,000 digits and products of up to 20 digits, of which GPT-6.1 Sol, the strongest of ten other models, solved 217. A symbolic runtime built on these procedures solves, expands and factors polynomials with every number computed by the model, and a multiplicative gate on the adapter recovers the base model exactly when the sheet is not in use.

AI.tldr: Sketchpad shows that a small vision-language model executing arithmetic step by step on a rendered sheet can be certified exact on all input lengths by checking a finite set of bounded views.
AI.motivation: Language models are accurate on most long-arithmetic problems, but their accuracy is estimated from samples with no guarantee for unseen inputs, while tool use is exact but moves computation outside the network.
AI.method: Qwen3.5-0.8B with a low-rank adapter executes arithmetic procedures on a rendered sheet, each forward pass reads a three-cell view and emits one step, and a fixed runtime moves the view; the authors prove in Lean that exactness on all inputs reduces to exactness on the finite set of views the runtime presents, and that the guarantee tolerates bounded numerical perturbation and extends to compositions.
AI.result: All 2,446 views pass on the deployment device, a laptop GPU running the model in a web browser; the certified model solves 200 of 200 pre-registered problems in the browser and 220 of 220 sums of up to 1,000 digits and products of up to 20 digits, where GPT-6.1 Sol, the strongest of ten other models, solved 217; a symbolic runtime built on these procedures solves, expands and factors polynomials.
AI.conclusion: Exactness at arbitrary input length can be made a finite, checkable property of a network when each step reads only a bounded view of external working memory.

title: Near-Zero Token Embeddings Silently Stall Training in Gated Sequence Models
summary: Among 291 surveyed open-weight language model repositories (280 distinct embedding tables), 52.6% of untied gated and hybrid checkpoints (20/38) contain reachable input embeddings with norms below $10^{-6}$, compared with 0% of weight-tied models. Such near-zero rows can arise during pretraining when unseen rare or template tokens receive zero input gradients while AdamW weight decay shrinks untied embeddings. In tested Transformer configurations, non-initial positions or a BOS token prevent this failure mode. In gated sequence models (Mamba, Gated DeltaNet, xLSTM), a near-zero token can amplify input-embedding gradients by more than 30 orders of magnitude (up to 35). At zero input, current-token readout factors (SiLU gates or linear queries) vanish, suppressing historical-state readout. Residual RMS values can then fall below the square root of the RMSNorm floor across consecutive layers, causing Pre-RMSNorm to amplify backward gradients by up to $10^3$ per layer. When a gradient entry exceeds $1.84 \times 10^{19}$, FP32 global-norm clipping in PyTorch, Hugging Face Trainer, and FSDP2 can overflow to infinity and zero the current batch's gradients. In Telugu continual pretraining of Nemotron-3-Nano-4B, this discards updates on approximately 20% of steps and leaves triggered rows frozen. We propose two remedies. For released checkpoints, GroupClip decouples input-embedding clipping using a 64-bit or rescaled norm; its rescaled implementation eliminates update loss and heals triggered rows in one step with negligible measured end-to-end overhead. For pretraining, GateFloor ($\mathrm{SiLU}(z) + \delta$, $\delta \in [0.01, 0.1]$) keeps the gate positive at zero input, reducing near-zero gradients by 28 orders of magnitude in experiments up to 370M parameters, with perplexity comparable to the baseline.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that near-zero input embeddings in untied gated and hybrid sequence models can amplify gradients and make global-norm clipping zero out batches, and proposes GroupClip and GateFloor as remedies.
AI.motivation: Near-zero token embeddings arise in pretraining when rare or template tokens receive no input gradient while weight decay shrinks untied embeddings, and their effects in gated sequence models were not understood.
AI.method: The authors survey 291 open-weight repositories, examine gradient amplification in Mamba, Gated DeltaNet and xLSTM, trace overflow in FP32 global-norm clipping in PyTorch, Hugging Face Trainer and FSDP2, and propose GroupClip (decoupled input-embedding clipping with a 64-bit or rescaled norm) for released checkpoints and GateFloor (SiLU(z) plus a small delta) for pretraining.
AI.result: 52.6% of untied gated and hybrid checkpoints (20 of 38) contain reachable input embeddings with norms below 10^-6, compared with 0% of weight-tied models; in Telugu continual pretraining of Nemotron-3-Nano-4B the failure discards updates on about 20% of steps; GroupClip eliminates update loss and heals triggered rows in one step; GateFloor reduces near-zero gradients by 28 orders of magnitude in experiments up to 370M parameters with perplexity comparable to baseline.
AI.conclusion: Near-zero embeddings are a silent failure mode in gated sequence models, and the two proposed fixes address it for released checkpoints and for pretraining.

title: Self-Privileged Fine-Tuning
summary: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is a key component of language model post-training, enabling effective task adaptation and serving as an important foundation for subsequent reinforcement learning. Recent methods seek to improve SFT by introducing token-level weights into the training objective, where these weights are typically derived from a model's output distribution at each token position. To better understand how such weighting schemes affect SFT, we analyze their optimization objectives and theoretically characterize the target distributions they induce. Our analysis shows that dynamic weighting methods, such as Dynamic Fine-Tuning (DFT), induce a heavily sharpened distribution, whereas static weighting methods fit a target distribution proportional to the product of the data distribution and a frozen prior. These findings suggest that static weighting provides a more stable training target, while its effectiveness critically depends on the quality of the prior distribution. Building on this observation, we propose Self-Privileged Fine-Tuning (SPFT), which uses a frozen copy of the initial model conditioned on privileged information (such as ground truth for mathematical questions) as a prior to provide guidance for token-level weighting during fine-tuning. Through a Bayesian decomposition, we further show that SPFT reweights the standard static prior according to how informative each target token is for predicting the ground-truth outcome, thereby assigning larger weights to more predictive tokens. Experiments on mathematical reasoning and code generation show that SPFT improves over standard SFT and other baselines across the main settings.

AI.tldr: Self-Privileged Fine-Tuning (SPFT) weights SFT tokens using a frozen copy of the initial model conditioned on privileged information such as ground truth, arguing that static weighting targets a more stable distribution than dynamic methods like DFT.
AI.motivation: Token-level weighted SFT methods derive weights from the model's own output distribution, and it was unclear how such weighting schemes change the target distribution during training.
AI.method: The authors analyze the optimization objectives and characterize the induced target distributions, showing dynamic weighting sharpens the distribution while static weighting fits a target proportional to the data distribution times a frozen prior; SPFT uses a frozen initial model conditioned on privileged information as that prior, with a Bayesian decomposition that weights tokens by how informative they are for the ground-truth outcome.
AI.result: Experiments on mathematical reasoning and code generation show that SPFT improves over standard SFT and other baselines across the main settings.
AI.conclusion: Static weighting gives a more stable training target, and its effectiveness depends critically on the quality of the prior, which SPFT supplies through privileged information.

title: Heads That Write, Not Just Point: Image Retrieval Heads in Vision-Language Models
summary: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) can process interleaved text and multiple images in a single context, but how they internally identify the image relevant to a question remains poorly understood. We study this grounding step as in-context image retrieval and introduce ICIR-MCQ, a controlled probe for head-level analysis of image retrieval. Using each head's attention mass over image-token spans, we first identify sparse pointer heads that reliably point to the target image. These heads transfer beyond the probe: a single pointer head is competitive with external vision-language retrievers on a naturalistic multi-image retrieval benchmark, showing that LVLMs contain a strong internal image retrieval signal. Attention alone, however, shows where a head reads from, not what its output passes on to later layers, so we introduce a complementary output-side analysis. For each head, we train a lightweight image retriever on its value-weighted output and use it to identify writer heads, whose outputs contain enough information to identify the target image. Surprisingly, the pointer and writer criteria select substantially different head sets, with only 35 to 47 heads overlapping among the top-100 heads under each criterion. Targeted set-partition ablations show that the heads most important for standard multi-image inference are concentrated in this pointer-writer intersection, while heads selected by only one criterion show less consistent separation from random-head controls. The most consistent causal effects arise from heads selected by both the attention-based pointer and output-side writer criteria. Code and data: this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies image retrieval heads in vision-language models, separating pointer heads that attend to the target image from writer heads whose outputs carry enough information to identify it, and finds the most causally important heads lie in their intersection.
AI.motivation: How large vision-language models internally identify the image relevant to a question is poorly understood, and attention alone does not show what a head passes on to later layers.
AI.method: The authors introduce ICIR-MCQ, a controlled probe; pointer heads are found from attention mass over image-token spans, writer heads by training a lightweight image retriever on each head's value-weighted output; set-partition ablations compare the heads selected by each criterion against random-head controls.
AI.result: A single pointer head is competitive with external vision-language retrievers on a naturalistic multi-image benchmark; the pointer and writer criteria select substantially different heads, with only 35 to 47 of the top 100 overlapping; heads important for multi-image inference concentrate in the pointer-writer intersection, and the most consistent causal effects come from heads selected by both criteria.
AI.conclusion: LVLMs contain a strong internal image retrieval signal, and grounding relies on heads that both attend to and write out the target image.

title: What Does the Model See? Representation Validity in Multimodal LLM-Based Video Analysis
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) allow social scientists to analyze video at scale, but researchers must decide which parts of a video to provide as input. We use the term representation validity to examine how text, audio, video, and combined inputs affect measurement and subsequent analysis. We compare input representations across six open-weight MLLMs and three human-annotated video datasets. No representation consistently performs best. On seven news-related constructs, native-video performance varies little across models (macro-F1 = .70-.77), while extracted-text performance ranges from .52 to .80. Three models perform better with text and three with video. Combining inputs rarely improves performance. Higher classification accuracy also does not reliably produce estimates closer to those based on human codes. The highest-F1 representation best reproduces human-coded regression coefficients in 17 of 42 comparisons. Even when each model uses its highest-F1 deployable representation, 45% of sample-prevalence estimates differ from the human-coded benchmark by more than ten percentage points. Input representation therefore requires validation for both the construct being measured and the quantity estimated from the resulting labels.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how the choice of input representation (text, audio, video or combined) for multimodal LLMs affects measurement validity in social-science video analysis, finding that no representation consistently performs best.
AI.motivation: Social scientists analyzing video at scale must decide which parts of a video to feed to a multimodal LLM, and this choice can change measurement and downstream estimates.
AI.method: Six open-weight MLLMs are compared across text, audio, video and combined inputs on three human-annotated video datasets, with classification performance and regression coefficients compared against human codes.
AI.result: On seven news-related constructs, native-video performance varies little across models (macro-F1 0.70-0.77) while extracted-text performance ranges from 0.52 to 0.80; three models do better with text and three with video; combining inputs rarely helps; the highest-F1 representation best reproduces human-coded regression coefficients in 17 of 42 comparisons; 45% of sample-prevalence estimates still differ from the human benchmark by more than ten percentage points.
AI.conclusion: Input representation must be validated both for the construct measured and for the quantity estimated from the resulting labels.

title: Reading Why: Born-Measured Attention with Exact Word Evidence on Light and Qubits
comment: 24 pages, 7 figures, 11 tables. Code, trained models, notebooks and the record of every IBM job: this https URL
summary: When a language model answers, we can usually only estimate why. We build a transformer in which every step is a Born measurement - attention $|\langle q|k\rangle|^4$ normalised over each row, a measured product in place of the feed-forward nonlinearity, and a Born readout. With its denominators held at their values for the input, each class probability is a polynomial in the word amplitudes, so its integrated-gradient evidence is computed by a finite quadrature with no quadrature error: the words' contributions sum to the class probability above its no-information share, to $10^{-11}$ or better. On e-SNLI natural language inference, with about 98k parameters outside the embedding, the model reaches $76.98 \pm 0.17$% test accuracy, level with a softmax transformer of the same size ($76.62 \pm 0.36$%). Deleting the word its evidence ranks first changes the answer in 45% of test pairs, out of the 53% any single deletion can change, against 32% for the softmax model explained the same way and 40% by its attention x gradient. Attention can look more like the words annotators highlighted, yet accounts for the answer less well: deleting the word it ranks first changes the Born Transformer's answer in 32% of pairs. The same weights compile exactly to optoelectronic optics and to qubits, and a coherent attention layer becomes one circuit equal to the model (852 CNOTs on 23 qubits). On IBM's ibm_kingston, reading only the attention overlaps by Hadamard tests, the device gave the model's answers on two short test pairs and kept or changed them under deletion as the model does; the evidence itself did not yet survive the device, and we work out the shots and calibration that measuring it on hardware would need.

AI.tldr: The paper builds a transformer whose every step is a Born measurement, making each class probability a polynomial in word amplitudes so that its integrated-gradient evidence is computed exactly, and reports matching accuracy to a softmax transformer on e-SNLI.
AI.motivation: Explanations of language model answers usually only estimate why a model answered as it did, and the authors want word-level evidence that is exact by construction.
AI.method: Attention uses |<q|k>|^4 normalised over each row, a measured product replaces the feed-forward nonlinearity, and a Born readout is used; with denominators held fixed, class probabilities are polynomials in word amplitudes, so integrated gradients are computed by finite quadrature; the same weights are compiled to optoelectronic optics and to a qubit circuit.
AI.result: On e-SNLI with about 98k non-embedding parameters the model reaches 76.98 +/- 0.17% test accuracy, level with a softmax transformer (76.62 +/- 0.36%); deleting the word its evidence ranks first changes the answer in 45% of test pairs, versus 32% for the softmax model explained the same way and 40% by attention times gradient; on IBM's ibm_kingston, the hardware reproduced the model's answers on two short test pairs for attention overlaps only, and the evidence did not yet survive the device.
AI.conclusion: Born-measured attention gives word evidence that accounts for the answer better than attention-based explanations, while measuring that evidence on hardware remains open.

title: Towards Automatic Heart Murmur Characterization from Multi-spot Phonocardiograms
summary: Cardiac auscultation traditionally detects the presence of a heart murmur, but clinicians further characterize it by timing, shape, pitch, quality, and grade. Most automatic phonocardiogram analysis systems stop at binary detection and do not estimate this richer description. In this work, we formulate automatic murmur characterization as five patient-level classification tasks and compare three multi-spot strategies on recordings from the aortic, pulmonary, mitral, and tricuspid auscultation locations. First, classical and deep-learning classifiers are trained independently at each location, and predictions are combined via a maximum-severity late-fusion rule. Second, a synchronous multi-input CNN jointly processes one representative segment per location for a single task. Third, a unified multi-input, multi-output CNN predicts all five attributes from one shared multi-spot representation. Using 735 patients from the CirCor DigiScope dataset with complete four-spot recordings, the best late-fusion configurations reach an unweighted mean sensitivity between 85.56% and 93.81% across the five tasks, with class-specific recalls between 80.00% and 100.00% for every relevant category. The multi-input CNN trails late fusion by 7-16 points depending on the task, while the multi-output model reaches values between 72.59% and 79.40%, estimating all five attributes from one shared representation. We further show that naively balancing training data by adding all minority-class segments degrades patient-level performance under the maximum-severity rule, since it introduces non-representative, noisy segments not filtered by the clustering-based segment selection used for evaluation. These results indicate multi-spot murmur characterization is feasible with both fusion-based and jointly learned architectures, outlining a path toward automatic, structured murmur reports complementing binary screening.

AI.tldr: The paper formulates heart murmur characterization as five patient-level classification tasks using multi-spot phonocardiograms, comparing late fusion of per-location models with two joint multi-input CNN designs on 735 CirCor DigiScope patients.
AI.motivation: Most automatic phonocardiogram systems stop at binary murmur detection, while clinicians also describe timing, shape, pitch, quality and grade.
AI.method: Classical and deep-learning classifiers are trained per auscultation location and combined by a maximum-severity late-fusion rule; a synchronous multi-input CNN processes one segment per location for a single task; a unified multi-input, multi-output CNN predicts all five attributes from one shared representation; the authors also test class balancing by adding all minority-class segments.
AI.result: The best late-fusion configurations reach unweighted mean sensitivity of 85.56% to 93.81% across the five tasks, with class-specific recalls of 80.00% to 100.00%; the multi-input CNN trails late fusion by 7-16 points depending on the task; the multi-output model reaches 72.59% to 79.40%; naive balancing degrades patient-level performance under the maximum-severity rule.
AI.conclusion: Multi-spot murmur characterization is feasible with both fusion-based and jointly learned architectures, and naive balancing of training data should be avoided.

title: Stress-Testing the Robustness of LLM-Based Causal Inference
summary: Why do some of the world's most powerful Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems still struggle to reason about cause and effect? Causal discovery, the ability to discern the underlying drivers of a system, is fundamental to scientific inquiry and has traditionally relied on structured data and statistical methods. Recently, Large Language Models (LLMs) have been explored as an alternative paradigm for causal inference, leveraging their broad knowledge and reasoning capabilities. Yet, despite their linguistic fluency, LLMs often rely on surface-level pattern recognition rather than genuine causal logic. While it is known that LLMs stumble in this domain, we lack a precise map of where, why, and how significantly these failures occur. In this paper, we propose a systematic stress-test framework across six critical dimensions: model scale, causal graph complexity, prompting strategy, metadata quality, data quality, and sensitivity to uncertainty. Our findings reveal a significant "optimism bias" in LLMs; models consistently overestimate causal links, leading to low precision across the board. Furthermore, we demonstrate that traditional evaluation metrics can be deceptive: while reasoning-heavy models lead in performance, the highest scores often occur when uncertainty in inference is overlooked. Once uncertainty is integrated into the evaluation, performance drops, providing a more honest reflection of causal reliability. We also find that, while scaling model size improves outcomes, these gains are fragile; performance degrades sharply as the quality of metadata decreases. This work serves as a practical guide to the blind spots of LLMs, offering a clear-eyed assessment of when these tools can be integrated into a causal discovery pipeline and when they are likely to lead researchers astray.

AI.tldr: The paper stress-tests LLM-based causal discovery across six dimensions and finds a systematic optimism bias, with models overestimating causal links and precision falling across the board.
AI.motivation: Although LLMs are explored as causal reasoners, the precise conditions under which their causal discovery fails were not mapped.
AI.method: A stress-test framework varies model scale, causal graph complexity, prompting strategy, metadata quality, data quality and sensitivity to uncertainty, and compares evaluation metrics with and without uncertainty integrated.
AI.result: Models consistently overestimate causal links, giving low precision across the board; reasoning-heavy models lead on traditional metrics, but their highest scores often occur when uncertainty is overlooked, and performance drops once uncertainty is integrated; scaling model size helps, but gains degrade sharply as metadata quality decreases.
AI.conclusion: LLM causal discovery needs uncertainty-aware evaluation and attention to metadata quality before it is used in a causal discovery pipeline.

title: Does the Trust Boundary Hold over Time? A Long-Horizon Benchmark for Receiver-Directed Federated Learning
comment: 8 pages, 2 figures, 7 tables. Code: this https URL (available upon acceptance)
summary: In receiver-directed federated learning, each site draws a trust boundary. For every source and model component it judges, on its own data, whether the transfer helps (admit), harms (reject) or cannot yet be told (abstain). We ask whether this boundary holds over hundreds of rounds. Our benchmark has a federation of thirteen semi-synthetic sites, an exact oracle for every evaluated transfer, paired seeds, an attack protocol, fourteen methods over 600 rounds and Qwen3-1.7B LoRA sites over 500. The answer depends on which boundary is measured. Across 20 paired CPU seeds, a gate judging against a fixed reference better identified transfers useful relative to the site's starting model. Yet it admitted 29% of transfers harmful to the model the site now has. A gate judging against the current model admitted 2% of harmful transfers on that target in the CPU tier, but missed many transfers useful to the starting model. Two short propositions explain these distinct failures. We also evaluate a held out audit that leaves gate verdicts intact. After training, it decides whether each final model is deployed or the site falls back to local training, and reports admissions that have gone stale. With independent audit data its guarantees hold after any training history. At 600 rounds the audit deployed 65 to 72% of models, none with negative benefit on its target, and kept 98% of the gain. No stale report had the wrong sign in our runs. With 20,000 audit observations, a variance-adaptive bound found 99% of stale transfers that cost at least 0.01 in log loss. A common-target Qwen3 comparison on 60 selected transfers shows the same tension over 100 rounds. With 38% adversarial sites, FedFomo and CS-Gate were the only evaluated methods with positive mean gain in every honest group.

AI.tldr: The paper benchmarks receiver-directed federated learning over 600 rounds, showing that a trust gate judging against a fixed reference and one judging against the current model fail in different ways, and proposes a held-out audit that decides deployment.
AI.motivation: In receiver-directed federated learning each site decides which transfers to admit, reject or abstain on, and it is unknown whether this trust boundary holds over hundreds of rounds.
AI.method: A federation of thirteen semi-synthetic sites with an exact oracle for every transfer, paired seeds, an attack protocol and fourteen methods over 600 rounds, plus Qwen3-1.7B LoRA sites over 500 rounds; a held-out audit leaves gate verdicts intact and decides whether each final model is deployed or the site falls back to local training.
AI.result: A gate judging against a fixed reference identified transfers useful to the starting model but admitted 29% of transfers harmful to the current model; a gate judging against the current model admitted 2% of harmful transfers but missed many useful ones; the audit deployed 65% to 72% of models at 600 rounds, none with negative benefit on its target, and kept 98% of the gain; with 38% adversarial sites, FedFomo and CS-Gate were the only evaluated methods with positive mean gain in every honest group.
AI.conclusion: The trust boundary depends on which boundary is measured, and an independent held-out audit is needed to keep admissions from going stale.

title: Auditing a Model-Hub Benchmark: Data Quality, Training Budgets, and Side Information in HuggingBench
comment: 12 pages, 10 tables, 2 figures. Code and data: this https URL
summary: Benchmarks built from model hubs combine interaction data, knowledge graphs (KGs) and resource documentation, but valid files do not ensure that these artifacts describe the same objects. Treating the release as a data product, we audit HuggingBench (SIGIR 2025), a benchmark for recommending Hugging Face resources, through data validation, a replication of its eleven recommendation methods and controlled experiments with three training seeds. In three of its four external KGs, the files pass key and range checks but violate the item-entity identity constraint on which KG recommenders rely. Correcting this join improves every KG-based method in every seed, by up to 73% in mean Recall@10, and consistently reverses ten of 27 comparisons between KG configurations. The protocol matters as well: the 100-epoch budget ends before early stopping in seven to eight of 29 validation-selected settings, and 21 of 23 such setting-seed pairs improve with a longer budget. The released item text, which no reported method uses, is the strongest signal: closed-form linear models with text and the item graph exceed the best reported Recall@10 by 18% while fitting in minutes on a CPU. Checks of other recommendation releases show that individually valid releases of one dataset can use incompatible identifiers. We release corrected files, mappings, validators and logs, and derive practices for preserving identity and provenance across the artifacts of benchmarks and model lakes.

AI.tldr: The paper audits the HuggingBench model-hub recommendation benchmark and finds that identifier mismatches between item text, knowledge graphs and interaction data distort results, and that correcting them changes method rankings.
AI.motivation: Benchmarks built from model hubs combine interaction data, knowledge graphs and documentation, but individually valid files may not describe the same objects.
AI.method: The authors audit HuggingBench through data validation, a replication of its eleven recommendation methods and controlled experiments with three training seeds, and check other recommendation releases for identifier compatibility.
AI.result: In three of four external KGs the files pass key and range checks but violate the item-entity identity constraint; correcting the join improves every KG-based method in every seed, by up to 73% in mean Recall@10, and reverses ten of 27 comparisons between KG configurations; 21 of 23 setting-seed pairs improve with a longer than 100-epoch budget; closed-form linear models with text and the item graph exceed the best reported Recall@10 by 18%.
AI.conclusion: Benchmarks should preserve identity and provenance across their artifacts, and the released item text is the strongest signal among those the audit examined.

title: SSPE: Robust Sequential Staypoint Extraction in Degraded Trajectory Data
summary: Extracting semantically meaningful staypoints from raw trajectory streams is a foundational prerequisite for mobility analytics. However, real-world trajectory data is frequently degraded by severe spatial noise and protracted temporal dropouts. Classic threshold-based extraction methods, such as the widely adopted sliding-window algorithm, are highly sensitive to these anomalies, routinely fracturing continuous stationary episodes into disjointed fragments. To overcome this limitation, we propose the Sequential Staypoint Extraction (SSPE) algorithm. SSPE employs a resilient, state-driven architecture that replaces static spatial anchors with a dynamic centroid and introduces an $n$-step lookahead heuristic to structurally tolerate transient coordinate drift. Concurrently, it utilizes temporal bridging mechanisms to prevent artificial fragmentation during prolonged signal loss. Since optimal extraction parameters vary significantly across datasets, we further introduce a fully unsupervised, consensus-based parameter estimation framework. This framework derives baseline statistical scales directly from the raw trajectory data and identifies the optimal parameter configuration by maximizing structural agreement, thereby eliminating the reliance on annotated ground truth. We evaluate SSPE on the ExtraSensory dataset, a real-world mobility corpus with manually verified ground-truth staypoints, against the sliding-window implementation of Trackintel, one of the most widely adopted extraction baselines in the field. Empirical results demonstrate that SSPE achieves superior accuracy, yielding higher F1-scores while simultaneously improving computational efficiency over this standard.

AI.tldr: SSPE is a state-driven staypoint extraction algorithm for degraded trajectory data that uses a dynamic centroid, n-step lookahead and temporal bridging, with consensus-based unsupervised parameter estimation, and outperforms the Trackintel sliding-window baseline on ExtraSensory.
AI.motivation: Classic threshold-based methods such as the sliding-window algorithm fracture continuous stationary episodes when trajectories have spatial noise and temporal dropouts.
AI.method: SSPE replaces static spatial anchors with a dynamic centroid, uses an n-step lookahead to tolerate transient drift, applies temporal bridging across signal loss, and selects parameters by maximizing structural agreement, with scales derived from the raw data and no annotated ground truth.
AI.result: Evaluated on ExtraSensory against the sliding-window implementation of Trackintel, SSPE yields higher F1-scores and improves computational efficiency.
AI.conclusion: SSPE gives more accurate and faster staypoint extraction than a widely used baseline on degraded trajectories without requiring labels for parameter tuning.

title: CaRe-KT: Continuity-Aware Retrieval-Augmented Reasoning for Knowledge Tracing
summary: Knowledge tracing (KT) estimates learners' evolving knowledge states from interaction histories to support adaptive learning. Retrieval-augmented KT improves these estimates using cross-learner behavioral evidence, but existing approaches typically separate evidence retrieval from downstream prediction. This creates a retrieval-inference alignment gap because evidence relevance varies with the learner's evolving state and prediction context. We propose CaRe-KT, a query-adaptive framework that maintains relevance continuity between evidence acquisition and inference without equating retrieval relevance with predictive utility. CaRe-KT introduces an Evidence-Graph Cache (EGC) that combines persistent question-level relational compatibility with interaction-level temporal validity to construct query-specific evidence subgraphs. Historical learning trajectories retrieved through these subgraphs are encoded alongside the target learner's history in a shared representation space using outcome-supervised contrastive learning. An attention mechanism combines acquisition relevance with learned query-evidence compatibility, allowing relevance to inform, rather than determine, each trajectory's predictive influence. Experiments across five benchmarks show that CaRe-KT outperforms strong KT baselines and remains robust under sparse-history and cold-start conditions. These findings support relevance continuity as a design principle for retrieval-augmented knowledge tracing.

AI.tldr: CaRe-KT is a retrieval-augmented knowledge tracing framework that keeps retrieved evidence consistent with prediction by using an evidence-graph cache and attention that weighs acquisition relevance against learned compatibility.
AI.motivation: Existing retrieval-augmented knowledge tracing methods separate evidence retrieval from prediction, creating an alignment gap because evidence relevance depends on the learner's evolving state and prediction context.
AI.method: CaRe-KT introduces an Evidence-Graph Cache combining persistent question-level compatibility with interaction-level temporal validity to build query-specific evidence subgraphs; retrieved trajectories are encoded with the target history in a shared space via outcome-supervised contrastive learning, and an attention mechanism combines acquisition relevance with learned query-evidence compatibility.
AI.result: CaRe-KT outperforms strong knowledge tracing baselines across five benchmarks and remains robust under sparse-history and cold-start conditions.
AI.conclusion: Relevance continuity between evidence acquisition and inference is a useful design principle for retrieval-augmented knowledge tracing.

title: Honest Small Decision Models for Finance: Scale, Specialization Collapse, and Mixed-Corpus Remediation
comment: ICAIF 2026: The 3rd Workshop on LLMs and Generative AI for Finance
summary: Financial workflows need fast, calibrated, auditable decisions, not just generated text. We train System-1 decision models, small language models fine-tuned to answer typed questions (choice/score/noul) with a probability in a single forward pass, across two model families (K2-Horizon and Qwen3.5/3.8) and nine rungs from 0.8B to 32B parameters, using one frozen LoRA recipe on a public decision benchmark and two new finance corpora: a programmatic-gold policy corpus (rule-reading with exact labels) and a reality-labeled outcome corpus (19,640 realized forward-return questions in walk-forward splits, plus a sealed 2026 test of 1,360 questions). Narrow fine-tuning costs general decision competence 9-45 percentage points, a data-mixture effect that shrinks with model scale and is associated with narrow-gradient volume. On reality-labeled questions, every trained rung from 0.8B to 32B lands at the horizon-conditioned prior baseline (accuracy 0.37-0.38, no detectable conditional edge under our controls); the models respond with flat, well-calibrated probabilities that track per-horizon base rates: naturally honest uncertainty, with a mid-scale calibration sweet spot (ECE 0.026 at 2B, degrading to 0.043-0.044 at 9-32B under prior drift). A mixed-corpus remediation carries all competencies in one adapter at modest cost: it matches or slightly exceeds the generalist specialist on the public benchmark while holding the policy ceiling and near-specialist outcome calibration, yielding a deployable artifact with per-domain temperature regimes and a band-dispatch escalation analysis: sharp, dispatchable bands where rules determine answers; flat, review-routing bands where reality does not.

AI.tldr: The paper trains small finance decision models (0.8B to 32B parameters) on typed questions and finds that on reality-labeled forward-return questions every trained model stays at the horizon-conditioned prior baseline, while its probabilities are well calibrated. A mixed-corpus adapter keeps several competencies in one deployable model.
AI.motivation: Financial workflows need fast, calibrated and auditable decisions, but narrow fine-tuning can erode general decision competence and it is unclear whether fine-tuned small models add real predictive edge on outcome data.
AI.method: System-1 decision models are small language models fine-tuned with one frozen LoRA recipe to answer choice, score and noul questions with a probability in a single forward pass, across two model families and nine sizes from 0.8B to 32B. Training uses a public decision benchmark, a programmatic-gold policy corpus and a reality-labeled outcome corpus of 19,640 walk-forward forward-return questions with a sealed 2026 test of 1,360 questions; a mixed-corpus remediation trains a single adapter on all competencies and a band-dispatch escalation analysis is added.
AI.result: Narrow fine-tuning costs general decision competence by 9 to 45 percentage points, an effect that shrinks with scale. On reality-labeled questions every trained rung from 0.8B to 32B reaches accuracy 0.37 to 0.38, the horizon-conditioned prior baseline, with no detectable conditional edge; calibration error (ECE) is 0.026 at 2B and 0.043 to 0.044 at 9B to 32B. The mixed-corpus adapter matches or slightly exceeds the generalist specialist on the public benchmark while holding policy ceiling and near-specialist outcome calibration.
AI.conclusion: Small fine-tuned models give honest, flat and well-calibrated uncertainty where outcomes are unpredictable, so the deployable artifact routes sharp rule-determined decisions automatically and sends unpredictable cases to human review.

title: Language Models Can Benefit from Domain-Specific Inductive Biases
comment: 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Position Paper Track
summary: Language models are typically trained with a single choice of architecture on diverse domains and data sources. Modern transformers have been extensively refined for such general-purpose learning, but are they equally effective across different subsets of the pretraining data? We investigate this question by training small language models from scratch on representative subsets of pretraining data such as web text, code, and mathematics. We introduce variants of transformers in which standard activation functions are replaced with learned splines tuned on specific datasets, providing a simple way to modify their inductive biases. Using a mix-and-match of architectures and datasets, we evaluate cross-domain transfer, i.e. how well does an architecture tuned for one domain perform on data from another? We find that the tuned transformer variants improve training efficiency or generalization on all seven of our tested datasets, but the gains are often domain-specific. For example, architectures tuned on a natural language dataset such as FineWeb perform well on TinyStories, whereas those tuned on mathematics perform poorly on natural language. We identify several mechanisms underlying these improvements, including wider loss basins and more abundant "lottery tickets". Our results show that different subsets of pretraining data can benefit from different learning mechanisms, highlighting a limitation of the prevailing trend towards a small set of general-purpose architectures and optimizers. This points to an opportunity to improve data efficiency by developing domain-specific learning strategies that retain the ability to train general-purpose models.

AI.tldr: The paper trains small language models from scratch on individual pretraining data domains with transformer variants whose activation functions are replaced by learned splines, and finds that the gains are domain-specific. Architectures tuned on one domain often transfer poorly to others.
AI.motivation: Language models are usually trained with one general-purpose architecture on all data, and it is unknown whether such architectures are equally effective across different subsets of the pretraining data.
AI.method: Small transformers are trained from scratch on subsets such as web text, code and mathematics. Standard activation functions are replaced by learned splines tuned on specific datasets, and architectures and datasets are mixed and matched to measure cross-domain transfer.
AI.result: The tuned variants improve training efficiency or generalization on all seven tested datasets, but the gains are often domain-specific. For example, a spline architecture tuned on FineWeb performs well on TinyStories, while one tuned on mathematics performs poorly on natural language. The improvements are associated with wider loss basins and more abundant lottery tickets.
AI.conclusion: Different pretraining subsets benefit from different learning mechanisms, which suggests that a small set of general-purpose architectures may leave data efficiency on the table and that domain-specific learning strategies are worth developing.

title: Quantifying out-of-distribution data severity with Wasserstein distances: benchmarking large language models for alloy property prediction
summary: As general-purpose Large Language Models (LLMs), such as Gemini and DeepSeek, exhibit increasingly advanced reasoning capabilities, a critical question arises: how do their property prediction abilities compare to those of domain-specific pretrained materials models? In this study, we evaluate predictions for Ti, steels, high-entropy alloy (HEA) and Al, demonstrating that general-purpose LLMs surprisingly outperform SteelBERT, MatSciBERT, and SciBERT. To further enhance performance, we introduce a hybrid approach that utilizes numerical priors from a prior model, such as CatBoost or SteelBERT, to guide the general LLMs (Deepseek V3.1, Gemini-2.5-Flash). By inputting these initial estimates from a prior model as prompts, the LLM acts as a reasoning corrector, achieving accuracy superior to the prior model and "unguided mode". Furthermore, we investigate the impact of data strategy using a similarity-based metric, revealing that data quality dominates quantity; using merely 5% of high-similarity reference data of training set as input yields performance similar to the results of using 100% of training set. Additionally, the LLMs demonstrate excellent uncertainty calibration, where self-reported "high" confidence strongly correlates with minimal deviation from ground truth. Our findings suggest that synergizing general-purpose LLMs with prior model numerical baselines and high-quality data curation creates a cost-effective and accurate paradigm for materials discovery, reducing the need for expensive domain-specific pretraining.

AI.tldr: The paper benchmarks general-purpose LLMs against materials-specific pretrained models for alloy property prediction and shows that LLMs can act as reasoning correctors over numerical priors from a prior model. Using only 5% of high-similarity training data gives performance similar to the full training set.
AI.motivation: It is unclear how general-purpose LLMs compare with domain-specific pretrained materials models for property prediction, and how much training data is needed for accurate predictions.
AI.method: Property predictions are evaluated for Ti, steels, high-entropy alloys and Al, comparing SteelBERT, MatSciBERT and SciBERT with general LLMs such as DeepSeek V3.1 and Gemini-2.5-Flash. A hybrid approach feeds numerical estimates from a prior model (CatBoost or SteelBERT) into the LLM as prompts, and a similarity-based metric is used to select reference data.
AI.result: General-purpose LLMs surprisingly outperform SteelBERT, MatSciBERT and SciBERT. The guided hybrid mode is more accurate than the prior model and the unguided mode. Using 5% of high-similarity reference data yields performance similar to 100% of the training set. The LLMs show good uncertainty calibration, with self-reported high confidence correlating with small deviation from ground truth.
AI.conclusion: Combining general LLMs with numerical baselines from prior models and careful data curation offers a cost-effective route to materials property prediction that reduces the need for expensive domain-specific pretraining.

title: Probabilistic Steering of Generative Priors for Lab-in-the-Loop Antibody Optimization
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS `26 GEM and NeurIPS `26 AI4DD
summary: Therapeutic antibody development is often framed as comprising two discrete stages: initial discovery of novel binders followed by iterative optimization to refine these hits into therapeutic-grade molecules. Models and methods often reflect these stages, with generative structure models applied to discovery and probabilistic black-box optimization methods applied to refinement. Here we propose to unify these stages by smoothly transitioning a generative discovery model into iterative optimization, allowing the handoff between the structure-based prior and supervision from wet lab data to be guided by the posterior uncertainty of a probabilistic surrogate. We show that this yields improvements in optimization efficiency in the low-N regime, as well as improved diversity amongst the optimized molecules.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a single framework that moves a generative structure-based discovery model smoothly into iterative optimization, with handoff governed by the posterior uncertainty of a probabilistic surrogate. It reports better optimization efficiency in the low-data regime and more diverse optimized molecules.
AI.motivation: Antibody development separates discovery with generative structure models from refinement with probabilistic black-box optimization, and the two stages are not unified.
AI.method: A generative discovery model is transitioned into iterative optimization. The handoff between the structure-based prior and supervision from wet-lab data is guided by the posterior uncertainty of a probabilistic surrogate model.
AI.result: The approach improves optimization efficiency in the low-N regime and yields improved diversity among the optimized molecules.
AI.conclusion: Unifying discovery and optimization in one lab-in-the-loop process is a practical way to use both structure priors and wet-lab feedback in therapeutic antibody development.

title: Dr. No: Feature Steering for Abstention in Vision-Language Models
summary: Large foundation models often answer even when the available visual or textual evidence is insufficient to support a reliable conclusion. This failure to abstain makes them hard to trust in high-stakes or information-seeking settings, where a confident but unsupported answer can be worse than no answer at all. It also raises a natural question: can the internal mechanisms behind this behaviour be identified and controlled at inference time? We present Dr. No, a feature-steering approach that mines sparse autoencoder (SAE) features associated with abstention and commitment, then modulates a small set of them during the prefill pass, without retraining the base model. Dr. No is evaluated on LLaVA-1.6 Mistral 7B across multimodal abstention benchmarks, including UNK-VQA and MM-UPD, and additionally benchmarked on language reasoning tasks using Qwen3.5-2B on AbstentionBench subsets. Against multiple uncertainty-based abstention baselines, feature steering achieves a more favourable balance between correct answering and appropriate abstention than post-hoc rejection methods. The gains are strongest on UNK-VQA and on MM-UPD cases involving image--question or question--answer incompatibility, and transfer most clearly to mathematical reasoning subsets of AbstentionBench. However, performance is more limited on absent-answer detection and retrieval-heavy multi-hop QA, such as MuSiQue. These results suggest that sparse internal features provide lightweight control handles for shaping uncertainty-aware behaviour in foundation models, while also showing that abstention control is source-dependent rather than governed by a single universal signal.

AI.tldr: Dr. No steers sparse autoencoder features at inference time, during the prefill pass, to make vision-language and language models abstain when evidence is insufficient. It gives a better trade-off between answering and abstaining than post-hoc rejection, though gains depend on the source of uncertainty.
AI.motivation: Foundation models often answer even when the evidence is insufficient, and existing uncertainty-based abstention methods are post-hoc and do not expose internal control handles.
AI.method: SAE features associated with abstention and commitment are mined and a small set is modulated during the prefill pass, without retraining. It is evaluated on LLaVA-1.6 Mistral 7B for UNK-VQA and MM-UPD, and on Qwen3.5-2B for AbstentionBench subsets.
AI.result: Feature steering gives a more favourable balance between correct answers and appropriate abstention than multiple uncertainty-based baselines and post-hoc rejection. Gains are strongest on UNK-VQA and on MM-UPD incompatibility cases, and transfer most clearly to mathematical reasoning subsets of AbstentionBench. Performance is weaker on absent-answer detection and on multi-hop QA such as MuSiQue.
AI.conclusion: Sparse internal features provide lightweight control handles for uncertainty-aware behaviour, but abstention control is source-dependent rather than governed by a single universal signal.

title: ExaTune: Exhaustive Hyperparameter Landscape Exploration at Scale
summary: Hyperparameter optimization (HPO) returns a single optimal configuration, systematically discarding the explored performance landscape that encodes how results depend on configuration choices. Fitness landscape analysis comprises a robust collection of methods from evolutionary computation offering ruggedness indices, autocorrelation functions, and fitness-distance correlation that have never been applied to machine learning hyperparameter spaces at scale, given that fine-grained ground-truth enumeration data has not existed. We present ExaTune, an open-source HPC system to produce a new artifact class: the hyperparameter landscape map. ExaTune exhaustively evaluates every point on a discretized hyperparameter grid via $K$-fold cross-validation, aggregates results into reproducible parquet benchmarks, and applies a suite of five formalized landscape metrics: spatial autocorrelation (Moran's $I$), ruggedness, local optima density, fitness-distance correlation (FDC), and variance-based parameter importance. We release a benchmark collection of 8 complete landscape maps (totalling 285,080 exhaustively evaluated configurations) spanning five model families (SVMs, random forests, XGBoost, ridge regression, and $k$-nearest neighbors) across six classification and two regression benchmarks, hosted on HuggingFace. Empirical analysis demonstrates that Bayesian optimization, Optuna, Hyperband, and Random Search at standard trial budgets systematically miss instability regions, secondary optima, and parameter interaction effects that are visible in complete landscapes; information that is structurally unavailable to any optimizer by design.

AI.tldr: ExaTune exhaustively evaluates discretized hyperparameter grids with K-fold cross-validation to build complete landscape maps and applies fitness landscape metrics to them. It releases 8 maps covering 285,080 configurations and shows that standard optimizers miss instability regions, secondary optima and parameter interactions.
AI.motivation: Hyperparameter optimization returns only a single best configuration and discards the performance landscape, and fitness landscape analysis has not been applied to ML hyperparameter spaces at scale because complete ground-truth enumerations did not exist.
AI.method: An open-source HPC system exhaustively evaluates every point of a discretized hyperparameter grid with K-fold cross-validation, stores results as parquet benchmarks and computes five landscape metrics: Moran's I, ruggedness, local optima density, fitness-distance correlation and variance-based parameter importance.
AI.result: The release contains 8 complete landscape maps (285,080 configurations) over five model families (SVMs, random forests, XGBoost, ridge regression and k-nearest neighbors) and eight classification and regression benchmarks, hosted on HuggingFace. Bayesian optimization, Optuna, Hyperband and random search at standard budgets systematically miss features visible in the complete landscapes.
AI.conclusion: Hyperparameter landscape maps are a new artifact class, and the information they reveal is structurally unavailable to any optimizer that samples a limited budget.

title: Embedding Semantic Entropy: NLI-Free Semantic Uncertainty Estimation with Geometry-Aware Clustering
comment: Large Language Models; Uncertainty Quantification; Semantic Entropy; Clus- tering; K-Medoids; Hallucination Detection
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) often generate fluent yet incorrect responses, making un- certainty estimation important for reliable deployment. Semantic Entropy (SE) estimates uncertainty by clustering responses based on semantic equivalence, but it relies on hard entailment-based clustering. We propose Embedding Semantic Entropy, which replaces entailment-based clustering with K-Medoids in semantic embedding space and uses dynamic cluster selection to account for intra-cluster compactness and inter-cluster separation. We evaluate the method on TriviaQA, SQuAD, NQ-Open, SVAMP, and BioASQ using Falcon- 7B-Instruct, LLaMA-2-7B, LLaMA-2-7B-Chat, and Gemma-7B. Results show competitive AUROC and AUARC performance, suggesting that NLI-based entailment clustering can be replaced with embedding-space clustering with limited degradation while improving the inspectability of semantic grouping. This matters because semantic uncertainty scores depend on underlying semantic groups; by making these groups explicit, compact, and separable in embedding space, Emb-SE turns uncertainty estimation from a black-box en- tailment decision into an inspectable clustering problem.

AI.tldr: Embedding Semantic Entropy replaces entailment-based clustering in semantic entropy with K-Medoids clustering in an embedding space, using dynamic cluster selection, and removes the need for an NLI model. It achieves competitive AUROC and AUARC on five QA and math datasets.
AI.motivation: Semantic entropy measures LLM uncertainty by clustering responses by meaning, but it relies on hard entailment-based clustering that is a black box.
AI.method: Responses are clustered with K-Medoids in a semantic embedding space, and dynamic cluster selection accounts for intra-cluster compactness and inter-cluster separation. It is evaluated on TriviaQA, SQuAD, NQ-Open, SVAMP and BioASQ with Falcon-7B-Instruct, LLaMA-2-7B, LLaMA-2-7B-Chat and Gemma-7B.
AI.result: The method gives competitive AUROC and AUARC, with limited degradation relative to entailment-based clustering.
AI.conclusion: Entailment clustering can be replaced by embedding-space clustering, which makes semantic groups explicit and inspectable at a limited cost in performance.

title: The Information Limits of Neural Controlled Differential Equations Under Sparse Observations
comment: Preliminary version. Further theoretical extensions are under development
summary: Neural controlled differential equations (Neural CDEs) evolve hidden states along continuous paths constructed by interpolating discrete observations. Sparse measurements leave the input between observation times undetermined, and admissible continuous paths consistent with the same data can produce different terminal states. We characterize this ambiguity for planar drivers with bounded speed. The set of compatible terminal states admits a leading-order zonotopic approximation determined by feasible signed areas and transported Lie brackets. Its projection onto a scalar prediction yields a computable, target-specific ambiguity certificate. We also study the number of measurements needed to reduce the remaining uncertainty. For nondegenerate planar CDEs, the optimal worst-case radius over deterministic adaptive sampling policies scales as $N^{-1}$ when speed is bounded and $N^{-2}$ when both speed and acceleration are bounded, where $N$ is the number of observation intervals. Synthetic experiments assess the certificate using admissible continuous completions and examine the role of path regularity.

AI.tldr: The paper characterizes how much sparse observations leave a neural CDE's terminal state undetermined for planar drivers with bounded speed. It gives a computable ambiguity certificate and shows that the optimal worst-case radius scales as N^-1 with bounded speed and N^-2 with bounded speed and acceleration.
AI.motivation: Neural CDEs interpolate sparse discrete observations into continuous paths, but many admissible paths consistent with the same data can yield different terminal states, and the uncertainty this creates was not characterized.
AI.method: The set of compatible terminal states is approximated to leading order by a zonotope determined by feasible signed areas and transported Lie brackets. Its projection onto a scalar prediction gives a target-specific ambiguity certificate, and the number of measurements needed is analysed over deterministic adaptive sampling policies.
AI.result: For nondegenerate planar CDEs the optimal worst-case radius scales as N^-1 when speed is bounded and as N^-2 when speed and acceleration are both bounded, where N is the number of observation intervals. Synthetic experiments check the certificate with admissible completions.
AI.conclusion: The ambiguity from sparse sampling can be certified and reduced at a rate set by path regularity, which gives guidance on how many measurements are needed.

title: When Latent Dynamics Meet Data Assimilation: A Benchmark of Koopman-Type Representations
summary: Koopman representations describe nonlinear dynamics through linear evolution in a transformed space, offering an attractive framework for their linear simplicity and generality. Yet these advantages do not necessarily translate into improved performance in deep latent data assimilation (LDA). We systematically compare seven representative methods and structural baselines across five systems spanning approximately periodic to strongly chaotic dynamics and a broad range of state dimensions. We evaluate forecast and assimilation accuracy, physical state recovery, latent-trajectory behavior, and dynamical consistency, and assess Gaussian error assumptions, objective convexity, and uniqueness of analysis solutions. Our results reveal a trade-off between representational flexibility and optimization tractability. Linear evolution of the latent state can stabilize short-term forecasts but restrict expressiveness in strongly chaotic and high-dimensional systems, without consistently improving assimilation accuracy. Parameterized linear operators offer greater flexibility, yet their joint optimization with the encoder--decoder remains nonconvex. Methods with closed-form analysis updates generally perform better and exhibit greater robustness in our experiments, although matrix inversion remains a computational bottleneck. These findings show that the practical benefits of Koopman structure depend on both sufficient observational information and the choice of assimilation procedure.

AI.tldr: The paper benchmarks seven Koopman-type latent representations in deep latent data assimilation across five dynamical systems. It finds that linear latent evolution does not reliably improve assimilation accuracy, and that methods with closed-form analysis updates perform best.
AI.motivation: Koopman representations promise linear simplicity for nonlinear dynamics, but it is unclear whether this helps in deep latent data assimilation.
AI.method: Seven representative methods and structural baselines are compared on five systems ranging from approximately periodic to strongly chaotic, across a range of state dimensions. Forecast and assimilation accuracy, physical state recovery, latent-trajectory behaviour and dynamical consistency are evaluated, along with Gaussian error assumptions, objective convexity and uniqueness of the analysis solution.
AI.result: Linear latent evolution can stabilize short-term forecasts but restricts expressiveness on strongly chaotic and high-dimensional systems without consistently improving assimilation. Parameterized linear operators are more flexible but their joint optimization with the encoder-decoder is nonconvex. Methods with closed-form analysis updates generally perform better and are more robust, although matrix inversion is a computational bottleneck.
AI.conclusion: The benefit of Koopman structure depends on sufficient observational information and on the choice of assimilation procedure, reflecting a trade-off between representational flexibility and optimization tractability.

title: Sequential auditing of connected forecast errors under partial observations
summary: Graph forecasting systems often rely on prediction intervals to quantify uncertainty across connected locations, but the true outcomes needed for evaluation may be only partially observed. We study how an auditor can selectively retrieve missing outcomes to determine whether there exists a connected group whose outcomes violate the same side of their respective forecast intervals. The audit stops when the observed labels determine the event or the query budget is exhausted. On three public graph time series, MOMS reduces mean queries by 19.6% to 38.5% relative to screened random acquisition when 30% of labels are hidden. Under localized masking on METR-LA, shortest witness finds more positive cases within ten queries, although the difference depends on node ordering. Direct component traversal reproduces all 9,696 screened random traces without enumerating connected subsets. The experiments show that reducing queries to a decision does not necessarily improve early event discovery or reduce local computation.

AI.tldr: The paper studies auditing of connected forecast-interval violations on graphs when outcomes are partly hidden, and proposes an adaptive query policy. On three public graph time series the MOMS policy reduces mean queries by 19.6% to 38.5% relative to screened random acquisition with 30% of labels hidden.
AI.motivation: Graph forecasting systems report prediction intervals, but the true outcomes needed to check them may be only partly observed, and an auditor needs to decide cheaply whether a connected group violates its intervals.
AI.method: The auditor adaptively retrieves missing outcomes until observed labels determine the event or the query budget runs out. MOMS is compared with screened random acquisition, with a shortest-witness strategy under localized masking on METR-LA, and with direct component traversal that avoids enumerating connected subsets.
AI.result: MOMS reduces mean queries by 19.6% to 38.5% when 30% of labels are hidden. Shortest witness finds more positive cases within ten queries on METR-LA, though the difference depends on node ordering. Direct traversal reproduces all 9,696 screened random traces.
AI.conclusion: Reducing the number of queries needed to reach a decision does not necessarily improve early event discovery or reduce local computation, so these objectives must be assessed separately.

title: Accelerating FastDEC Clustering Algorithm with GPUs
summary: Fast Dominance Estimation Clustering (FastDEC) is an efficient variant of Density Peak Clustering (DPC) that achieves high clustering quality through dominance-based density estimation, but remains constrained by the computational cost of exact k-nearest-neighbor (k-NN) construction and dominance component (DC) processing. We present SymWarp-FastDEC, a GPU-accelerated implementation of FastDEC. At its core is SymTrikNN, an exact self-k-NN kernel that exploits search symmetry using upper-triangular traversal and warp-cooperative top-k selection. We also introduce WP-DC, a warp-parallel DC reduction algorithm designed for modern GPUs. Combined with memory-adaptive execution planning and stream scheduling, WP-DC eliminates DC reduction as a runtime bottleneck. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show that SymWarp-FastDEC produces clustering outputs identical to the original FastDEC on all evaluated equivalence benchmarks. Compared with a FastDEC variant using FAISS GpuIndexFlatL2 for exact k-NN search, our approach achieves approximately 1.7x to 4.9x higher end-to-end performance, with the advantage generally increasing with dimensionality. Compared with the original single-threaded Python FastDEC implementation, speedups reach approximately 2.5 x 10^4 in a very high-dimensional case where its k-d-tree-based search degrades; this extreme result is not representative of typical acceleration.

AI.tldr: SymWarp-FastDEC is a GPU implementation of the FastDEC density peak clustering algorithm that uses an exact symmetric k-NN kernel and a warp-parallel dominance component reduction. It produces identical clustering outputs and runs 1.7x to 4.9x faster than a FAISS GPU baseline.
AI.motivation: FastDEC is efficient but its exact k-NN construction and dominance component processing remain costly, which limits its scalability.
AI.method: SymTrikNN is an exact self-k-NN kernel that uses upper-triangular traversal and warp-cooperative top-k selection. WP-DC is a warp-parallel dominance component reduction, combined with memory-adaptive execution planning and stream scheduling.
AI.result: Outputs are identical to the original FastDEC on all evaluated equivalence benchmarks. End-to-end speedups over a FastDEC variant using FAISS GpuIndexFlatL2 are about 1.7x to 4.9x, growing with dimensionality. Speedups over the single-threaded Python FastDEC reach about 2.5 x 10^4 in one very high-dimensional case, which the abstract describes as not representative.
AI.conclusion: The GPU design removes the dominance component reduction as a runtime bottleneck while keeping exact clustering results, and the typical gains are substantial but much smaller than the extreme case.

title: Forget What Comes Next: LLM Unlearning via Statistical Independence
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can memorize and reproduce fragments of their training data, raising privacy and legal concerns that motivate machine unlearning. Yet poisoned training examples can remain statistically detectable after unlearning, which raises the question of whether current unlearning objectives remove what the model has memorized at all. In this work, we introduce PINT, a novel algorithm for machine unlearning that uses the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC) to reduce the statistical dependence between tokens to be forgotten and the internal representations used to predict them. We formally relate our HSIC-based objective to Exact Memorization through a computable upper bound, connecting the training objective directly to the model's ability to reproduce the forgotten tokens. In extensive experiments, we compare forgetting-utility trade-offs across eight settings with models up to 7B parameters and demonstrate scalability to 70B parameter models. Our evaluations cover unlearning Gaussian poisons, personal information, hazardous knowledge in biology and cybersecurity, and copyrighted books and news articles. PINT achieves the strongest forgetting-utility trade-off on average and is the only method to make Gaussian poisons undetectable while maintaining near-original model utility. Code is available at: this https URL

AI.tldr: PINT is an unlearning method that minimizes HSIC-based statistical dependence between the tokens to forget and the representations used to predict them. It removes the detectability of Gaussian poisons while keeping near-original utility and scales to 70B models.
AI.motivation: Poisoned examples can remain statistically detectable after unlearning, which suggests that current unlearning objectives may not remove what the model memorized.
AI.method: The Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion is used to reduce dependence between forget tokens and internal representations, and a computable upper bound links this objective to Exact Memorization. Eight settings with models up to 7B and a 70B scale-up cover Gaussian poisons, personal information, hazardous biology and cybersecurity knowledge, and copyrighted books and news.
AI.result: PINT gives the strongest average forgetting-utility trade-off and is the only method that makes Gaussian poisons undetectable while maintaining near-original utility.
AI.conclusion: Dependence-based unlearning objectives can remove memorized content more thoroughly than standard approaches, and the bound connects the training objective directly to reproduction of forgotten tokens.

title: Sampling Interventional Distributions with Orthogonal MMD Flow
summary: Many causal inference problems require sampling from interventional outcome distributions rather than estimating low-dimensional summaries. Existing approaches often rely on fitting generative models of the target distribution together with additional nuisance components, which can be computationally demanding for high-dimensional outcomes.
