summary: Machine unlearning aims to erase the influence of a designated forget set from a trained model while preserving strong utility on the retain set. Approximate unlearning methods efficiently achieve this goal without full retraining, but their effectiveness is primarily assessed using dataset-level aggregate metrics. These aggregate metrics can mask deviations from retraining at the level of individual samples. In this work, we focus on per-sample unlearning effectiveness. We introduce SALA (Sample-grained Likelihoods ALignment), a plug-in optimization framework that enables approximate unlearning methods to operate at the level of individual samples by steering each example toward its correct target distribution. To quantitatively assess this behavior, we further propose the sample-grained distribution gap, a metric that captures per-sample discrepancies between approximate unlearning and exact retraining output distributions. We provide theoretical guarantees showing that SALA contracts this gap and yields a bounded per-sample discrepancy to retraining. To make this framework practical, we develop a low-cost estimation method for the member and non-member target distributions. Extensive experiments on classification and generation tasks demonstrate that SALA reduces the sample-grained distribution gap by up to $86.67\%$ when paired with existing approximate unlearning baselines, while also improving robustness to unlearning hyperparameters.

AI.tldr: SALA is a plug-in optimization framework that steers each forget-set example toward its correct target distribution, so that approximate unlearning can be checked per sample. It reduces the sample-grained distribution gap by up to 86.67% when paired with existing baselines, with theoretical bounds on per-sample discrepancy to retraining.
AI.motivation: Aggregate unlearning metrics can mask deviations from exact retraining at the level of individual samples.
AI.method: A sample-grained distribution gap metric is defined to measure per-sample discrepancy between approximate unlearning and retraining output distributions. SALA aligns sample-level likelihoods to member and non-member target distributions, estimated with a low-cost method, and is tested on classification and generation tasks.
AI.result: SALA contracts the sample-grained distribution gap and yields bounded per-sample discrepancy to retraining, reducing the gap by up to 86.67% when paired with existing approximate unlearning baselines. It also improves robustness to unlearning hyperparameters.
AI.conclusion: Per-sample evaluation and alignment can make approximate unlearning closer to retraining than aggregate metrics indicate.

title: Variational Learning with Lie Group Exponential Families
summary: Variational Bayesian learning for deep neural networks offers many potential benefits. The difficulty in implementation arises from constraints on the parameters of the variational distributions, as well as the need for low-variance gradient estimators. Our recent work proposes Lie group methods for multiplicative or affine groups that naturally overcome such difficulties. Lie groups are essentially parameter spaces with a binary operator such as addition or multiplication, which allows for natural updates within the parameter space. In this article, we streamline and extend our Lie group framework to any general Lie group, and give an explicit relation to standard natural-gradient variational learning methods such as the Bayesian learning rule (BLR). In particular, we prove that linear approximations of the Lie group algorithm give generalizations of the BLR. The key ingredient is the harmonic exponential family, a general class of Lie group exponential families associated to representations of Lie groups. Our work provides a systematic method to construct from such representations efficiently implementable algorithms for variational learning.

AI.tldr: The paper extends Lie group methods for variational learning to general Lie groups and shows that linear approximations of the resulting algorithm generalize the Bayesian learning rule. The key ingredient is the harmonic exponential family associated with group representations.
AI.motivation: Variational Bayesian learning for deep networks is hard to implement because of parameter constraints and high-variance gradient estimators, and earlier Lie group methods were limited to multiplicative or affine groups.
AI.method: The Lie group framework is streamlined and extended to any general Lie group, with an explicit relation to natural-gradient variational methods such as the Bayesian learning rule. The harmonic exponential family, which is associated with representations of Lie groups, gives a systematic construction of implementable algorithms.
AI.result: Linear approximations of the Lie group algorithm are proved to give generalizations of the Bayesian learning rule.
AI.conclusion: Representations of Lie groups provide a systematic way to construct efficiently implementable variational learning algorithms.

title: The Price of List Replicability: Tight Bounds for Bias Estimation
summary: We study the sample complexity of list replicable algorithms for estimating the biases of $d$ coins. An algorithm is $(k,\varepsilon,\delta)$-list replicable if for every bias vector $\mathbf{p}\in[0,1]^d$, there is a set of outputs $L_{\mathbf{p}}\subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ of at most $k$ elements such that every $\mathbf{y}\in L_{\mathbf{p}}$ satisfies $\lVert\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{p}\rVert_\infty\leq\varepsilon$, and the algorithm output is in $L_{\mathbf{p}}$ with probability at least $1-\delta$. Prior work gave a $(d+1,\varepsilon,\delta)$-list replicable algorithm with sample complexity $\widetilde{O}\left(\frac{d^3}{\varepsilon^2}\right)$, but no nontrivial sample complexity lower bound was known. We establish the first non-trivial sample complexity lower bound for this problem and give an improved algorithm that matches it up to polylogarithmic factors. Together, these results determine the optimal sample complexity for list size $d+1$ to be $\widetilde{\Theta}\left(\frac{d^2}{\varepsilon^2}\right)$, showing that the quadratic dependence on dimension is inherent up to polylogarithmic factors. More generally, for every $k\in[d+1,2^d]$, we establish matching upper and lower bounds of $\widetilde{\Theta}\left(\frac{d^2}{\varepsilon^2\log k}\right)$ on the total sample complexity.

AI.tldr: This paper gives the first non-trivial sample complexity lower bound for list replicable bias estimation of d coins and an improved algorithm that matches it up to polylogarithmic factors, determining the optimal sample complexity for list size d+1 as d^2/eps^2.
AI.motivation: Prior work gave a list replicable algorithm for list size d+1 with sample complexity about d^3/eps^2, but no nontrivial lower bound was known, so the optimal dependence was unclear.
AI.method: The authors prove a sample complexity lower bound for (k,eps,delta)-list replicable bias estimation and design an improved algorithm, extending the analysis to every list size k in [d+1, 2^d].
AI.result: For list size d+1 the optimal total sample complexity is Theta-tilde(d^2/eps^2), and for every k in [d+1, 2^d] matching upper and lower bounds of Theta-tilde(d^2/(eps^2 log k)) are established.
AI.conclusion: The quadratic dependence on dimension is inherent up to polylogarithmic factors, so the price of list replicability for bias estimation is now characterised tightly.

title: Curriculum unlearning in humans and neural networks
summary: During learning, humans often benefit from curricula that teach simple rules before exceptions. However, we lack a computational explanation for this phenomenon. Here, using a canonical behavioural task and modelling with neural networks, we develop and test a theory for why simple-to-complex curricula succeed. We show that during learning, both humans and neural networks show simplicity biases, a tendency to learn simple rules that are underfit to the data. In neural networks this bias is accompanied by compression of neural representations. Simple-to-complex curricula help both types of learners overcome this compression, developing representations (and policy) with appropriate dimensionality for the task. We test and confirm a further prediction from this theory: learners that have been pre-exposed to simple tasks and with more compressed initial representations benefit more from curricula. These findings suggest that curricula help with ``unlearning'' of simple rules.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a theory that simple-to-complex curricula help learners by undoing a simplicity bias and the representation compression that comes with it, and tests the theory in both humans and neural networks.
AI.motivation: Humans often benefit from curricula that teach simple rules before exceptions, but there is no computational explanation for why such simple-to-complex curricula succeed.
AI.method: Using a canonical behavioural task, the authors model human learners and neural networks, measure simplicity biases and representation compression, and test a prediction about pre-exposure to simple tasks and compressed initial representations.
AI.result: Both humans and neural networks show simplicity biases, and in networks these coincide with compression of neural representations; simple-to-complex curricula overcome this compression, and learners pre-exposed to simple tasks with more compressed initial representations benefit more from curricula.
AI.conclusion: Curricula help learners unlearn simple rules by restoring representations of appropriate dimensionality for the task, giving a computational account of why simple-to-complex teaching works.

title: Ground-Wing: A Parametric 3D Wing-in-Ground-Effect Dataset for Benchmarking Neural Surrogate Models
summary: This paper presents a CFD dataset of a highly parametrized 3D wing operating in ground effect, designed for benchmarking neural surrogate models for aerodynamic prediction, using a wing shape and flow conditions typically encountered in motorsport applications. The dataset comprises 770 RANS simulations of 194 unique wing configurations, sampled across 27 airfoil profile variants and 4 distances from the ground, spanning variations in wing sweep, chord, taper, angle of attack, and tip twist. Six neural network architectures representing distinct paradigms --- convolutional (DoMINO), graph-based (X-MeshGraphNet), transformer-based (AB-UPT, GeoTransolver, GAOT), and JEPA-based (AeroJEPA) --- are evaluated on their ability to predict surface pressure coefficient and wall shear stress distributions, from which integral drag and lift coefficients are recovered. The dataset is intended to be used as a challenging benchmark for surrogate CFD models, due to the uniqueness of the ground effect being absent from other wing and airfoil datasets.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Ground-Wing, a CFD dataset of 770 RANS simulations of a parametrised 3D wing in ground effect, designed as a benchmark for neural surrogate models of aerodynamics.
AI.motivation: Existing wing and airfoil datasets do not include the ground effect, which is important for motorsport aerodynamics, so surrogate models lack a challenging benchmark for it.
AI.method: The dataset covers 194 unique wing configurations sampled across 27 airfoil profiles and 4 ground distances, varying sweep, chord, taper, angle of attack and tip twist; six neural architectures (DoMINO, X-MeshGraphNet, AB-UPT, GeoTransolver, GAOT, AeroJEPA) predict surface pressure coefficient and wall shear stress, from which drag and lift are recovered.
AI.result: The abstract reports the dataset size and the evaluation of six surrogate architectures spanning convolutional, graph, transformer and JEPA paradigms, but no specific accuracy numbers.
AI.conclusion: Ground-Wing is intended as a challenging benchmark for surrogate CFD models because the ground effect is absent from other wing and airfoil datasets.

title: SCANO: Restoring Boundary-Condition Completeness in Sampled Meshes with a Sliced-Cross-Attention Neural Operator for 3D Thermal Fields
summary: Training neural operators on million-cell meshes can exceed GPU memory limits. Models are therefore trained on subsamples and deployed on whole meshes or selected regions. However, subsampling can distort boundary information, degrading accuracy. We ask when boundary conditioning under sampling stays consistent with whole-mesh training, and how to aggregate and inject boundary data. Representing the solution as an integral of boundary data against type-dependent measures, we show that subsampling distorts this conditioning in three ways: incomplete boundary coverage or a sample-dependent global state, face weighting by count rather than area, and compression of boundary inputs into a low-dimensional vector. This analysis yields four measurable consistency conditions checkable before training. We satisfy them with two backbone-agnostic modules. Boundary Quadrature Attention (BQA) aggregates all boundary faces, typed and area-weighted, into slice tokens that every query point reads at every layer. Anchored Global State (AGS) estimates the global state from anchors independent of the sampled points. Adding both to a scalable message-passing and slice-attention backbone yields SCANO. We evaluate the approach on controlled and public benchmarks and a data-centre thermal simulation dataset (DCTS) containing million-cell meshes. On both benchmarks, BQA improves every backbone, reducing whole-mesh error up to 15-fold. On all three datasets, AGS aligns regional with whole-mesh predictions, cutting regional error at least tenfold for most backbones on the public benchmark. Together, the modules nearly halve the best original backbone's whole-mesh error on both benchmarks. SCANO predicts a room-scale field in under one second, over 100 times faster than whole-room anchor self-attention.

AI.tldr: SCANO is a neural operator for 3D thermal fields that restores boundary-condition completeness when training on subsampled meshes, using two backbone-agnostic modules, Boundary Quadrature Attention and Anchored Global State.
AI.motivation: Neural operators trained on subsampled million-cell meshes can lose boundary information, since subsampling distorts boundary conditioning and degrades accuracy when deployed on whole meshes or regions.
AI.method: The authors derive four measurable consistency conditions from an integral representation of the solution over boundary data; BQA aggregates all boundary faces, typed and area-weighted, into slice tokens read by every query, and AGS estimates the global state from anchors independent of the sampled points, both added to a message-passing and slice-attention backbone.
AI.result: On controlled and public benchmarks BQA improves every backbone and reduces whole-mesh error up to 15-fold, AGS cuts regional error at least tenfold for most backbones on the public benchmark, and together they nearly halve the best backbone's whole-mesh error; SCANO predicts a room-scale field in under one second, over 100 times faster than whole-room anchor self-attention.
AI.conclusion: Restoring boundary conditioning under sampling makes training on subsamples consistent with whole-mesh behaviour, enabling accurate and fast thermal field prediction at million-cell scale.

title: CAPSkip: Cancellation-Aware Prefix Skipping for Selective Backpropagation
summary: Per-step selective back-propagation forwards every example of a mini-batch but back-propagates only some of them. Most rules rank examples by loss or gradient magnitude, but such scalar scores ignore cancellation between per-example gradients: the gradient removed by a set can be much smaller than its individual magnitudes suggest. We introduce CAPSkip (Cancellation-Aware Prefix Skipping). Among the examples the model already classifies correctly, CAPSkip skips the longest prefix, in increasing order of last-layer gradient norm, whose vector sum stays within a relative budget $b$ of the batch's last-layer gradient. In exact arithmetic this bounds the change of the raw final-layer gradient, using rank-one contributions already available from the forward pass; the bound does not extend to deeper layers, optimizer updates, or the training trajectory. Because the cumulative distortion is not monotone in the prefix length, CAPSkip scans all prefixes; a factorised Gram matrix makes the scan cheap and keeps it on the device. With activation reuse and selected-row backward, CAPSkip fine-tunes DeiT-S on CIFAR-100 for 103 epochs in 0.576x the time of 103-epoch dense training, and is +0.25 pp [+0.08, +0.42] above an approximately time-matched 59-epoch dense run (n=3).

AI.tldr: CAPSkip is a selective backpropagation rule that skips back-propagation for correctly classified examples in a cancellation-aware way, bounding the change of the final-layer gradient, and speeds up fine-tuning of DeiT-S on CIFAR-100.
AI.motivation: Rules that rank examples by loss or gradient magnitude ignore cancellation between per-example gradients, so the gradient removed by a set can be much smaller than its individual magnitudes suggest.
AI.method: Among correctly classified examples, CAPSkip skips the longest prefix, in increasing order of last-layer gradient norm, whose vector sum stays within a relative budget b of the batch gradient, scanning all prefixes with a factorised Gram matrix and using activation reuse and selected-row backward.
AI.result: CAPSkip fine-tunes DeiT-S on CIFAR-100 for 103 epochs in 0.576 times the time of dense training and is +0.25 pp [+0.08, +0.42] above a roughly time-matched 59-epoch dense run (n=3).
AI.conclusion: The bound is exact only for the raw final-layer gradient and does not extend to deeper layers, optimiser updates or the training trajectory, so the efficiency gain is shown empirically rather than guaranteed.

title: Policy Network Diffusion
summary: Diffusion models have shown remarkable progress in AI-generated content, including images and videos. In this paper, we explore whether diffusion models can generate the parameters of policy networks in reinforcement learning (RL), and whether the generated policies exhibit generalization capabilities. To achieve this, we propose Diffusion-based Conditional Policy Network Parameter Generation (DPPG), which consists of a Transformer-based autoencoder and a task-conditioned diffusion model. The autoencoder achieves a high compression rate by patchifying network parameters, while the task-conditioned diffusion model generates corresponding parameters conditioned on different environments. Our experiments demonstrate that, with a single unified DPPG model, we can synthesize high-quality policies across a diverse set of tasks from different environment domains, including Classic Control, Atari games, and MuJoCo. Additionally, our method can generate networks with a larger number of parameters compared to previous approaches. Furthermore, we find that in previously unseen environments, DPPG can generate parameters that achieve faster convergence and reach competitive performance, showcasing the potential future applications of parameter generation via diffusion.

AI.tldr: DPPG uses a Transformer autoencoder and a task-conditioned diffusion model to generate policy network parameters for reinforcement learning, producing policies that work across Classic Control, Atari and MuJoCo with one unified model.
AI.motivation: The paper asks whether diffusion models can generate policy network parameters in RL and whether the generated policies generalise, which prior parameter generation approaches have not shown at this scope.
AI.method: A Transformer-based autoencoder compresses network parameters by patchifying them, and a task-conditioned diffusion model generates the parameters conditioned on the environment.
AI.result: A single DPPG model synthesises high-quality policies across tasks from different environment domains, can generate networks with more parameters than previous approaches, and in unseen environments produces parameters with faster convergence and competitive performance.
AI.conclusion: Diffusion-based parameter generation is a promising route to producing and transferring RL policies, though the abstract does not quantify performance against specific baselines.

title: Exploiting Biases in Attention for Transformers
summary: Attention is known to be sparse in vision transformers. In particular, we analyze the unequal relevance of attention-matrix columns to the final computation and show that this phenomenon becomes increasingly pronounced with network depth. This can be interpreted as saying that tokens have an absolute importance for the attention process, independently of queries. Inspired by this, we propose a reformulation of the attention formula that makes this phenomenon explicit by adding an input-dependent bias to the query-key dot product. We show that this new term gives each token a scalar value indicating its anticipated influence on other tokens during the attention process, and can thus serve as a proxy for pruning attention maps. Across multiple transformer model sizes, this allows us to substantially reduce the computational cost of attention, in terms of both FLOPs and inference latency, while retaining most of the original classification accuracy. We publicly released the code and models at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that attention in vision transformers is sparse because tokens have an input-dependent absolute importance, and adds a per-token bias to the query-key product to prune attention maps and cut computation.
AI.motivation: Attention is known to be sparse in vision transformers, and the unequal relevance of attention columns grows with depth, but the mechanism behind this sparsity is not made explicit in the standard formulation.
AI.method: The authors reformulate attention by adding an input-dependent bias term to the query-key dot product, which gives each token a scalar score of its anticipated influence and serves as a proxy for pruning attention maps.
AI.result: Across several transformer sizes the method substantially reduces attention cost in FLOPs and inference latency while retaining most of the original classification accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The per-token bias provides a simple and principled proxy for attention pruning, making attention cheaper with modest accuracy loss; code and models are released.

title: Leakage-free evaluation of residual graph convolutional networks for network intrusion detection
summary: Graph neural networks are increasingly proposed for network intrusion detection, yet many reported results come from protocols in which test flows shape the graph used for training, duplicated flows sit on both sides of the split, or a single split is reported. This study measures what a residual graph convolutional network gains over simpler models once these sources of optimism are removed. CICIDS2017 and NF-UNSW-NB15-v2 were cleaned with label-aware removal of exact duplicates, removing 69% of NF-UNSW-NB15-v2 flows. Flows were linked in a nearest-neighbour graph built from training flows only, and validation and test flows were attached to their nearest training flows at prediction time. A two-layer residual network was compared with eight models under the same settings, including a nearest-neighbour vote over the same graph, gradient-boosted trees and a random forest, over three seeds that each draw a new split, with ablations, leave-one-family-out and feature-noise tests. On CICIDS2017 the residual network reached a binary F1 of 98.11% (SD 0.18) and on NF-UNSW-NB15-v2 90.57% (0.38), indistinguishable from a multilayer perceptron without the graph and from other graph networks. Tree ensembles were 1.48 to 1.57 F1 points higher on CICIDS2017 and led on the area under the precision-recall curve on both datasets; their CICIDS2017 multiclass macro-F1 reached 93.08% against 64.51%, a gap mainly from benign flows the residual network assigned to small attack classes. No ablation, including transductive graph construction, changed F1 beyond seed variation. Under Gaussian feature noise (SD 0.5), the residual network kept an F1 of 96.16%, while XGBoost fell to 0.67%. Under a leakage-controlled protocol, message passing over flow graphs adds no measurable accuracy over a perceptron, and tree ensembles remain stronger on both; the advantage of graph models lies in robustness to feature noise.

AI.tldr: Under leakage-free evaluation of residual graph convolutional networks for intrusion detection, the graph model adds no measurable accuracy over a perceptron, tree ensembles remain stronger, and the main benefit of graphs is robustness to feature noise.
AI.motivation: Many reported graph-based intrusion detection results rely on protocols with leakage, such as test flows shaping the training graph, duplicate flows across splits, or single splits, so the true gain of graph models is unclear.
AI.method: The authors clean CICIDS2017 and NF-UNSW-NB15-v2 by label-aware removal of exact duplicates, build a nearest-neighbour graph from training flows only, attach validation and test flows at prediction time, and compare a two-layer residual network with eight models over three seeds, with ablations, leave-one-family-out and feature-noise tests.
AI.result: The residual network reaches binary F1 98.11% (SD 0.18) on CICIDS2017 and 90.57% (0.38) on NF-UNSW-NB15-v2, indistinguishable from an MLP without the graph; tree ensembles are 1.48 to 1.57 F1 points higher on CICIDS2017, and under Gaussian feature noise (SD 0.5) the residual network keeps 96.16% F1 while XGBoost falls to 0.67%.
AI.conclusion: Message passing over flow graphs adds no measurable accuracy under a leakage-controlled protocol, and the practical advantage of graph models is robustness to feature noise rather than accuracy.

title: Feature-Based and Deep Learning Methods for Astronomical Light Curve Classification
comment: 14 pages, 5 figures. Submitted to Moscow University Physics Bulletin (DLCP-2026 special issue)
summary: We compare feature-based machine learning and end-to-end deep learning for variable star classification using the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) StarEmbed dataset, which contains about 40,000 objects across seven imbalanced classes. Classical models trained on physically motivated features consistently outperform deep networks trained directly on raw light curves. We find that limited labeled data contributes to the performance gap, while the multivariate, irregularly sampled, and morphologically diverse nature of light curves poses additional challenges for deep learning models. While deep learning holds promise for learning representations directly from observations, our results indicate that current models fail to generalize with the available training set size. These findings motivate further investigation of the benefits of scaling labeled datasets and self-supervised pretraining on large unlabeled surveys. This work establishes a quantitative baseline for future research and highlights the need for further innovations to unlock the potential of deep learning in astronomical time series analysis.

AI.tldr: On the ZTF StarEmbed variable star dataset, classical models using physically motivated features outperform deep networks trained on raw light curves, with limited labelled data identified as a main cause.
AI.motivation: Deep learning promises representations learned directly from astronomical observations, but its performance on irregularly sampled, multivariate light curves with few labels has not been established against feature-based methods.
AI.method: The authors compare feature-based machine learning with end-to-end deep learning on about 40,000 ZTF StarEmbed objects across seven imbalanced variable star classes.
AI.result: Classical models trained on physically motivated features consistently outperform deep networks trained directly on raw light curves, and the deep models fail to generalise at the available training set size.
AI.conclusion: The work sets a quantitative baseline and motivates scaling labelled datasets and self-supervised pretraining on large unlabelled surveys before deep learning can match feature-based methods.

title: FedCSGA: Client Selection Based on Genetic Algorithm for Federated Learning
summary: Federated Learning (FL) enables collaborative training of machine learning models across distributed clients while preserving data privacy. In practical deployments, FL relies on selecting a subset of clients in each communication round to reduce communication cost, mitigate stragglers, and improve training efficiency under heterogeneous data and system conditions. In heterogeneous edge computing environments, both statistical heterogeneity and system heterogeneity significantly affect convergence efficiency and model performance. However, existing client selection methods often address these factors independently, overlooking their coupled and dynamic impact across communication rounds. To address this limitation, we propose FedCSGA, a Client Selection method for Federated learning based on a Genetic Algorithm. FedCSGA encodes client subsets as chromosomes and evaluates these subsets through a non-linear fitness function that jointly integrates resource-aware metrics and history-aware participation weighting. This design captures subset-level interactions, mitigates persistent selection bias, and balances statistical utility with system efficiency. Extensive experiments on FMNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR- 100, and Tiny-ImageNet demonstrate that FedCSGA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across diverse heterogeneity settings, achieving accuracy improvements of up to 7.0% and faster convergence with fewer communication rounds. These results validate the effectiveness of jointly modeling statistical and system factors to achieve robust and efficient learning in heterogeneous federated environments.

AI.tldr: FedCSGA selects clients for federated learning with a genetic algorithm whose fitness jointly scores resource-aware metrics and history-aware participation, improving accuracy by up to 7.0% over state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing client selection methods treat statistical heterogeneity and system heterogeneity separately, overlooking their coupled and dynamic effect across communication rounds.
AI.method: Client subsets are encoded as chromosomes and evaluated by a non-linear fitness function that combines resource-aware metrics with history-aware participation weighting to capture subset-level interactions and limit selection bias.
AI.result: On FMNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and Tiny-ImageNet FedCSGA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across heterogeneity settings, with accuracy gains of up to 7.0% and faster convergence in fewer communication rounds.
AI.conclusion: Jointly modelling statistical and system factors yields more robust and efficient federated learning under heterogeneous conditions.

title: Sheaf-MPNN: A Library for Sheaf Neural Networks as Message Passing
summary: Standard Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) implicitly assume that neighboring nodes share the same feature space, which contributes to oversmoothing and poor performance on heterophilic graphs. Sheaf Neural Networks (SNNs) remove this assumption by giving each node and edge its own vector space and learning restriction maps that transform features as they move between neighbors. These maps define a sheaf Laplacian that drives diffusion over the graph, but existing implementations often assemble it explicitly as a global sparse block matrix, which adds memory and computational overhead and can hinder scalability. In this paper, we introduce Sheaf-MPNN, a PyTorch Geometric library that reformulates sheaf diffusion as local incidence-wise transport and aggregation, eliminating the need to construct the global Laplacian. Sheaf-MPNN implements fifteen families of SNNs under a unified message-passing framework, each supporting both homogeneous and heterogeneous graphs, and directed and undirected settings, with diagonal, general, orthogonal, and low-rank restriction maps and attention-based predictors. We further provide a unified benchmarking suite covering node- and graph-level tasks, heterogeneous graph learning, and computational efficiency, enabling systematic and reproducible comparisons across architectures. We establish theoretical equivalence between these message-passing formulations and their original counterparts and identify the architectural mechanisms needed to preserve their propagation dynamics. This unified perspective provides a principled foundation for implementing, comparing, and extending sheaf-based architectures within standard graph learning frameworks. Source code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Sheaf-MPNN is a PyTorch Geometric library that implements fifteen families of sheaf neural networks as local message passing, avoiding construction of the global sheaf Laplacian, with a unified benchmarking suite.
AI.motivation: Sheaf neural networks address oversmoothing and heterophily by learning restriction maps, but existing implementations assemble a global sparse sheaf Laplacian, which adds memory and compute cost and hinders scalability.
AI.method: The authors reformulate sheaf diffusion as local incidence-wise transport and aggregation under a unified message-passing framework supporting homogeneous and heterogeneous, directed and undirected graphs and diagonal, general, orthogonal and low-rank restriction maps.
AI.result: The abstract reports theoretical equivalence between the message-passing formulations and their original counterparts, identifies the architectural mechanisms needed to preserve propagation dynamics, and provides a benchmarking suite for node-level, graph-level, heterogeneous and efficiency tasks, but gives no numerical benchmark results.
AI.conclusion: The library offers a principled and reproducible foundation for implementing, comparing and extending sheaf-based architectures within standard graph learning frameworks.

title: Surrogate Models for Stochastic Al-Cu Phase-Field Solidification
comment: Accepted at the AI4Mat workshop at NeurIPS 2026. Includes supplementary material
summary: Phase-field models resolve microstructural evolution during rapid alloy solidification, but their computational cost limits long trajectories, stochastic ensembles, and studies across process conditions. We present a variance-preserving denoising diffusion bridge model (VP-DDBM) for state-conditioned prediction of two-dimensional Al-Cu solidification. Given the current phase, concentration, and prescribed temperature fields, the model predicts the subsequent state and is applied autoregressively. Across two held-out thermal gradients, VP-DDBM produces lower long-horizon errors than deterministic U-Net and SI-ConvNeXt baselines in domain-mean phase, domain-mean Cu concentration, and leading-tip position. It also retains fine dendritic structure over long rollouts, whereas the deterministic U-Net progressively smooths the morphology. VP-DDBM predicts the phase and concentration evolution approximately $73\times$ faster than the phase-field solver, showing potential for faster process-condition screening and ensemble-based microstructure studies.

AI.tldr: A variance-preserving denoising diffusion bridge model (VP-DDBM) predicts two-dimensional Al-Cu phase-field solidification autoregressively, giving lower long-horizon errors than deterministic baselines and running about 73 times faster than the phase-field solver.
AI.motivation: Phase-field simulations of rapid alloy solidification are too expensive for long trajectories, stochastic ensembles and studies across process conditions.
AI.method: Conditioned on the current phase, concentration and prescribed temperature fields, a VP-DDBM predicts the next state and is applied autoregressively, and it is evaluated on two held-out thermal gradients against U-Net and SI-ConvNeXt baselines.
AI.result: VP-DDBM gives lower long-horizon errors than the deterministic U-Net and SI-ConvNeXt baselines in domain-mean phase, domain-mean Cu concentration and leading-tip position, retains fine dendritic structure where the U-Net smooths morphology, and predicts phase and concentration about 73 times faster than the solver.
AI.conclusion: The surrogate offers a path to faster process-condition screening and ensemble-based microstructure studies.

title: Beyond Local Refinement: Wide-Area Precise Cross-View Localization
summary: Fine-grained cross-view localization aims to precisely localize a ground camera against geo-referenced aerial imagery, but current methods typically assume a narrow geographic prior, substantially limiting their applicability when upstream localization remains coarse. To bridge this gap, we study this task over much larger aerial regions. However, this seemingly simple extension fundamentally changes the localization problem: the growing disparity in spatial extent between ground and aerial views makes reliable cross-view matching difficult to establish directly, while the increasing number of look-alike locations in larger regions introduces substantial visual ambiguity. To address these challenges, we propose RingMatch, a search-and-verification framework for wide-area cross-view localization. RingMatch first leverages predictive uncertainty to uncover plausible locations and progressively zooms into their surroundings to obtain increasingly fine-grained evidence, yielding a compact set of promising candidates. We then introduce the depth ring, a novel geometric representation that reveals subtle variations in the spatial layout around a location and serves as a view-shared spatial signature for an LVLM verifier to resolve residual ambiguity. To benchmark this setting, we construct VIGOR-Pro by composing VIGOR aerial tiles into contiguous regions with spatial extents of up to 400 m. Experiments show that RingMatch maintains strong localization performance as the aerial region expands, consistently outperforming representative end-to-end and retrieval-based methods.

AI.tldr: RingMatch performs fine-grained cross-view localisation of a ground camera over wide aerial regions by searching with predictive uncertainty, verifying with a depth-ring geometric signature and an LVLM, and is benchmarked on VIGOR-Pro regions up to 400 m.
AI.motivation: Existing fine-grained cross-view localisation assumes a narrow geographic prior, which breaks when upstream localisation is coarse, because larger regions enlarge the ground-aerial extent gap and add look-alike locations.
AI.method: RingMatch is a search-and-verification framework that uses predictive uncertainty to find plausible locations, zooms progressively into them to form a compact candidate set, and uses a depth-ring representation as a view-shared spatial signature for an LVLM verifier; the VIGOR-Pro benchmark is built by composing VIGOR aerial tiles into regions up to 400 m.
AI.result: The abstract reports that RingMatch keeps strong localisation performance as the aerial region grows and consistently outperforms representative end-to-end and retrieval-based methods, without giving specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Search-and-verification with a geometric signature makes precise cross-view localisation practical over wide areas where coarse priors are all that is available.

title: Pixel-space video generation with U-JiT
summary: Latent diffusion and flow matching models are ubiquitous in state-of-the-art generative video models. While highly effective, relying on pretrained autoencoders to compress the data into a lower-dimensional latent space also comes with drawbacks. First, training proceeds in two stages: autoencoder pretraining, with compression and reconstruction objectives, followed by latent generative model training, precluding fully end-to-end training. Second, autoencoders also lead to an inherent loss of signal, and the trade-off between reconstruction quality and generative performance in the latent space is still an active area of research. In this paper we explore the viability of generative video models directly in pixel space. We analyze recent approaches in pixel-space generative modeling of images that rely on basic transformer designs, and identify several shortcomings that limit their effectiveness for the high-dimensional pixel-space video generation. To overcome these limitations, we propose a UNet-like transformer architecture along with improvements to the training recipe and sampling strategy. We conduct controlled experiments, training latent and pixel-space models from scratch on Kinetics-600. For the standard frames-to-video task at 128 resolution, our U-JiT model improves generative FVD by 27% over prior state-of-the-art results, and by 14% against the JiT pixel-space baseline. Scaling to higher 256 resolution, we find the improvement over pixel-space and latent-based models grows as we increase the spatiotemporal compression rate up to $64 \times 64 \times 8$. Finally, we find that U-JiT improves per-frame FID by 27% over latent models and 61% over pixel-space models on class-to-video generation, with respectively 9% and 56% reduction in FVD.

AI.tldr: U-JiT is a UNet-like transformer for pixel-space video generation that avoids autoencoders, improving generative FVD by 27% over prior state of the art at 128 resolution and showing gains grow with spatiotemporal compression at 256 resolution.
AI.motivation: Latent video diffusion and flow matching need pretrained autoencoders, which split training into two stages and lose signal, while basic transformer pixel-space designs do not scale to high-dimensional video.
AI.method: The authors propose a UNet-like transformer architecture with improved training recipe and sampling strategy, and train latent and pixel-space models from scratch on Kinetics-600 for controlled comparison.
AI.result: At 128 resolution on frames-to-video, U-JiT improves FVD by 27% over prior state of the art and by 14% over the JiT pixel-space baseline; at 256 resolution the advantage grows up to 64x64x8 compression; on class-to-video it improves per-frame FID by 27% over latent models and 61% over pixel-space models, with FVD reductions of 9% and 56%.
AI.conclusion: Pixel-space video generation is viable and can outperform latent approaches, with the gains increasing as the compression rate grows.

title: NightIQA: A Comprehensive Dataset and Benchmark for MLLM-Based Nighttime Image Quality Assessment
comment: Accepted to WACV 2027. 25 pages including supplementary material
summary: Nighttime images are inherently susceptible to complex, compound degradations, making accurate quality assessment exceptionally challenging. Score-based IQA methods condense quality into a single number, lacking the multi-dimensional, language-grounded reasoning required for nighttime evaluation. Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) offer a more comprehensive alternative, yet remain constrained by a critical data gap: existing real-world IQA datasets are overwhelmingly daytime-centric and often built from outdated captures, while synthetic alternatives lack nighttime-specific degradation modeling, yielding artifacts far removed from authentic nighttime conditions. To bridge this gap, we present NightIQA, a dataset and benchmark suite purpose-built for MLLM-based nighttime IQA. It comprises three core components: NightIQA-Real, a real-world dataset of 1,769 high-resolution images that we captured ourselves with modern equipment, encompassing six canonical distortion types and structured multi-dimensional annotations; NightIQA-Bench, a benchmark of 1,078 visually grounded multiple-choice questions tailored to MLLM-based nighttime IQA, organized around a four-level evaluation hierarchy spanning Perception, Technical Assessment, Localization, and Reasoning; and NightIQA-Syn, an inherently scalable, scene-aware synthesis pipeline that jointly models global-level and instance-level degradations, with an initial release of 80k high-fidelity images alongside the full generation code. Fine-tuned on NightIQA with Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), Qwen3-VL-8B outperforms open-source IQA methods and achieves higher overall accuracy than leading closed-source models, highlighting the value of domain-specific data and structured supervision.

AI.tldr: NightIQA provides a real-world nighttime image quality dataset, a multiple-choice benchmark and a synthesis pipeline for MLLM-based quality assessment, and an SFT plus GRPO fine-tuned Qwen3-VL-8B beats open-source IQA methods and some closed-source models.
AI.motivation: MLLM-based image quality assessment lacks nighttime data, since existing real-world IQA datasets are mostly daytime and outdated, and synthetic data lacks realistic nighttime degradations.
AI.method: NightIQA has three parts: NightIQA-Real with 1,769 self-captured high-resolution images with six distortion types and multi-dimensional annotations; NightIQA-Bench with 1,078 visually grounded multiple-choice questions over four levels (Perception, Technical Assessment, Localization, Reasoning); and NightIQA-Syn, a scene-aware synthesis pipeline with an initial 80k images.
AI.result: Qwen3-VL-8B fine-tuned on NightIQA with SFT and GRPO outperforms open-source IQA methods and achieves higher overall accuracy than leading closed-source models.
AI.conclusion: Domain-specific data and structured supervision are valuable for nighttime quality assessment with multimodal language models.

title: Radial distortion homography estimation from affine-covariant or orientation-covariant features
summary: We present minimal solvers for joint homography and radial distortion estimation using affine- or orientation-covariant features. The core contribution is a set of novel constraints that exploit local feature geometry inherent to affine descriptors, enabling solvers that require fewer correspondences than point-based methods. Using modern robust estimation frameworks, we demonstrate that the proposed solvers are advantageous to the current state-of-the-art with a significant speed-up in the presence of outliers while maintaining comparable or superior estimation accuracy. The proposed solvers are tested on both synthetic and real images containing challenging fisheye distortions.

AI.tldr: The paper gives minimal solvers for jointly estimating a homography and radial distortion from affine- or orientation-covariant features, needing fewer correspondences than point-based methods and running faster under outliers.
AI.motivation: Joint homography and radial distortion estimation with point correspondences needs many matches, which is costly under outliers and with challenging fisheye distortion.
AI.method: The core contribution is new constraints derived from the local feature geometry of affine or orientation-covariant descriptors, used in minimal solvers within modern robust estimation frameworks.
AI.result: The solvers are advantageous over the current state of the art on synthetic and real fisheye images, giving a significant speed-up in the presence of outliers with comparable or superior accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting local feature geometry reduces the minimal sample size and speeds up robust estimation with distortion-aware homography.

title: OCR in the Foundation Model Era: From Specialist Models to Unified Models
comment: 21 pages, 7 figures, 7 tables. Resources: this https URL
summary: Optical Character Recognition (OCR) is among the oldest and most widely deployed applications of artificial intelligence. This survey reviews its development, focusing on the Foundation Model Era. We define OCR through faithful transcription: within a specified visual scope, OCR should completely reconstruct the text, notation, and document structure observable in the source image, and every textual, notational, or structural element in the output must be verifiable from visual evidence in that image. We trace the development from specialist OCR models toward unified models, examining joint text detection and recognition, structured sequence generation, and the use of pretrained vision-language models (VLMs). We organize contemporary OCR systems into five coexisting families: modular toolkits and task-specific models, specialized document VLMs, hybrid workflows, general-purpose VLMs, and commercial products and managed services. We compare their architectures, data, and training, examining hallucination and omission, insufficient spatial grounding, and inference cost in generative OCR. We review evaluation from character and scene text recognition to parsing individual structural elements and full-page transcription, highlighting gaps in consistent output definitions, attribution of performance to individual components, and coverage of real capture conditions and visible content and structure. Finally, we summarize the challenges facing OCR and discuss directions for future research. We continuously track related work at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This survey reviews OCR in the foundation model era, organising systems into five families and defining OCR by faithful transcription that every output element must be verifiable from the image.
AI.motivation: OCR has evolved from specialist models toward unified VLM-based systems, but evaluation and output definitions are inconsistent, and generative OCR suffers from hallucination, omission and weak spatial grounding.
AI.method: The authors trace the development from specialist models to unified models, compare architectures, data and training of five families (modular toolkits, specialised document VLMs, hybrid workflows, general-purpose VLMs, commercial services), and review evaluation from character recognition to full-page transcription.
AI.result: The survey identifies gaps in consistent output definitions, attribution of performance to individual components, and coverage of real capture conditions and visible content and structure; the abstract gives no numerical results.
AI.conclusion: It summarises open challenges and future directions for OCR, and the authors continuously track related work online.

title: MiCaDe: Online LiDAR-Camera Miscalibration Change Detection for Autonomous Driving
summary: Reliable multi-sensor perception in autonomous vehicles requires accurate calibration between cameras and LiDAR. However, calibration drift is often unavoidable in long-term deployments: vibrations, thermal effects, and minor mechanical shocks may alter the relative pose between sensors, leading to systematic errors in downstream fusion tasks. We propose MiCaDe (Miscalibration Change Detection), an online solution detecting when the extrinsic LiDAR-camera calibration parameters are no longer accurate by means of sequential change detection. MiCaDe requires no calibration targets, or modification of the perception stack, providing low false-alarm rates with negligible computational overhead. Our key insight is that 3D and 2D bounding boxes produced by standard object detectors should remain geometrically consistent under correct calibration. By matching cross-modal detections, we derive geometric consistency metrics that serve as sensitive indicators of extrinsic drift. These metrics are aggregated into fixed-size batches and scored against a reference distribution, producing a likelihood stream that is monitored by a Change Point Model (CPM). Crucially, the CPM accumulates statistical evidence over time, enabling detection of subtle drifts that would otherwise go unnoticed. Experiments on multiple long-sequence datasets and on a real-world dataset with physically induced miscalibration confirm reliable detection under diverse conditions. Code available at: this https URL.

AI.tldr: MiCaDe detects online when LiDAR-camera extrinsic calibration has drifted, using geometric consistency between matched 3D and 2D detections aggregated by a change point model, with no calibration targets required.
AI.motivation: Vibration, thermal effects and mechanical shocks cause calibration drift in long-term autonomous vehicle deployments, leading to systematic errors in fusion, and existing approaches need targets or changes to the perception stack.
AI.method: The method matches cross-modal object detections, derives geometric consistency metrics, aggregates them into fixed-size batches scored against a reference distribution, and feeds the likelihood stream to a Change Point Model that accumulates evidence over time.
AI.result: Experiments on multiple long-sequence datasets and on a real-world dataset with physically induced miscalibration confirm reliable detection under diverse conditions, with low false-alarm rates and negligible overhead.
AI.conclusion: Consistency between standard detector outputs under correct calibration provides a practical signal for monitoring extrinsic drift online.

title: EP-LVMQA: Evidence-Preserving Coarse-to-Fine Localization for Low-Quality Long Video Moment Question Answering
summary: Long instructional videos are increasingly used in medical education, industrial training, and procedural knowledge transfer, yet their evidence is often incomplete or unreliable: subtitles may be missing, ASR noisy, OCR sparse, and decisive actions briefly shown without narration. Existing VideoQA systems typically return labels or free-form text, making answer support difficult to inspect. We study Long Video Moment Question Answering (LVMQA), where a system returns timestamped answer-supporting evidence. We propose EP-LVMQA, an evidence-preserving coarse-to-fine framework comprising an Uncertainty-Aware Multimodal Evidence Timeline, a Coarse Evidence Planner, and an Evidence-Conditioned Fine Localizer. An evidence card transfers planner scores, matched cues, source-confidence proxies, modality-specific evidence, neighboring context, and a temporal prior between the latter two modules. On MedVidQA, EP-LVMQA achieves 26.1 R1@0.5 and 31.8 mIoU, improving the strongest non-ours results by 6.3 and 5.1 points. It raises Suff.@2 and Ver.@2 to 25.4 and 22.6, gains of 9.5 and 8.8 points. Under matched low-quality perturbations, average relative degradation is reduced from the strongest non-ours value of 14.6% to 11.1%. On Ego4D-NLQ and QVHighlights, EP-LVMQA remains broadly comparable to established task-specific localization methods.

AI.tldr: EP-LVMQA is a coarse-to-fine framework for long video moment question answering that returns timestamped answer-supporting evidence, improving over the strongest non-ours methods on MedVidQA and remaining comparable on Ego4D-NLQ and QVHighlights.
AI.motivation: Long instructional videos often have missing subtitles, noisy ASR, sparse OCR and briefly shown actions, and existing VideoQA systems return labels or free text, which makes answer support hard to inspect.
AI.method: The framework combines an Uncertainty-Aware Multimodal Evidence Timeline, a Coarse Evidence Planner and an Evidence-Conditioned Fine Localizer, linked by an evidence card that passes planner scores, cues, source-confidence proxies and a temporal prior between the two modules.
AI.result: On MedVidQA it achieves 26.1 R1@0.5 and 31.8 mIoU, 6.3 and 5.1 points above the strongest non-ours results; Suff.@2 and Ver.@2 rise to 25.4 and 22.6, gains of 9.5 and 8.8 points; under low-quality perturbations average relative degradation falls from 14.6% to 11.1%; on Ego4D-NLQ and QVHighlights it is broadly comparable to task-specific methods.
AI.conclusion: Preserving and passing evidence through the pipeline makes long video answers more verifiable and more robust to low-quality inputs.

title: Behind Video Generation: Observations and Insights on Multimodal Understanding from Kling
summary: Video generation has progressed from isolated clips to coherent short-form audiovisual sequences, and the bottleneck is shifting from rendering to semantic control. This report summarizes the observations and insights on multimodal understanding gained from successive generations of Kling. We argue that generation quality is the projection of multimodal understanding through the entire data--conditioning--alignment--evaluation chain, and we examine this chain module by module. Kling-MLLM, a shared multimodal foundation model that unifies image, video, audio, synchronized audio--video, and interleaved inputs, is specialized for each downstream module. Because a DiT is trained on far fewer training samples than a language model, we treat captioning as a semantic contract that maximizes description density, and extend it to reference-grounded captioning that makes reference bindings explicit. Prompt enhancement translates user intent into this caption distribution: basic PE is derived from captions of compelling videos and refined with text-level and generator-in-the-loop reinforcement learning, while agentic PE refines the story and retrieves compelling examples. We show that a reliable text encoder comes from perceptual training rather than from stronger language ability, and that candidates can be screened from text alone before end-to-end training. Reward modeling pairs a general reward model for explainable, localized critiques with a decision reward model for fast multidimensional scoring, treating perceptual bandwidth as a first-class design parameter. Finally, we review task-specific automatic evaluation, focusing on protocols that expose scoring shortcuts and help trace failures to their upstream source. We hope these lessons offer practical guidance for building the understanding stack behind controllable video generation.

AI.tldr: This report from Kling summarises lessons on multimodal understanding behind video generation, covering captioning, prompt enhancement, text encoders, reward modelling and evaluation across a shared multimodal foundation model.
AI.motivation: Video generation is shifting from rendering to semantic control, so the authors argue that generation quality reflects multimodal understanding along the whole data, conditioning, alignment and evaluation chain.
AI.method: The report examines each module of the chain, including Kling-MLLM as a shared foundation model specialised per module, reference-grounded captioning, basic and agentic prompt enhancement, a general reward model and a decision reward model, and task-specific automatic evaluation.
AI.result: The abstract reports qualitative observations rather than quantitative results, including that a reliable text encoder comes from perceptual training and that candidates can be screened from text alone before end-to-end training.
AI.conclusion: The lessons are offered as practical guidance for building the understanding stack behind controllable video generation.

title: VISTA: Vision-Language Integrated Semantic Triage Architecture for Online Face Clustering in Long Videos
comment: Accepted at ACM Multimedia 2026 (MM '26). 17 pages, including 8 pages of supplementary material
summary: Clustering faces by identity in long, continuous video streams is a challenging task that serves as a building block for human-centric video analysis. The majority of existing face clustering models are offline, i.e., they assume the entire data to be available altogether. In many practical scenarios, however, the entire data is either unavailable or poses computational challenges to be processed in its entirety. A handful of online methods that exist rely on geometric visual features and simple thresholding techniques, which fail when the faces exhibit significant appearance variations in long, unconstrained videos. To this end, we present VISTA, the first vision language framework for online face clustering in long videos. VISTA leverages semantic reasoning in a controlled, uncertainty aware fashion to maintain both high cluster purity and long range identity continuity. This makes it robust to the variations in illumination, pose, and costume changes that the faces and characters exhibit in long real world videos. Extensive experiments on the VPCD benchmark dataset (with 15 full episodes from The Big Bang Theory [2007-2019], Buffy the Vampire Slayer [1997-2003], and Sherlock [2010-2017]) demonstrate that VISTA achieves a robust precision and recall balance, consistently improving over the strongest matched online unsupervised baseline (COFC) under identical detector, embeddings, and evaluation protocol. Code and supplementary material: this https URL.

AI.tldr: VISTA is a vision-language framework for online face clustering in long videos that uses uncertainty-aware semantic reasoning to keep cluster purity and long-range identity continuity, improving over the online baseline COFC on the VPCD benchmark.
AI.motivation: Existing online face clustering methods rely on geometric features and simple thresholds, which fail when appearance changes substantially in long unconstrained videos.
AI.method: VISTA leverages semantic reasoning from a vision-language model in a controlled, uncertainty-aware fashion to decide cluster assignments in an online setting.
AI.result: On VPCD, built from 15 full episodes of The Big Bang Theory, Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Sherlock, VISTA achieves a robust precision and recall balance and consistently improves over the strongest matched online unsupervised baseline, COFC, under identical detector, embeddings and protocol.
AI.conclusion: Semantic reasoning makes online face clustering more robust to illumination, pose and costume changes in long real-world videos.

title: Robustness Verification against Patch Attacks via Group-Lasso Semidefinite Relaxation
summary: Robustness verification is essential for ensuring the safety and security of neural networks, but current methods focus heavily on norm-ball attacks, which do not adequately model typical real-world threats that present physical perturbations, known as patch attacks. A naive approach requires computationally prohibitive enumeration of all possible patch positions. To address the challenge, we propose a novel neural network verification method specialized to the patch-attack threat. Instead of enumerating patch locations, we first model the patch attack with group-wise sparsity and formulate its verification methods as a mixed-integer semidefinite program (MISDP) by applying SDP relaxation to the neural network. We then propose three relaxations, including Group-Lasso relaxation, that remove the integer variables while preserving the sparse, group-wise structure of the original attack, enabling substantially efficient verification. Our empirical analysis demonstrates that the proposed relaxations require less than 3% of the computation time of the original MISDP, while the Group-Lasso relaxation incurs only a 0.34\% average increase in the objective value over the original formulation. Furthermore, Group-Lasso achieves a verified rate of 91%, compared with under 70% for prior methods.

AI.tldr: The paper verifies neural networks against patch attacks by modelling the attack as group-wise sparsity and proposing SDP relaxations, including a Group-Lasso relaxation, that avoid enumerating patch positions and cut computation to under 3% of the original MISDP.
AI.motivation: Robustness verification mostly targets norm-ball perturbations, not physical patch attacks, and exact patch verification needs prohibitively expensive enumeration of all patch positions.
AI.method: The patch attack is modelled with group-wise sparsity and formulated as a mixed-integer semidefinite program through SDP relaxation of the network; three relaxations, including Group-Lasso, remove the integer variables while preserving the group-sparse structure.
AI.result: The relaxations need less than 3% of the computation time of the original MISDP, Group-Lasso increases the objective by only 0.34% on average, and Group-Lasso achieves a verified rate of 91% compared with under 70% for prior methods.
AI.conclusion: Relaxing the integer variables while keeping group sparsity gives a scalable and tighter route to certifying patch-attack robustness.

title: HTNN-MSC: Multi-view Subspace Clustering with a Hyperbolic Tangent Tensor Low-Rank Surrogate
summary: High-order dependencies among views can be modeled by tensor singular value decomposition (t-SVD) in multi-view subspace clustering. However, the tensor nuclear norm often used with this framework assigns the same asymptotic marginal penalty to singular values of different magnitudes, which may excessively shrink dominant components that encode cluster structure. We propose HTNN-MSC, which replaces this norm with a bounded hyperbolic tangent tensor rank surrogate. The surrogate is strictly concave on the positive half-axis and has a Lipschitz continuous derivative. Its marginal penalty decreases as singular values grow. We develop an alternating direction method of multipliers solver in which the tensor subproblem decomposes into scalar frequency-domain shrinkage problems. Safeguarded multi-start Newton iterations and candidate-objective comparison implement the resulting hyperbolic tangent thresholding operator. The shape parameter is scaled by the input spectrum. We also establish o-minimal definability of the augmented objective. Under explicit boundedness, descent, relative-error, and exact-block conditions, the Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz framework guarantees convergence of the full sequence to a KKT point. On 23 datasets, HTNN-MSC achieves a mean clustering accuracy of 0.8404 and an average accuracy rank of 2.78 against nine representative methods. Friedman tests and Holm-adjusted Wilcoxon comparisons reveal significant overall differences, although several pairwise differences remain nonsignificant. HTNN-MSC records 19 wins, one tie, and three losses against the convex t-SVD-MSC skeleton. A same-skeleton ablation also shows that the proposed surrogate does not uniformly outperform alternative nonconvex penalties.

AI.tldr: HTNN-MSC replaces the tensor nuclear norm in t-SVD multi-view subspace clustering with a bounded hyperbolic tangent rank surrogate that penalises large singular values less, and reports convergence to a KKT point under the KL framework.
AI.motivation: The tensor nuclear norm gives the same asymptotic marginal penalty to all singular values, which may over-shrink dominant components that encode cluster structure.
AI.method: The surrogate is strictly concave on the positive half-axis with a Lipschitz continuous derivative and a decreasing marginal penalty; an ADMM solver decomposes the tensor subproblem into frequency-domain scalar shrinkage problems solved with safeguarded multi-start Newton iterations.
AI.result: On 23 datasets HTNN-MSC achieves mean clustering accuracy 0.8404 and average accuracy rank 2.78 against nine methods, with significant overall differences by Friedman tests and 19 wins, one tie and three losses against the convex t-SVD-MSC; the surrogate does not uniformly beat other nonconvex penalties.
AI.conclusion: The hyperbolic tangent surrogate improves over the convex norm on most datasets, with convergence guarantees, but its advantage over alternative nonconvex penalties is not uniform.

title: Learning Where to Look: Observation Policy Optimization for Thinking with Images
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Project page: this https URL
summary: Complex visual question answering often requires vision-language models to think with images, i.e., actively acquire local visual evidence by zooming into informative regions of high-resolution images. Our error analysis shows that many failures in this setting originate from incorrect observation actions, where the model fails to localize key regions or obtain crops that contain sufficient evidence for answering. We further observe that bounding-box tokens exhibit substantially higher generation entropy than ordinary language tokens, indicating high uncertainty when the model decides where to look. However, existing reinforcement learning methods based on final-answer rewards provide only trajectory-level feedback, making it difficult to assign precise credit to the observation actions. We propose Observation Policy Optimization (OPO), an RL algorithm for optimizing observation actions in tool-augmented thinking with images. OPO consists of two core modules. First, Uncertainty-Guided Observation Branching (UOB) treats each image zoom-in tool call as an observation event and selectively branches at high-uncertainty, low-redundancy events during rollout, enabling efficient exploration of alternative cropping decisions and their resulting visual evidence. Second, Evidence-Localized Advantage Attribution (ELAA) compares sibling branches using local evidence-sufficiency rewards and assigns credit only to the corresponding observation-action tokens. By decoupling observation-action optimization from trajectory-level outcome supervision, OPO improves visual evidence acquisition and further enhances visual reasoning performance. Experiments show that OPO consistently improves Qwen3-VL models across scales and achieves competitive performance against larger models and tool-augmented baselines. Code is publicly available.

AI.tldr: Observation Policy Optimization (OPO) is an RL algorithm for thinking-with-images in vision-language models that assigns credit to zoom-in observation actions through uncertainty-guided branching and local evidence-based advantages, improving Qwen3-VL models.
AI.motivation: Many failures in thinking with images come from wrong observation actions, and final-answer rewards give only trajectory-level feedback, so credit for where the model looks is poorly assigned.
AI.method: Uncertainty-Guided Observation Branching (UOB) branches rollouts at high-uncertainty, low-redundancy zoom-in events to explore alternative crops, and Evidence-Localized Advantage Attribution (ELAA) compares sibling branches with local evidence-sufficiency rewards, assigning credit only to observation-action tokens.
AI.result: OPO consistently improves Qwen3-VL models across scales and is competitive with larger models and tool-augmented baselines; the abstract reports no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling observation-action optimisation from outcome supervision improves visual evidence acquisition and reasoning in tool-augmented VLMs.

title: How Well Does Webcam Eye Tracking Work "in the Wild"? A Large-Scale Validation of Chiasm and a Comparison with WebGazer
summary: Webcam eye tracking can greatly accelerate data collection in basic and applied research by reaching large, diverse samples of participants online. However, its spatial performance is considered well below that of hardware-based systems, limiting its use. We evaluated the first-generation Chiasm webcam eye tracker in a large online study ($N = 505$) spanning diverse participants, devices, and recording conditions. Chiasm achieved a mean spatial accuracy of 2.39 cm ($\approx 2.28^\circ$ at 60 cm), spatial precision (SD) of 1.05 cm ($\approx 1.00^\circ$ at 60 cm), and sample-to-sample precision (RMS-S2S) of 1.29 cm ($\approx 1.23^\circ$ at 60 cm). For the 91% of participants who met a 3 cm calibration criterion, spatial accuracy was 2.15 cm ($\approx 2.05^\circ$ at 60 cm). After three minutes of a task that encouraged head movement, spatial accuracy declined by 0.59 cm, while the gaze center at each target shifted by a mean distance of only 0.37 cm. On the validation block, the offset was 0.30 cm larger for men than for women. Age, region of residence, face luminance, and Michelson contrast showed no reliable relationship with spatial accuracy. A higher eye aspect ratio, a more open eye, was associated with a smaller offset. Wearing glasses decreased spatial accuracy on every validation block. In a comparison between a random subsample ($N = 101$) and a separate sample tested with the open-source tracker WebGazer ($N = 101$) using an identical protocol, Chiasm showed better spatial accuracy (2.18 vs. 4.51 cm) and spatial precision (SD; 1.01 vs. 1.55 cm). WebGazer showed better sample-to-sample precision (RMS-S2S; 0.79 vs. 1.26 cm), which likely reflects conservative, over-smoothed estimates rather than superior stability. These results suggest that Chiasm is narrowing the gap between webcam and hardware-based eye tracking, making large-scale gaze research "in the wild" a reality.

AI.tldr: A large online study (N = 505) finds that the Chiasm webcam eye tracker reaches about 2.39 cm spatial accuracy and outperforms WebGazer in accuracy and precision, though WebGazer has better sample-to-sample precision.
AI.motivation: Webcam eye tracking could accelerate large-scale research, but its spatial performance is assumed to be well below hardware-based systems, which limits its use.
AI.method: The first-generation Chiasm webcam tracker was evaluated in an online study with diverse participants, devices and recording conditions, and compared with WebGazer on a separate 101-person sample using an identical protocol.
AI.result: Chiasm achieved mean spatial accuracy 2.39 cm, precision SD 1.05 cm and RMS-S2S 1.29 cm; accuracy fell by 0.59 cm after three minutes of head movement; against WebGazer it had better accuracy (2.18 vs. 4.51 cm) and precision (SD 1.01 vs. 1.55 cm), while WebGazer had better RMS-S2S (0.79 vs. 1.26 cm); wearing glasses reduced accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Chiasm is narrowing the gap between webcam and hardware eye tracking, making large-scale gaze research in the wild practical.

title: PATTS: Parallel-Aware Test-Time Scaling for Thought-Image Generation in Multimodal Discrete Diffusion LLMs
summary: Test-time scaling (TTS) improves generative models by allocating additional inference-time computation to sampling, search, and verification. Existing image generation approaches, however, typically rank completed images or image-centric intermediate states. We study TTS for parallel multimodal discrete diffusion language models, in which reasoning tokens and image tokens are decoded jointly within a single generation trajectory. We first diagnose a limitation of conventional final-image selection: on GenEval, a CLIP-style image-prompt score is weakly aligned with within-prompt compositional correctness, leaving substantial headroom between verifier selection and oracle selection. We then propose PATTS, a novel parallel-aware TTS framework that searches over intermediate thought-image states using cross-modal verifier signals. PATTS uses a state-dependent reliability weight, derived from model-internal trajectory diagnostics, to modulate the influence of external semantic verification during generation. In the fixed N=32 evaluation on MMaDA-Parallel, the PATTS reaches a GenEval score of 0.844, compared with 0.628 without TTS, 0.787 for Best-of-N, and 0.810 for FKD. These results show that reliability-aware trajectory verification can improve test-time selection for parallel thought-image co-generation under the evaluated search budget. Our code release is at this https URL

AI.tldr: PATTS is a parallel-aware test-time scaling framework that searches over intermediate thought-image states in multimodal discrete diffusion LLMs, reaching a GenEval score of 0.844 on MMaDA-Parallel versus 0.628 without test-time scaling.
AI.motivation: Image test-time scaling usually ranks completed images, and a CLIP-style image-prompt score is only weakly aligned with compositional correctness on GenEval, leaving a gap between verifier and oracle selection.
AI.method: PATTS searches over intermediate thought-image states using cross-modal verifier signals and a state-dependent reliability weight derived from model-internal trajectory diagnostics, which modulates the influence of external semantic verification during generation.
AI.result: With N=32 on MMaDA-Parallel PATTS reaches a GenEval score of 0.844, compared with 0.628 without test-time scaling, 0.787 for Best-of-N and 0.810 for FKD.
AI.conclusion: Reliability-aware trajectory verification improves test-time selection for parallel thought-image co-generation under the evaluated search budget.

title: DPAGait: Dynamic Pose-Knowledge-Aware Network for Robust Gait Recognition in the Wild
summary: Gait biometrics aims at identity recognition by appearance or pose features captured during unconstrained human walking. Existing methods predominantly rely on binary silhouette images, inherently characterized by low information entropy, and fail to fully utilize the dynamic information in gait sequences, limiting their ability to handle cross-time variations effectively. Consequently, these methods encounter significant challenges in the wild. They are susceptible to variations in clothing, carried objects, and viewpoints, as well as dynamic environmental conditions, all of which lead to substantial degradation in recognition accuracy and robustness. To overcome these challenges, we propose a pose-knowledge-aware approach specifically designed for robust gait recognition in the wild. First, we propose a novel Dynamic Pose-Parsing enhanced Silhouette gait representation paradigm that substantially enhances the information entropy and effectively captures fine-grained behavioral cues by integrating pose-parsing cues with traditional silhouettes. Subsequently, we develop a dual-branch Dynamic Pose-Knowledge-Aware Gait network. The framework consists of two complementary branches: (1) a 2D dynamic pose-aware branch that extracts pose-enhanced features from our proposed DPPS representations, and (2) a 3D Skinned Multi-Person Linear branch that leverages the 3D SMPL model to capture rich and comprehensive 3D dynamic pose information. Finally, the features are integrated to facilitate accurate and robust gait recognition. Extensive experiments on four challenging in-the-wild gait datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and generalizability of the proposed DPPS representation. The complete framework is further evaluated on SUSTech1K, CCPG, and Gait3D, where SMPL information is available or can be consistently estimated, achieving competitive performance under diverse real-world conditions.

AI.tldr: DPAGait improves gait recognition in the wild by enriching silhouettes with pose-parsing cues and fusing a 2D pose branch with a 3D SMPL branch, reporting competitive results on four in-the-wild gait datasets.
AI.motivation: Binary silhouettes have low information entropy and miss dynamic cues, so gait recognition degrades with clothing, carried objects, viewpoint and environmental changes in unconstrained walking.
AI.method: The authors propose a Dynamic Pose-Parsing enhanced Silhouette (DPPS) representation and a dual-branch Dynamic Pose-Knowledge-Aware Gait network, with a 2D dynamic pose-aware branch on DPPS and a 3D Skinned Multi-Person Linear branch, with features integrated for recognition.
AI.result: The DPPS representation is shown to be effective and generalisable across four in-the-wild gait datasets, and the full framework is evaluated on SUSTech1K, CCPG and Gait3D with competitive performance; the abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Combining pose knowledge with silhouettes gives a more robust gait representation for real-world identification.

title: Lightweight graph transformers for clutter and target classification in automotive radar
comment: Accepted to the IEEE Sensors Journal Volume 26 Issue 6
summary: Radar is a core sensor modality for scene perception to achieve higher levels of autonomy in automotive driving. A common occurrence in automotive radars is clutter - detections of non-existent moving objects, that can adversely impact target detection and classification performance and subsequent driving actions.
