AI.result: GSCV++ reports over 20% intra- and 60% inter-prediction rate-distortion gains against state-of-the-art methods, and it also produces 2D maps and encodes and decodes faster than other state-of-the-art methods using the same codec type.
AI.conclusion: Standard video codecs can be exploited more effectively for Gaussian Splatting sequence compression with low complexity, and the ablations are presented as insights for later work.

title: Visibility-Aware Reference Generation for Benchmarking Visual 3D Reconstruction in Vegetation-Rich Environments
summary: Reliable evaluation of visual 3D reconstruction and depth estimation in vegetation-rich outdoor environments is limited by the scarcity of geometric ground-truth data and the cost of complete scanner surveys. We present a LiDARbased reference-generation pipeline for evaluating the zero-shot performance of feed-forward visual-geometry models alongside conventional structure-from-motion (SfM) methods. The pipeline reuses camera images, LiDAR scans, and reference poses from existing multi-sensor localization datasets to generate per-view depth maps and visible reference point clouds. To address visibility errors in accumulated LiDAR scans, we introduce the LargeDepth-Gap Visibility Score (LDGVS) for point-wise visibility filtering and automatic scale selection in Hidden Point Removal(HPR). Experiments on TartanAirV2 and TartanGround show that, compared with Poisson surface reconstruction, which is an approach suited to completed scan surveys, the combined HPR and LDGVS filtering retains approximately three times the point density at comparable absolute relative error. We also apply the pipeline to the BotanicGarden dataset to systematically compare depth estimation and 3D reconstruction methods. Feedforward methods produce dense depth predictions efficiently, but their 3D reconstructions can contain duplicated structures. Conventional SfM generally produces more coherent geometry, but its reconstructions remain sparse and more prone to failure in challenging vegetated scenes. The benchmark toolkit and datasets will be released.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a LiDAR-based pipeline that generates visibility-aware depth and point-cloud references for benchmarking feed-forward and structure-from-motion 3D reconstruction in vegetation-rich outdoor scenes.
AI.motivation: Evaluating visual 3D reconstruction and depth estimation in vegetated environments is limited by scarce geometric ground truth and the cost of complete scanner surveys.
AI.method: The pipeline reuses camera images, LiDAR scans and reference poses from existing multi-sensor localisation datasets, and introduces the LargeDepth-Gap Visibility Score (LDGVS) for point-wise visibility filtering and automatic scale selection in Hidden Point Removal (HPR).
AI.result: On TartanAirV2 and TartanGround, HPR combined with LDGVS keeps about three times the point density of Poisson surface reconstruction at comparable absolute relative error; on BotanicGarden, feed-forward methods give dense but sometimes duplicated 3D structures while conventional SfM gives more coherent but sparse geometry that fails more often in vegetation.
AI.conclusion: The reference-generation pipeline enables systematic comparison of depth and reconstruction methods in vegetated scenes, and the benchmark toolkit and datasets are to be released.

title: CoReMatch: Recurrent Continuous Coordinate Refinement for Real-Time Robotic Feature Matching
summary: Feature matching underpins many robotic perception tasks, including visual localization, mapping, SLAM, and autonomous navigation. Existing semi-dense matchers predict confidence on fixed grids, limiting correspondences to predefined locations and requiring costly high-resolution grids for precise localization. We present CoReMatch (Coordinate Refinement Match), a recurrent framework that refines correspondences directly in continuous coordinate space rather than predicting discrete confidence maps. CoReMatch progressively improves correspondence estimates by propagating information across iterations. At the coarse stage, a Deep Aggregated Transformer captures global context and iteratively updates correspondence coordinates, while a lightweight regression head further sharpens their localization. Experiments on indoor and outdoor benchmarks show that CoReMatch strikes a strong balance between accuracy and efficiency, outperforming Efficient LoFTR in accuracy while running more than 10x faster on embedded edge hardware. These results demonstrate that recurrent coordinate refinement offers an efficient and scalable approach to real-time feature matching for robotic perception.

AI.tldr: CoReMatch is a recurrent real-time feature matcher that refines correspondence coordinates in continuous space instead of predicting confidence on fixed grids, and runs over 10x faster than Efficient LoFTR on embedded hardware.
AI.motivation: Semi-dense matchers predict confidence on fixed grids, which restricts correspondences to predefined locations and requires costly high-resolution grids for precise localisation.
AI.method: A Deep Aggregated Transformer captures global context at the coarse stage and iteratively updates correspondence coordinates across recurrent iterations, and a lightweight regression head sharpens their localisation.
AI.result: On indoor and outdoor benchmarks, CoReMatch outperforms Efficient LoFTR in accuracy while running more than 10x faster on embedded edge hardware.
AI.conclusion: Recurrent continuous coordinate refinement is presented as an efficient and scalable approach to real-time feature matching for robotic perception.

title: A Novel Conditional Adversarial Diffusion Model for High-Fidelity OCT-to-OCT Image Translation and Precise Anti-VEGF Therapy Response Prediction in Diabetic Macular Edema
comment: 18 pages, 8 figures, 6 tables, Submitted to IEEE Journal of Biomedical and Health Informatics
summary: Diabetic macular edema (DME) is a leading cause of severe vision loss among working-age adults. Although intravitreal anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) injections currently serve as the first-line therapy for DME, a notable subset of patients fails to respond despite the substantial cost and clinical burden, suggesting they may benefit more from alternative interventions. Automated, noninvasive pre-treatment response assessment could therefore spare non-responders from the current trial-and-error treatment paradigm. In this study, we propose a novel conditional adversarial diffusion framework that synthesizes post-treatment optical coherence tomography (OCT) images from baseline scans, enabling the derivation of each patient's initial response to anti-VEGF therapy. The model was developed with subject-level 5-fold cross-validation on a US cohort (n = 127) and externally validated on an independent Iranian cohort (n = 44). Benchmarked against fourteen baseline and state-of-the-art translation models, the proposed model achieved the best treatment-response prediction performance among the methods evaluated for that task on both cohorts, with balanced accuracies of 85.7% and 93.0% on the US cohort and 85.2% and 95.3% on the external Iranian cohort at the 10% and 20% central subfield thickness reduction thresholds, respectively. Ultimately, this framework offers a decision-support tool to help ophthalmologists anticipate initial anti-VEGF outcomes in DME prior to treatment initiation, toward personalized therapy selection. The source code will be made publicly available upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: A conditional adversarial diffusion model synthesises post-treatment OCT images from baseline scans to predict anti-VEGF treatment response in diabetic macular edema, with balanced accuracies of 85% to 95% on two cohorts.
AI.motivation: A notable subset of DME patients do not respond to first-line anti-VEGF injections, and non-invasive pre-treatment response assessment could spare non-responders from trial-and-error treatment.
AI.method: The authors propose a conditional adversarial diffusion framework that translates baseline OCT to post-treatment OCT, evaluated with subject-level 5-fold cross-validation on a US cohort (n = 127) and external validation on an Iranian cohort (n = 44), and benchmarked against fourteen baseline and state-of-the-art translation models.
AI.result: The model achieves balanced accuracies of 85.7% and 93.0% on the US cohort and 85.2% and 95.3% on the external Iranian cohort at the 10% and 20% central subfield thickness reduction thresholds, and the best treatment-response performance among the evaluated methods on both cohorts.
AI.conclusion: The framework is presented as a decision-support tool that could help ophthalmologists anticipate initial anti-VEGF outcomes before treatment starts, toward personalised therapy selection.

title: Evaluating the Impact of Nonlinear Registration on Longitudinal PET Analysis in a Rodent Stroke Model
comment: Accepted for presentation at the 2nd International Conference on Artificial Intelligence, Security and Networking (CAISN 2026)
summary: Longitudinal rodent positron emission tomography (PET) studies of stroke and neuromodulation rely on accurate registration to a common atlas space to detect group-level effects. Prior work applying ultra-high frequency low-intensity magnetic stimulation (UHF-LiMS) to a rat model of chronic capsule infarct used affine normalization to a Sprague Dawley MRI template without evaluating that choice. We compare a two-stage (affine and nonlinear) pipeline against an affine- only one for rat PET-to-atlas alignment on the same dataset. Across 32 longitudinal [18F]-FDG PET scans (8 rats, 4 timepoints), the nonlinear stage gave a higher Dice similarity coefficient on every scan, and the gain was significant at the rat level. Jacobian determinants showed no folding on the sampling grid. Group-level linear mixed-effects maps of change from baseline (AFNI 3dLME), computed identically under both pipelines, differ in the size, number and location of their suprathreshold clusters. In this dataset, the registration pipeline is therefore a variable that can change the interpretation of downstream group-level analyses.

AI.tldr: In a rat PET stroke study, adding a nonlinear registration stage to affine normalisation to atlas space increases Dice on every scan and changes the size, number and location of group-level statistical clusters.
AI.motivation: Prior longitudinal rodent PET work on stroke and neuromodulation used affine-only normalisation to an MRI template without evaluating that choice, so its effect on group-level results was unknown.
AI.method: The authors compare a two-stage affine plus nonlinear pipeline against an affine-only pipeline on 32 longitudinal [18F]-FDG PET scans from 8 rats at 4 timepoints, check Jacobian determinants for folding, and compare group-level linear mixed-effects change maps computed with AFNI 3dLME under both pipelines.
AI.result: The nonlinear stage gives a higher Dice on every scan and the gain is significant at the rat level, Jacobian determinants show no folding on the sampling grid, and the suprathreshold clusters of the group-level maps differ in size, number and location between pipelines.
AI.conclusion: In this dataset the registration pipeline is a variable that can change the interpretation of downstream group-level analyses, so it should be evaluated rather than assumed.

title: DUNEDepth: Bronchoscopic Depth and Pose Estimation via Hybrid Adaptation of a 3D-Vision Foundation Model
comment: 10 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables. Accepted to MICAD 2026 (International Conference on Medical Imaging and Computer-Aided Diagnosis), Edinburgh, UK, Oct. 22-24, 2026. To appear in Springer Lecture Notes
summary: State-of-the-art bronchoscopy guidance systems and computer-aided diagnosis methods have emerged as important tools for early lung cancer detection. Effective use of these tools depends on being able to accurately link a patient's bronchoscopic airway exam video to their pre-operative 3D chest CT scan. Unfortunately, the derivation of such links, which include bronchoscope depth and camera motion, from the exam video remains an open problem. Building on recently proposed 3D-vision foundation models, we propose DUNEDepth, a hybrid architecture that combines a shared DUNE ViT encoder, a twin MASt3R cross-attention decoder structure, and a prediction head that includes elements of the MASt3R and Reloc3r models. To fine-tune the architecture to our application, we utilize an integrated hybrid synthetic-supervised/self-supervised training strategy that draws on both bronchoscopic video and CT-derived virtual bronchoscopic views. Experiments drawing on bronchoscopic video sequences demonstrate that DUNEDepth more accurately derives depth information and camera motion trajectories than previously proposed self-supervised methods.

AI.tldr: DUNEDepth estimates bronchoscope depth and camera pose from airway exam video by adapting a 3D-vision foundation model with a hybrid synthetic and self-supervised training strategy.
AI.motivation: Linking a bronchoscopic exam video to the patient's pre-operative chest CT requires depth and camera motion, which remains an open problem for lung cancer guidance systems.
AI.method: DUNEDepth combines a shared DUNE ViT encoder, a twin MASt3R cross-attention decoder and a prediction head with elements of MASt3R and Reloc3r, and is fine-tuned with hybrid synthetic-supervised and self-supervised training using bronchoscopic video and CT-derived virtual bronchoscopic views.
AI.result: Experiments on bronchoscopic video sequences show that DUNEDepth derives depth and camera motion trajectories more accurately than previously proposed self-supervised methods; the abstract gives no numerical values.
AI.conclusion: Adapting 3D-vision foundation models with hybrid training is presented as a way to improve video-to-CT linkage for bronchoscopic guidance.

title: An automated photometric pipeline for measuring the corotation radius of spiral galaxies
summary: The corotation radius R_CR of a spiral galaxy marks the radius where the angular speed of the spiral pattern matches the orbital speed of the disk material. Despite its importance for understanding spiral structure and galaxy evolution, very few galaxies have corotation measurements, often derived using heterogeneous techniques. We present an automated photometric pipeline that identifies corotation radii by tracking the azimuthal phase offset between young and old stellar populations. Building on the color-gradient framework of \citet{Puerari1997}, we extract azimuthal brightness profiles from deprojected dual-band images, fit periodic models to the profiles, and identify corotation candidates at radii where the phase difference between the two stellar tracers changes sign. Each candidate is assigned an adaptive uncertainty interval and reported with a goodness-of-fit metric. We benchmark the method against a cross-method literature compilation, scoring every technique -- including our own -- against a reference built from the published measurements alone and evaluated leave-one-out. Over the $90$ galaxies for which such a reference exists, the pipeline places a correct corotation radius in $80.0\%$ of them, recovers $63.6\%$ of their known corotation radii, and reaches a harmonic mean of recall and purity of $0.58$, the highest values of any method in the comparison. Unlike the published methods, each of which was applied to a small, curated set of galaxies, our pipeline is run on the entire reference sample without any pre-selection, a sample two to six times larger than existing methods. The pipeline is scalable to large surveys, flexible with respect to spiral mode, and naturally recovers multiple corotation radii in galaxies with complex spiral structure, providing a uniform framework for studying disk resonances across diverse galaxy populations.

AI.tldr: An automated photometric pipeline identifies corotation radii of spiral galaxies from azimuthal phase offsets between young and old stellar populations, and is run on a sample two to six times larger than previous methods.
AI.motivation: Corotation radii are known for very few galaxies, and the published measurements come from heterogeneous techniques applied to small curated samples.
AI.method: The pipeline extracts azimuthal brightness profiles from deprojected dual-band images, fits periodic models, and identifies candidates where the phase difference between the two stellar tracers changes sign, assigning each an adaptive uncertainty interval and goodness-of-fit metric; it is benchmarked leave-one-out against a literature compilation.
AI.result: Over 90 galaxies with a reference, the pipeline places a correct corotation radius in 80.0% of them, recovers 63.6% of known corotation radii, and reaches a harmonic mean of recall and purity of 0.58, the highest among the compared methods.
AI.conclusion: The method provides a scalable, uniform framework for studying disk resonances across galaxy populations and can recover multiple corotation radii in galaxies with complex spiral structure.

title: COSMIO: A Benchmark for Cross-Survey Modality Imputation
summary: Large-scale astronomical surveys define a heterogeneous, partially observed multi-survey learning setting: each object is observed by only a subset of surveys, while survey observations differ in resolutions, wavelength coverage, noise characteristics, and footprints. This setting gives rise to a natural machine learning problem: given observations of an object in some surveys, how to infer its appearance in other surveys. We formalize this as the problem of cross-survey modality imputation and introduce COSMIO, a multi-survey benchmark of aligned observations obtained by forward-rendered shared astrophysical scenes across LSST, Euclid, and Roman under survey-specific instrument characteristics. The benchmark enables systematic evaluation of imputation across source-target survey combinations and missing-survey patterns. We evaluate a broad range of machine learning methods for imputation, which reveal a clear domain gap: methods developed for existing imputation settings transfer poorly to the survey setting. We identify rare-event imputation as a central challenge. This regime arises in the early stages of new surveys, when rare but scientifically valuable phenomena may be available only from prior surveys. We use strong gravitational lensing, where light from a background galaxy is gravitationally deflected by a foreground galaxy, as a representative rare-event setting. We evaluate model performance on zero-shot imputation of gravitational lenses and on downstream scientific tasks using the imputed lens observations. On our constructed evaluation set of galaxy-galaxy strong lenses, performance degrades under rare-event distribution shift, and this degradation further propagates to the downstream lens-detection task. Code: this https URL.

AI.tldr: COSMIO is a benchmark for cross-survey modality imputation, showing that existing imputation methods transfer poorly to multi-survey astronomy and that rare-event imputation, such as strong lens recovery, degrades under distribution shift.
AI.motivation: Astronomical surveys observe each object with only some instruments that differ in resolution, wavelength coverage, noise and footprint, and imputation methods developed for other settings are not known to work in this survey setting.
AI.method: The authors formalise cross-survey modality imputation and build COSMIO, an aligned benchmark of forward-rendered shared scenes across LSST, Euclid and Roman with survey-specific instrument characteristics, evaluating many imputation methods, zero-shot lens imputation and a downstream lens-detection task.
AI.result: The evaluated methods show a clear domain gap, and on a constructed set of galaxy-galaxy strong lenses performance degrades under rare-event distribution shift, with this degradation propagating to the downstream lens-detection task.
AI.conclusion: Rare-event imputation is identified as a central challenge for new surveys, where rare phenomena may appear only in prior surveys.

title: RAFT: Reasoning-Aligned Fine-Tuning Improves Robustness of VLA Post-Training
summary: Adapting a generalist vision-language-action (VLA) policy to a target task with limited demonstrations can improve nominal task success while reducing robustness to variations in appearance, objects, and instructions. We introduce reasoning-aligned fine-tuning (RAFT), a two-stage post-training procedure: RAFT first trains low-rank adapters on task-relevant reasoning annotations, then freezes them while fine-tuning the policy on action demonstrations. On a physical DROID robot, RAFT achieves $75.0\%$ out-of-distribution success, compared with $27.9\%$ for plain fine-tuning; on a multi-stage bimanual YAM task, it reaches $70.0\%$ mean success, compared with $36.0\%$ for the strongest baseline. RAFT also improves success under visual, object, and instruction shifts in simulated pick-and-place and open-drawer tasks. Compared with plain fine-tuning, RAFT policies place more attention on annotated task regions and yield higher linear-probe accuracy for object identity in later layers. A broader reasoning-data mixture further improves downstream success across demonstration budgets.

AI.tldr: RAFT is a two-stage post-training procedure for vision-language-action policies that first trains low-rank adapters on reasoning annotations and then fine-tunes the policy on actions, improving robustness to distribution shifts.
AI.motivation: Adapting a generalist VLA policy with few demonstrations raises nominal success but can reduce robustness to changes in appearance, objects and instructions.
AI.method: RAFT trains low-rank adapters on task-relevant reasoning annotations, freezes them, and then fine-tunes the policy on action demonstrations, with a broader reasoning-data mixture also evaluated.
AI.result: On a physical DROID robot RAFT achieves 75.0% out-of-distribution success versus 27.9% for plain fine-tuning, and on a multi-stage bimanual YAM task it reaches 70.0% mean success versus 36.0% for the strongest baseline; RAFT also improves success under visual, object and instruction shifts in simulation, and its policies attend more to annotated regions and give higher linear-probe object identity accuracy in later layers.
AI.conclusion: Aligning post-training with reasoning annotations improves robustness of VLA policies under shifts, and a broader reasoning mixture further improves success across demonstration budgets.

title: Hybrid Quantum--Classical Pauli-Correlator Architecture for Image Reconstruction
summary: We introduce the Pauli-Correlator Autoencoder (PCAE), a hybrid quantum--classical architecture for image reconstruction. PCAE splits an image into patches and compresses each patch as a matrix product state (MPS). A small quantum circuit turns each compressed patch into a few measured numbers, and a classical neural network rebuilds the patch from these numbers and the patch position. A learnable energy term, taken from physics, is added to training and tracked as training proceeds. Two versions place the six qubits on a line (PCAE1D) or on a grid (PCAE2D). An averaging step makes the PCAE2D features follow rotations and reflections of the image exactly. Trained on one image at a time, PCAE2D rebuilds images from six public datasets with a peak signal-to-noise ratio of 25.8 to 41.6 decibels. On CIFAR-10 images not used in training, a formula-based stand-in for the PCAE2D features performs within 1 decibel of several simpler classical methods. Five trained models also run on real IBM quantum computers without retraining, and rebuild images at 25.90 to 31.52 decibels. A short argument and a synthetic test show that, with a linear final layer, measuring qubits in pairs is needed for targets built from products of inputs. These results show that PCAE works as a hybrid model that rebuilds varied images and runs on today's quantum hardware at the six-qubit scale.

AI.tldr: PCAE is a hybrid quantum-classical autoencoder that compresses image patches as matrix product states, measures a six-qubit circuit and reconstructs images with a classical network, and it also runs on real IBM quantum hardware.
AI.motivation: Quantum image reconstruction models need to work on today's small quantum devices, and existing hybrid approaches have not shown reconstruction of varied images at this scale on real hardware.
AI.method: The image is split into patches, each compressed as a matrix product state and passed through a small quantum circuit whose measured values, along with patch position, feed a classical network; two variants place six qubits on a line (PCAE1D) or a grid (PCAE2D), with an averaging step making PCAE2D exactly equivariant to rotations and reflections.
AI.result: Trained on one image at a time, PCAE2D reconstructs images from six public datasets at 25.8 to 41.6 dB PSNR; on unseen CIFAR-10 images a formula-based stand-in for its features is within 1 dB of several simpler classical methods; five trained models run on IBM quantum computers without retraining at 25.90 to 31.52 dB.
AI.conclusion: PCAE works as a hybrid model that reconstructs varied images on current six-qubit quantum hardware, and measuring qubits in pairs is argued and tested to be needed for certain product-type targets with a linear final layer.

title: Hybrid Particle-Voxel Dynamics for Multimodal 3D World Simulation
summary: Predicting how the world evolves in response to robot actions is central to policy learning, evaluation, and planning. However, many action-conditioned world models predict future observations in 2D image or video space without explicitly modeling the underlying 3D scene, making spatial consistency across viewpoints and over long-horizon interactions challenging. We introduce 3D World Simulator, an action-conditioned multimodal world modeling framework that jointly predicts appearance, geometry, and tactile observations from a unified 3D representation. Our approach combines a hybrid particle-voxel autoencoder that compresses point clouds into compact 3D voxel latents with an action-conditioned latent dynamics model that predicts their evolution. The shared 3D representation supports geometrically consistent rendering from arbitrary viewpoints and flexible integration of spatially aligned tactile signals. Our experiments demonstrate interactive, long-horizon, multimodal prediction at 50 Hz. We then show how our model enables scalable data generation for policy training and evaluation using tactile and multi-view visual observations, including wrist-mounted and novel camera views. Furthermore, we scale our method to large datasets containing diverse objects and demonstrate model-based planning with unseen objects and robot configurations. Together, these results highlight the potential of hybrid particle-voxel dynamics as a foundation for multimodal 3D world simulation.

AI.tldr: 3D World Simulator is an action-conditioned world model that jointly predicts appearance, geometry and tactile observations through a hybrid particle-voxel latent representation, supporting consistent multi-view rendering and planning.
AI.motivation: Action-conditioned world models that predict 2D images or video do not explicitly model the 3D scene, which makes spatial consistency across viewpoints and long horizons difficult.
AI.method: A hybrid particle-voxel autoencoder compresses point clouds into compact 3D voxel latents, and an action-conditioned latent dynamics model predicts their evolution; the shared representation supports rendering from arbitrary viewpoints and aligned tactile signals.
AI.result: The model shows interactive, long-horizon, multimodal prediction at 50 Hz, enables scalable data generation for policy training and evaluation with tactile and multi-view observations, and supports model-based planning with unseen objects and robot configurations on large datasets.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid particle-voxel dynamics is presented as a foundation for multimodal 3D world simulation.

title: Sparse-View 3D Coronary Reconstruction from Vessel Segmentations Using a Diffusion Prior
summary: Reconstructing three-dimensional (3D) coronary anatomy from sparse angiographic views could support percutaneous coronary intervention, but limited angular coverage and imperfect vessel segmentations introduce substantial geometric ambiguity. We propose a vessel-specific reconstruction framework combining a learned 3D diffusion prior, visual-hull initialization, and projection-based data consistency. The unconditional diffusion model is trained on coronary vessel masks without paired 2D--3D data and reused across different view counts without retraining. During inference, a scaled visual hull initializes reconstruction, while projection-based updates constrain diffusion refinement using patient-specific vessel observations. We evaluated the framework on simulated angiograms derived from ImageCAS computed tomography angiography volumes using two, four, and eight views at two contrast levels. Across 50 evaluation coronary-tree cases, the proposed method achieved higher mean Dice and clDice than visual hull, deep image prior (DIP), and hash-grid implicit neural representation (INR) at all view counts under reduced contrast. With eight views, improvements over DIP, the best-performing baseline at lower contrast, were approximately 0.13 in Dice and 0.22 in clDice. At higher contrast, performance remained competitive with hash-grid INR, the best-performing eight-view baseline. The preferred diffusion starting timestep depended on observation quality and view count, with excessive refinement reducing accuracy at higher contrast. Projection guidance improved both metrics across all conditions. Averaging stochastic reconstructions further improved accuracy, while sample disagreement localized errors with average-precision gains of 0.14--0.21 over error prevalence. These findings support diffusion-prior reconstruction from sparse vessel observations, although clinical validation remains necessary.

AI.tldr: The paper reconstructs 3D coronary trees from two, four or eight angiographic views by combining a trained unconditional 3D diffusion prior with visual-hull initialisation and projection-based data consistency.
AI.motivation: Sparse-view coronary reconstruction has large geometric ambiguity from limited angular coverage and imperfect vessel segmentations, which hampers its use in percutaneous coronary intervention.
AI.method: The unconditional diffusion model is trained on coronary vessel masks without paired 2D-3D data and reused across view counts; inference initialises from a scaled visual hull and applies projection-based updates to constrain diffusion refinement using patient-specific observations.
AI.result: On 50 simulated evaluation cases from ImageCAS, the method achieves higher mean Dice and clDice than visual hull, deep image prior and hash-grid INR at all view counts under reduced contrast, with eight-view gains over DIP of about 0.13 in Dice and 0.22 in clDice; at higher contrast it stays competitive with hash-grid INR.
AI.conclusion: Diffusion-prior reconstruction from sparse vessel observations is supported, though the authors state that clinical validation remains necessary.

title: LIPS-PC: Learning Illumination Patterns for Single-Pixel Classification
summary: In single-pixel (ghost) imaging, known illumination patterns probe an object and a detector with no spatial resolution returns one number per pattern. Each measurement costs acquisition time and photons and, for ionizing probes, contributes to delivered dose. Motivated by automated radiographic defect screening, where a class label suffices, we introduce Learning Illumination Patterns for Single-Pixel Classification (LIPS-PC). The patterns are learned end-to-end while the measurement operator remains one fixed linear matrix, identical for every input. We parameterize it as a residual correction to a two-dimensional discrete cosine transform (2D-DCT), $D=D_{\mathrm{base}}+\Delta$, and jointly train the correction and a compact classifier using cross-entropy, without a reconstruction objective. This yields a task-driven linear embedding through optimization. We evaluate LIPS-PC numerically on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST under a controlled protocol, then on RIAWELC, a real industrial X-ray weld-radiograph dataset. Across five budgets, $M\in{8,16,32,64,128}$, corresponding to sampling ratios from below 1% to 12.5%, the learned operator outperforms the best tested fixed transform by 9-15 percentage points at $M=8$ on all three datasets. Its eight-measurement accuracy requires roughly 16-32 measurements with the best fixed transform, indicating a $2\times$ to $4\times$ saving at comparable accuracy. The advantage generally shrinks as $M$ increases, with a small reversal on RIAWELC at higher budgets. These results show that learning what to measure is especially valuable when measurements are scarce.

AI.tldr: LIPS-PC learns illumination patterns end-to-end for single-pixel classification, parameterising the fixed measurement matrix as a learned residual on a 2D DCT, and outperforms fixed transforms when measurements are scarce.
AI.motivation: Each single-pixel measurement costs acquisition time and dose for ionising probes, and for defect screening only a class label is needed, not a reconstruction.
AI.method: The measurement operator is D = D_base + Delta, a residual correction to a 2D-DCT, trained jointly with a compact classifier under cross-entropy loss without any reconstruction objective.
AI.result: At M = 8 the learned operator outperforms the best tested fixed transform by 9-15 percentage points on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST and RIAWELC, an industrial X-ray weld dataset; the fixed transform needs roughly 16-32 measurements to match its eight-measurement accuracy, and the advantage generally shrinks as M grows, with a small reversal on RIAWELC at higher budgets.
AI.conclusion: Learning what to measure is especially valuable when measurements are scarce, and the advantage narrows at larger measurement budgets.

title: Trusting Imagined Futures: Auditing Imagined Rewards for VLA Post-Training
summary: Video world models enable candidate actions to be evaluated through imagined outcomes, but high predicted rewards can favor trajectories with poor execution quality. We introduce Trusting Imagined Futures (TIF), an offline supervision selection method for vision-language-action (VLA) post-training that audits predicted rewards using execution feedback. A multidimensional reward model predicts a utility score for candidate ranking and five dimensions of execution quality. An auditor uses reward predictions and uncertainty to identify overestimation patterns learned from paired imagined videos and real executions. TIF accepts the candidate with the highest predicted utility when its advantage over the existing trajectory exceeds a margin and its audit risk passes a threshold; otherwise, it retains the existing supervision. The retained real trajectories then supervise behavior cloning. Across four LIBERO suites and three training seeds, TIF achieves a mean success rate of 76.25%, improving over training on the existing trajectories by 3.00 percentage points with the same trajectory count and training budget. Adding audit gating yields 1.47 percentage points with the reward model and advantage margin held fixed. The gains persist against advantage ranking and logistic regression risk selection at matched replacement counts. On recorded videos from three real robot tasks, TIF increases clean completion among selected trajectories from 58.33% to 70.00% across 60 candidate pools.

AI.tldr: TIF audits the predicted rewards of a video world model before using imagined trajectories for VLA post-training, keeping a candidate only when its advantage and audit risk pass thresholds, and improves behaviour cloning success on LIBERO.
AI.motivation: High predicted rewards from video world models can favour trajectories with poor execution quality, so imagined outcomes need checking against execution feedback before they supervise a policy.
AI.method: A multidimensional reward model predicts a utility score and five execution-quality dimensions, and an auditor uses predictions and uncertainty to flag overestimation patterns learned from paired imagined and real videos; TIF accepts the top candidate when its advantage exceeds a margin and its audit risk passes a threshold, otherwise it keeps the existing trajectory, and retained real trajectories supervise behaviour cloning.
AI.result: Across four LIBERO suites and three seeds, TIF reaches a mean success rate of 76.25%, 3.00 points above training on existing trajectories at the same count and budget, and audit gating adds 1.47 points; on recorded real robot videos, clean completion among selected trajectories rises from 58.33% to 70.00%.
AI.conclusion: Auditing imagined rewards before selecting supervision improves VLA post-training, and the gains persist against advantage ranking and logistic-regression risk selection.

title: Federated Transfer Learning for Medical Image Classification under Mixed Skew
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures and 2 tables. Presented at 4th IEEE International Conference on Federated Learning Technologies and Applications (FLTA 2026)
summary: Deep learning in medical imaging is constrained by data scarcity and by privacy regulations that make centralizing patient data across institutions impractical. Federated Learning (FL) addresses these constraints by keeping data local, but its distributed nature exposes training to strong statistical heterogeneity. Multicentric medical data is particularly affected, exhibiting a mixed skew that combines feature, label, concept, and quantity shifts across centers. Personalized FL mitigates heterogeneity by tailoring a model to each client, yet most methods assume training from scratch, which is unrealistic given the high dimensionality of medical features relative to the limited data available. We propose the Personalized Aligner Federated Pretrained (PAFP) framework, a personalized FL approach built on a pre-trained backbone. PAFP inserts client-specific Feature Alignment modules before the fine-tuned blocks to realign hidden feature distributions toward a server-aggregated target. On the FedISIC benchmark, PAFP attains the highest unweighted balanced accuracy while reducing inter-client performance variance roughly six-fold relative to the strongest baseline, yielding accuracy and cross-client equity jointly. Our code is publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: PAFP is a personalised federated learning framework that uses a pretrained backbone with client-specific feature alignment modules to handle mixed skew in multicentre medical imaging.
AI.motivation: Multicentre medical data have mixed feature, label, concept and quantity shifts, and most personalised federated methods train from scratch, which is unrealistic for high-dimensional medical features with limited data.
AI.method: PAFP inserts client-specific Feature Alignment modules before fine-tuned blocks of a pretrained backbone, realigning hidden feature distributions toward a server-aggregated target.
AI.result: On the FedISIC benchmark, PAFP attains the highest unweighted balanced accuracy and reduces inter-client performance variance roughly six-fold relative to the strongest baseline.
AI.conclusion: The approach is presented as achieving both accuracy and cross-client equity in federated medical image classification under mixed skew.

title: Label-Preserving Fourier Domain Adaptation with Generative-AI and Real Style Donors for 3D Mitral Valve Segmentation
comment: 7 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables, submitted to IEEE for possible publication
summary: Accurate segmentation of the mitral valve from three-dimensional transesophageal echocardiography (3D TEE) is severely restricted by the scarcity of publicly available expert- annotated volumetric datasets. To address this critical limitation, we investigated Fourier Domain Adaptation (FDA), utilizing general-purpose generative-AI images (from platforms like Chat- GPT, Google Gemini, and Microsoft MAI) as annotation-free style donors for 3D mitral valve segmentation. We employed a DeepMitral residual U-Net model on the public MVSeg2023 dataset, comparing six conditions over three runs: real-only training, traditional augmentation, FDA with each generative source, and a non-AI FDA control using real-image style donors, plus an optimization-matched real-only control and a \b{eta} sensitivity analysis. Case-level paired testing showed that FDA with these generative sources led to significant reductions in boundary- and surface-related errors across all three donor conditions relative to the primary real-only baseline. However, the impact on the core segmentation metric, Generalized Dice Score (GDS), proved generator-dependent. ChatGPT-FDA showed a significant GDS advantage over the optimization-matched control but not over the primary baseline, and Gemini-FDA showed no significant GDS difference. Notably, only MAI-FDA provided a statistically robust and significant increase in GDS compared to the primary baseline. The \b{eta} sensitivity was not robust across training runs. These findings confirm that FDA remains an important augmentation mechanism. While generative-AI images offer a practical means of acquiring style diversity without new annotations, the non-AI control performed comparably to ChatGPT-FDA, so we do not conclude that this approach is superior to training with real-image donors.

AI.tldr: Fourier Domain Adaptation with generative-AI images as style donors improves 3D mitral valve segmentation, but the gain in the main overlap metric depends on which generator supplies the donors.
AI.motivation: Public expert-annotated 3D transesophageal echocardiography datasets are scarce, and general-purpose generative-AI images may offer annotation-free style diversity for augmentation.
AI.method: The authors train a DeepMitral residual U-Net on the public MVSeg2023 dataset under six conditions over three runs, comparing real-only training, traditional augmentation, FDA with ChatGPT, Gemini and MAI images, a non-AI FDA control with real-image donors, an optimisation-matched control and a beta sensitivity analysis, with case-level paired tests.
AI.result: FDA with all generative sources significantly reduces boundary and surface errors relative to real-only training; for Generalized Dice Score, only MAI-FDA gives a statistically robust significant increase over the primary baseline, ChatGPT-FDA is significant only against the optimisation-matched control, Gemini-FDA shows no difference, and the non-AI control performs comparably to ChatGPT-FDA.
AI.conclusion: FDA remains a useful augmentation mechanism, but the authors do not conclude that generative-AI donors are superior to real-image donors.

title: What Does It Mean to Remove an Edge? Intervention-Aware Fidelity for Graph Neural Network Explanations
summary: Graph neural network explanations are often evaluated via deletion fidelity, i.e., by deleting their top-ranked edges and measuring the resulting change in model output. Yet, in a message-passing GNN, "deleting an edge" does not specify a unique intervention. Structural deletion removes the edge from the graph and recomputes quantities such as degree normalization and attention, whereas message suppression leaves this structural context intact while blocking the message carried by the edge. The meaning of deletion fidelity therefore depends on what the intervention targets in the model computation. We formalize this distinction and derive sufficient conditions for exact equivalence. The two interventions coincide for additive message passing with edge-set-independent coefficients, but can diverge when aggregation depends on the presence of zero messages or when removing an edge changes the coefficients applied to surviving messages. We then construct intervention-specific edge attributions and evaluate each resulting ranking under both interventions, testing whether their relative fidelity changes with the evaluation intervention. Across nine datasets and a panel of GIN, GCN, and GATv2 models at depths 2--5, all nine GIN controls satisfy the equivalence predicted by the theory. On the target logit, the relative fidelity of the two rankings depends on the evaluation intervention in 10 of 11 reportable GCN and GATv2 cells, and in nine of them each ranking has the larger deletion area under the intervention it was built with. Deletion fidelity is thus not a property of an edge ranking alone. Evaluation protocols should explicitly report the intervention, output functional, target, and perturbation unit, and test alternative intervention semantics when the scientific question does not uniquely determine one.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that deleting an edge in a GNN is not a unique intervention and shows that structural deletion and message suppression can give different deletion-fidelity rankings, so fidelity must state its intervention.
AI.motivation: Graph neural network explanations are commonly evaluated by deletion fidelity, but in message-passing models "deleting an edge" can mean structural removal or suppression of its message, and the meaning of the metric depends on which is used.
AI.method: The authors formalise the distinction, derive sufficient conditions for exact equivalence of the two interventions, build intervention-specific edge attributions, and evaluate each ranking under both interventions across nine datasets and GIN, GCN and GATv2 models at depths 2 to 5.
AI.result: All nine GIN controls satisfy the predicted equivalence, while on the target logit the relative fidelity of the two rankings depends on the evaluation intervention in 10 of 11 reportable GCN and GATv2 cells, with each ranking usually having the larger deletion area under its own intervention.
AI.conclusion: Deletion fidelity is not a property of an edge ranking alone, and evaluation protocols should report the intervention, output functional, target and perturbation unit.

title: Non-Interfering Asymmetric AdamW Updates for Constrained Exploration of Equifinality in Hybrid Models
summary: Hybrid models let neural networks supply the unresolved parameters of a process-based simulator, and are fitted to observations that constrain aggregate fluxes and storages but not the internal partitioning that produces them. Such a fit is equifinal: configurations indistinguishable in the observed aggregates can disagree substantially about the unobserved internals, and therefore about the mechanism they attribute to the same data. We study evapotranspiration, whose total flux is observed while its split into transpiration and evaporation is not. A model ensemble built from random seeds alone spans only a narrow band of the partitionings the data admit. We produce the spread deliberately, training members under auxiliary repulsion on transpiration, subject to the fit to observations not degrading. Non-interference is usually arranged by making the auxiliary gradient orthogonal to the main one, but under AdamW the applied step is a preconditioned momentum direction, so orthogonality between raw gradients no longer implies it. We introduce Non-interfering Asymmetric Network Optimization (NANO), an update whose first-order effect on the main loss is exactly that of the main objective alone, whose auxiliary step is bounded, and which concentrates repulsion in the coordinates the main gradient leaves idle.

AI.tldr: NANO is an AdamW-compatible update for training an ensemble of hybrid evapotranspiration models that spreads transpiration-evaporation partitionings while leaving the main fit objective's first-order effect unchanged.
AI.motivation: Hybrid models fitted to total evapotranspiration are equifinal, so configurations matching the observed flux can disagree about its unobserved split, and random seeds alone produce only a narrow spread of partitionings.
AI.method: Members are trained with auxiliary repulsion on transpiration subject to the main fit, and NANO, a non-interfering asymmetric optimisation update, is designed so that under AdamW its first-order effect on the main loss equals that of the main objective, its auxiliary step is bounded, and repulsion concentrates in coordinates the main gradient leaves idle.
AI.result: The abstract describes the method's properties but reports no numerical results.
AI.conclusion: Under AdamW, orthogonality of raw gradients does not guarantee non-interference, and NANO provides a non-interfering alternative for deliberately exploring equifinal solutions.

title: Koopman Generative Operators for Efficient Probabilistic Time-Series Forecasting
summary: Probabilistic time-series forecasting requires models that simultaneously capture structured temporal dynamics, expressive uncertainty, and efficient inference, yet existing approaches fall short of this goal: latent dynamical models impose structure but rely on restrictive generation mechanisms, while modern generative methods such as diffusion and flow matching achieve flexibility at the cost of iterative and computationally expensive sampling. We introduce the Koopman Generative Operator (KGO), a probabilistic forecasting method that conceptualizes prediction as the evolution of structured uncertainty. KGO integrates three core components: (1) Koopman Patch Embedding (KoPE) for temporally consistent latent trajectory extrapolation; (2) Koopman Flow Matching (KoFM), which enables fast, single-step generation through a closed-form matrix exponential in a Koopman latent space, bypassing iterative sampling; and (3) an Adaptive Uncertainty Gate (AUG), which provides probabilistic forecasts by adapting uncertainty per-variable and per-horizon, corresponding to a learned decomposition of aleatoric uncertainty without manual tuning. By unifying these components, KGO achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on 13/17 ProbTS benchmarks in CRPS and 16/17 in NMAE. Further, by eliminating iterative sampling, KGO delivers at least a 25$\times$ reduction in inference time compared to iterative generative models. These results position KGO as a practical and principled framework that advances the accuracy-efficiency trade-off in probabilistic time-series forecasting, combining leading accuracy on the evaluated benchmarks with fast, single-step generation.

AI.tldr: Koopman Generative Operator (KGO) is a probabilistic time-series forecaster that uses a Koopman latent space to generate forecasts in a single step, reporting state-of-the-art accuracy on most ProbTS benchmarks and at least 25x faster inference than iterative generative models.
AI.motivation: Latent dynamical models impose structure but use restrictive generation, while diffusion and flow-matching models are flexible but need costly iterative sampling.
AI.method: KGO combines Koopman Patch Embedding for latent trajectory extrapolation, Koopman Flow Matching that generates in one step through a closed-form matrix exponential in Koopman latent space, and an Adaptive Uncertainty Gate that adapts uncertainty per variable and per horizon.
AI.result: KGO achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on 13 of 17 ProbTS benchmarks in CRPS and 16 of 17 in NMAE, and delivers at least a 25x reduction in inference time compared with iterative generative models.
AI.conclusion: KGO is presented as a practical framework that improves the accuracy-efficiency trade-off in probabilistic time-series forecasting.

title: Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Submodular Trajectory Rewards
summary: We study cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning with decoupled dynamics and a monotone submodular reward function over joint trajectories. Due to the non-additive reward, an optimal policy may depend on the history of all agents. This dependence makes exact optimization exponential in the horizon and the number of agents. To overcome this challenge while retaining theoretical guarantees, we introduce pre-window curvature $c_m$, which quantifies how states visited more than $m$ steps earlier reduce current marginal gains. Using this curvature to control the error from restricting the policy of each agent to depend only on its last $m+1$ states, we propose a greedy algorithm that exploits the decoupled dynamics to optimize local policies sequentially. For fixed $m$, the algorithm achieves a $\frac{1-c_m}{2-c_m}$ approximation guarantee up to estimation error, and its computation time is polynomial in the number of agents and the horizon. We recover the known $1/2$-factor approximation for time-additive rewards and obtain an approximation factor no smaller than the known total-curvature bound for a single agent. We formulate multi-agent traffic monitoring as an example of this framework and evaluate our algorithm on it.

AI.tldr: The paper gives a greedy algorithm for cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning with submodular trajectory rewards, with an approximation guarantee governed by a new pre-window curvature parameter.
AI.motivation: With non-additive joint-trajectory rewards, the optimal policy can depend on the full history of all agents, making exact optimisation exponential in the horizon and the number of agents.
AI.method: The authors define pre-window curvature c_m, which measures how states visited more than m steps earlier reduce current marginal gains, restrict each agent's policy to its last m+1 states, and optimise local policies sequentially with a greedy algorithm that exploits decoupled dynamics.
AI.result: For fixed m the algorithm achieves a (1 - c_m)/(2 - c_m) approximation guarantee up to estimation error in polynomial time, recovers the known 1/2 factor for time-additive rewards, and gives a factor no smaller than the known total-curvature bound for a single agent; it is evaluated on multi-agent traffic monitoring.
AI.conclusion: Bounded-memory local policies with a curvature-based guarantee offer a tractable approach to submodular cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning.

title: Training Specialist LLMs on Your Phone: Forward-Only Optimization via Block-Spectral Coordinates
summary: Large language models (LLMs) on personal devices keep user data local, but limited memory restricts their general capability. Since most user-specific tasks do not require the breadth of frontier models, a practical solution is to adapt a shared on-device model into lightweight specialists. However, backpropagation is prohibitive in memory, and users rarely provide labeled data. We present MobileSpec, a system that trains specialists with forward passes alone and learns from automatically checked task outcomes, as in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Because forward-only updates are built from random perturbations, training is efficient only when these perturbations resemble the weight changes of RLVR, which largely preserve the singular values of pretrained weights and rotate their singular vectors. The core algorithm of MobileSpec, FuRA-S, produces such perturbations while training only the block-spectral coordinates of pretrained weights, namely the singular values of their column blocks. As we show theoretically and empirically, rescaling these blocks independently shifts their relative contributions to each weight matrix and thereby rotates its singular vectors. Since this update can be rewritten as a transformation of the layer input, FuRA-S also adapts INT4 models without modifying their weights. With specialists of only 1-5 MB that update 0.015-0.05% of the parameters, MobileSpec raises the success rate of a phone-use agent from 6-23% up to 89-100% and trains a personalized 8B model on an iPhone 16 Pro overnight. On RLVR benchmarks, FuRA-S is competitive with full-parameter evolution strategies (ES) and outperforms ES over LoRA adapters and quantized ES on INT4 models.

AI.tldr: MobileSpec trains task-specific on-device LLM specialists using forward passes only, learning from automatically checked outcomes, and it raises phone-use agent success from 6-23% to 89-100%.
AI.motivation: Backpropagation is too memory-hungry for on-device LLM adaptation, and users rarely provide labelled data, so specialists must be trained from forward passes and verifiable outcomes.
AI.method: The FuRA-S algorithm trains only the block-spectral coordinates of pretrained weights, the singular values of their column blocks, to produce random perturbations resembling RLVR weight changes, and it also adapts INT4 models by rewriting the update as a transformation of the layer input.
AI.result: Specialists of 1-5 MB update 0.015-0.05% of parameters and raise the success rate of a phone-use agent from 6-23% to 89-100%; a personalised 8B model is trained overnight on an iPhone 16 Pro, and on RLVR benchmarks FuRA-S is competitive with full-parameter evolution strategies and outperforms ES over LoRA adapters and quantised ES on INT4 models.
AI.conclusion: Forward-only, block-spectral training makes on-device specialisation of LLMs practical in memory and data terms.

title: On the Complexity of Finite-Sum Nonconvex-Strongly-Concave Minimax Optimization with Exact Proximal Oracles
comment: 50 pages, including appendices and references. Lean 4 formalization of the lower bounds in the ancillary files
summary: Finite-sum nonconvex-strongly-concave minimax problems arise in adversarial training and distributionally robust learning. Their known lower bounds cover only linear-span algorithms, zero-respecting algorithms, or a restricted proximal protocol. They leave open the power of exact component proximal steps, whose responses are global saddle points of regularized component problems and can expose directions that gradients do not reveal. We show that neither unrestricted adaptivity nor exact proximal access improves the polynomial complexity. We consider $n$ components with joint mean-squared smoothness $L$ and condition number $\kappa$, started from a point with primal gap at most $\Delta$ and joint gradient norm at most $\sqrt{2L\Delta}$. For $\varepsilon^2/(L\Delta)$ below a universal constant, every randomized adaptive algorithm with exact component values, gradients, and proximal responses needs $\Omega(n+\min\{\sqrt n\,\kappa,n^{3/4}\sqrt\kappa\}L\Delta/\varepsilon^2)$ component queries in the worst case to find an $\varepsilon$-stationary point of the value function. A method using only component gradients attains this rate up to a factor $\log^2(2+\kappa)$, including initialization. Zhou (arXiv:2610.04944) concurrently proves the same rate for zero-respecting first-order methods. In our hard instances, every component admits proximal steps with the same step sizes, and a response for a component reveals hidden directions only up to the first one assigned to another component.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that, for finite-sum nonconvex-strongly-concave minimax problems with exact proximal oracles, the polynomial complexity cannot be improved, with a matching lower bound and a near-optimal gradient-only method.
AI.motivation: Known lower bounds cover only linear-span, zero-respecting or restricted proximal algorithms, leaving open whether exact component proximal steps and unrestricted adaptivity can reduce complexity.
AI.method: The authors prove a lower bound for randomised adaptive algorithms with exact component values, gradients and proximal responses under joint mean-squared smoothness L and condition number kappa, using hard instances in which proximal responses reveal hidden directions only up to a limited point.
AI.result: The lower bound is Omega(n + min{sqrt(n) kappa, n^(3/4) sqrt(kappa)} L Delta / epsilon^2) component queries for an epsilon-stationary point, and a method using only component gradients attains this up to a log^2(2 + kappa) factor.
AI.conclusion: Neither unrestricted adaptivity nor exact proximal access improves the polynomial complexity, and the same rate was concurrently proven for zero-respecting first-order methods by Zhou (arXiv:2610.04944).

title: Sleep-Disordered Breathing Detection with Quantum Recurrent Neural Networks
summary: This work investigates the application of Quantum Recurrent Neural Networks to the binary classification of sleep-disordered breathing events in time-series data, aiming to distinguish between apneic and normal breathing episodes. A variational classical--quantum architecture is proposed and evaluated against classical Recurrent Neural Network models. Experiments were conducted on multiple real-world datasets with varying levels of complexity to assess the strengths and limitations of the quantum approach. In the comparative analysis, both classical and quantum models showed comparable performance. The quantum model achieved superior performance on the smallest dataset, while yielding slightly weaker results in the most complex setting. However, the quantum approach exhibited notable strengths, such as competitive performance despite a drastically reduced parameter count and low-qubit regime, as well as good generalization capabilities. These results suggest that, despite current hardware and algorithmic limitations, variational quantum recurrent models represent a promising alternative for time-series classification as Quantum Computing technologies continue to mature.

AI.tldr: A variational quantum recurrent network is compared with classical RNNs for binary classification of apneic versus normal breathing in time-series data, with comparable performance and far fewer parameters.
AI.motivation: Sleep-disordered breathing detection from time series could benefit from quantum recurrent models, and their practical value at current hardware scale is unclear.
AI.method: A variational classical-quantum recurrent architecture is proposed and evaluated against classical RNN models on several real-world datasets of differing complexity.
AI.result: Classical and quantum models perform comparably overall; the quantum model is better on the smallest dataset and slightly weaker on the most complex setting, with competitive results despite a drastically reduced parameter count and a low-qubit regime, as well as good generalisation.
AI.conclusion: Variational quantum recurrent models are presented as a promising alternative for time-series classification as quantum hardware matures, despite current limitations.

title: Anomaly Detection on Resource-Constrained Devices with Reservoir Computing
summary: Anomaly detection at the edge requires the deployment of models that achieve competitive performance, while minimizing computational cost and memory footprint. In this article, we investigate the suitability of the Mahalanobis Distance of Reservoir States (MDRS), an unsupervised time-series anomaly detection method, for resource-constrained devices and propose two optimizations to reduce its computational requirements. Specifically, we replace random reservoir connectivity (MDRS-Rand) with a circular shift (MDRS-Circ) and show that the anomaly score for an entire time series can be computed from the final reservoir state alone. Furthermore, we show that exploiting the reservoir's temporal memory enables more efficient input preprocessing, further reducing computational cost. We evaluate the MDRS variants on the MLPerf Tiny anomaly detection benchmark against the reference autoencoder and other anomaly detection methods, and deploy their inference kernels on a NUCLEO-F401RE microcontroller to assess latency, estimate energy consumption, and measure memory footprint. Among the evaluated methods, only MDRS and the autoencoder meet the benchmark's performance target, with MDRS requiring fewer operations and smaller models. With optimized preprocessing, MDRS achieves an ROC AUC of 0.869, a model size of 24 KB, an estimated energy consumption of 24 uJ per inference, and a latency of 0.32 ms, corresponding to a 75.9x speedup over the autoencoder with standard preprocessing.

AI.tldr: MDRS with a circular-shift reservoir and reduced preprocessing achieves MLPerf Tiny anomaly detection performance on a microcontroller with a 24 KB model, 0.32 ms latency and 75.9x speedup over the autoencoder.
AI.motivation: Edge anomaly detection needs models that are accurate yet cheap in computation and memory, and the reservoir-based MDRS method has not been adapted for resource-constrained devices.
AI.method: The authors replace random reservoir connectivity with a circular shift (MDRS-Circ), compute the whole-series anomaly score from the final reservoir state, exploit reservoir temporal memory for cheaper input preprocessing, and deploy inference kernels on a NUCLEO-F401RE microcontroller.
AI.result: On the MLPerf Tiny anomaly detection benchmark, only MDRS and the autoencoder meet the performance target; with optimised preprocessing MDRS achieves ROC AUC 0.869, 24 KB model size, an estimated 24 uJ per inference and 0.32 ms latency, a 75.9x speedup over the autoencoder with standard preprocessing.
AI.conclusion: MDRS with the proposed optimisations is a lightweight option for edge anomaly detection, requiring fewer operations and smaller models than the autoencoder.

title: DLER: Dual-Logit Experience Replay for Online Continual Learning
summary: Online continual learning aims to continuously train neural networks on a non-stationary data stream in a single pass. Rehearsal-based methods alleviate catastrophic forgetting by replaying stored samples, but the imbalance between current and previous data often leads to predictions biased toward current classes. Many approaches have been proposed to overcome the forgetting problem by correcting the bias; however, they still need to be improved in an online fashion. By decomposing the dot-product logits into an angle factor and a norm factor, our analysis reveals that the angle factor efficiently captures novel knowledge but is particularly susceptible to prediction bias, whereas the norm factor helps preserve historical knowledge. Based on these observations, we propose Dual-Logit Experience Replay (DLER), which exploits dual-logits for both model optimization and memory management. Specifically, DLER learns current samples using cosine logits and incorporates additional dot-product logits when replaying previous samples to mitigate prediction bias. To strengthen dual-logit learning under limited replay memory, an auxiliary supervised contrastive objective promotes angular compactness within each class, extending corrections learned from limited replay samples to other samples of the same class. Meanwhile, we introduce a memory update strategy that preferentially retains samples for which dot-product prediction assigns a higher probability to the correct class than cosine prediction, aligning sample selection with dual-logit training. Extensive experiments on three datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of DLER, particularly under limited memory budgets.

AI.tldr: DLER is a rehearsal method for online continual learning that uses cosine logits for current data and dot-product logits for replayed data, with a memory policy that retains samples favoured by the dot-product prediction.
AI.motivation: In online continual learning, replay leaves predictions biased toward current classes, and existing bias corrections are not yet effective in a single-pass online setting.
AI.method: Logits are decomposed into an angle factor and a norm factor; DLER learns current samples with cosine logits, adds dot-product logits when replaying previous samples, adds an auxiliary supervised contrastive objective for angular compactness within each class, and uses a memory update that keeps samples where the dot-product prediction gives higher probability to the correct class than the cosine prediction.
AI.result: The abstract reports that extensive experiments on three datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of DLER, particularly under limited memory budgets, without giving specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Dual-logit learning, combined with a memory policy aligned to it, is presented as an effective way to reduce prediction bias in online continual learning, especially with small replay memories.

title: Attending to Memory Writes Reduces Seed Variability in Recurrent Length Generalization
summary: Recurrent memory requires learning useful updates, but attention added to assist learning can also compromise length generalization. We study bounded delta attention: causal attention over uncorrected update proposals whose bounded correction enters the recurrent update. Its implementation in TraceRelay combines additive phase recurrence with attention computed before a parallel scan. On prefix-supervised modulo-5, trained at lengths 1--40, three findings characterize its behavior at length 80. First, upper delta attention attains $70.81\pm8.26$% accuracy across seven seeds, versus $69.21\pm22.42$% for the local-attention recurrent baseline (mean $\pm$ sample SD): a 63.2% reduction in SD with a similar mean. Upper state attention also reduces variation, reaching $74.75\pm6.24$%, so this benefit is not unique to update-level attention. Disabling the upper delta correction retains $70.62\pm8.60$%. Second, blocking gradients at the delta-attention inputs changes accuracy to $65.25\pm12.40$% in the matched seven-seed comparison, increasing SD by 50.2%. It also delays a 99% validation threshold on average among the same six seeds that reach it; the 95% threshold is reached earlier on average with input-gradient blocking across all seven seeds. Third, lower delta attention exhibits substantially less extrapolation degradation than lower state attention: 62.60% versus 19.40%, against a 71.06% baseline. Removing its correction reduces accuracy to 22.56%; its advantage over lower state attention also persists under input-gradient blocking. These observations motivate bounded update-level attention as a recurrent learning scaffold, combining reduced seed variation with less severe degradation in a placement where state attention fails.

AI.tldr: Bounded delta attention over uncorrected update proposals reduces seed variability in recurrent length generalisation on modulo-5, while keeping accuracy at length 80 comparable to the local-attention baseline.
AI.motivation: Attention added to recurrent memory to aid learning can harm length generalisation, and recurrent models trained on short sequences are sensitive to random seeds.
AI.method: The authors study bounded delta attention, which is causal attention over uncorrected update proposals whose bounded correction enters the recurrent update, implemented in TraceRelay with additive phase recurrence and attention computed before a parallel scan, and compare it on prefix-supervised modulo-5 trained at lengths 1 to 40 across seven seeds.
AI.result: Upper delta attention reaches 70.81 ± 8.26% accuracy at length 80 versus 69.21 ± 22.42% for the local-attention baseline, a 63.2% reduction in standard deviation; blocking input gradients raises the standard deviation by 50.2%, and lower delta attention degrades less under extrapolation (62.60% versus 19.40% for lower state attention, against a 71.06% baseline).
AI.conclusion: Bounded update-level attention is presented as a recurrent learning scaffold that reduces seed variation and degrades less under length extrapolation than state attention.

title: Cool Graphs: Active Property Search Towards Quantum Nano-Refrigerators
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 20 pages. Code: this https URL (archived at this https URL)
summary: Nanodevices that absorb energy from their thermal environment can act as quantum refrigerators. Finding suitable configurations, however, is a needle-in-a-haystack problem: the many-body state space scales exponentially with the size of the device, where each candidate configuration requires an expensive quantum-chemical computation. We introduce a search framework that couples a Graph Variational Autoencoder (GVAE) with an uncertainty-driven Active Learning (AL) loop to efficiently identify energy-absorbing configurations in electronic junctions with a 2D "working material" to be optimized. The GVAE maps physical parameters - site energies, coupling matrices, temperature - into a smooth latent space that distinguishes cooling from dissipative parameter regimes, achieving a classification discriminability of $0.920 \pm 0.004$ on held-out configurations and $0.895 \pm 0.010$ on unseen extrapolation topologies. An AL pipeline based on Monte Carlo dropout then targets the decision boundary, iteratively selecting the candidates where the model is least certain for simulation. Over 32 AL cycles, the uncertainty-driven strategy discovers energy absorbing systems at rates consistently exceeding the random baseline across all tested topologies (where only 1.9-8.4% of configurations exhibit the desired property), providing a data-efficient pathway for navigating a combinatorically large design space. The learned latent space organizes configurations along physically interpretable axes, that correlate with underlying microscopic model parameters. This hints at the existence of "cooling coordinates" - low-dimensional, physically interpretable quantities separating cooling from non-cooling regimes. Our framework, thus, paves a new way towards effective cooling of nanoscale electronic information processing devices, to reduce the environmental footprint of high performance computing.

AI.tldr: The paper couples a Graph Variational Autoencoder with an uncertainty-driven active learning loop to search for electronic-junction configurations that absorb energy from their thermal environment, i.e. act as quantum refrigerators. The search reaches energy-absorbing systems at rates consistently above a random baseline across all tested topologies.
AI.motivation: Finding cooling configurations is a needle-in-a-haystack problem because the many-body state space grows exponentially with device size and each candidate needs an expensive quantum-chemical computation.
AI.method: A GVAE maps physical parameters (site energies, coupling matrices, temperature) into a smooth latent space, and Monte Carlo dropout active learning iteratively selects the candidates where the model is least certain, targeting the decision boundary.
AI.result: The GVAE reaches classification discriminability of 0.920 +/- 0.004 on held-out configurations and 0.895 +/- 0.010 on unseen extrapolation topologies. Over 32 AL cycles the uncertainty-driven strategy beats random sampling on all topologies, where only 1.9-8.4% of configurations have the desired property.
AI.conclusion: The learned latent space separates cooling from dissipative regimes along physically interpretable axes that correlate with microscopic model parameters, which the authors read as hints of "cooling coordinates" and as a data-efficient route to designing cooling in nanoscale electronics.

title: Modulating Merging Strengths via Joint Loss Estimation for LoRA-based Continual Learning
summary: Continual learning (CL) aims to adapt models to new tasks while preserving previously learned knowledge. Recently, Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), a representative Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) method, has gained increasing attention in CL due to its efficiency and scalability. Several LoRA-based merging methods maintain a single inference model by scaling the newly learned LoRA update with one coefficient and merging it into the previous weights after each task. However, they usually control the whole update with a shared scalar factor, although different update elements may affect previous and current tasks in different ways. To address this issue, we propose Merging Strength Modulation via Joint Loss Estimation (M2LE). It consists of Hessian Information-guided Adaptive Merging (HIM) and Task Simulation Perturbation for Merging (TSP). Instead of searching for a global merge coefficient, HIM directly solves for the target merged update under a joint objective over previous and current tasks. Solving this objective gives an analytic solution that naturally takes the form of element-wise modulation over the current task LoRA update. To improve the stability of the learned update under subsequent merging, we introduce TSP which simulates different tasks interference. Experiments on multiple benchmarks show that M2LE consistently outperforms existing PEFT-based continual learning methods. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes M2LE, which replaces the single shared scalar that scales a new LoRA update with element-wise modulation derived from a joint loss over previous and current tasks. It reports consistent gains over existing PEFT-based continual learning methods on multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing LoRA-based merging methods scale the whole new update with one shared coefficient, although different update elements may affect previous and current tasks in different ways.
AI.method: M2LE combines Hessian Information-guided Adaptive Merging (HIM), which solves analytically for the merged update under a joint objective over previous and current tasks, with Task Simulation Perturbation for Merging (TSP), which simulates task interference to stabilise the learned update under later merges.
AI.result: HIM yields an analytic solution in the form of element-wise modulation of the current task LoRA update. M2LE consistently outperforms existing PEFT-based continual learning methods on multiple benchmarks; the abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Element-wise, loss-informed merging is presented as a better alternative to a global merge coefficient for keeping a single LoRA-based model across sequential tasks.

title: Deep Neural Operator Learning for stochastic heat equations and applications
summary: In this paper, we establish a universal approximation theorem for solution operators of semilinear stochastic heat equations in spatial dimension \(d\ge2\), extending deep neural operator approximation results to SPDEs with distribution-valued Gaussian forcing. A smooth Fourier cutoff reduces the forcing to finitely many measurements, while Besov and Schauder estimates control the resulting solution error. The finite-dimensional solution map is then approximated by ReLU branch networks together with grid-based trunk functions, yielding explicit bounds on the numbers of forcing measurements and trunk functions and approximation in every finite stochastic moment. For linear equations, the reduction coincides with truncation of the first Wiener chaos. Lastly, as an application, we prove a high-probability local-in-time approximation theorem for stochastic Navier--Stokes equations, with finite measurements of both the initial condition and forcing and an explicit sensing rate.

AI.tldr: The paper proves a universal approximation theorem for solution operators of semilinear stochastic heat equations in spatial dimension d >= 2 with distribution-valued Gaussian forcing, and extends it to a local-in-time result for stochastic Navier-Stokes equations. The approximation uses finitely many forcing measurements.
AI.motivation: Deep neural operator approximation results were available for deterministic PDEs but had not been extended to SPDEs with rough, distribution-valued Gaussian forcing.
AI.method: A smooth Fourier cutoff reduces the forcing to finitely many measurements, Besov and Schauder estimates control the solution error, and the finite-dimensional solution map is approximated by ReLU branch networks combined with grid-based trunk functions.
