This equation accounts for nonlinearity, \(\eta\), and attenuation, \(\gamma\). To solve this equation, we observe that traditional solvers may struggle to do so correctly. This is due to the difficulties arising from the nonlinear nature of the equation. We solve the equation by defining three synthetic cases - linear (\(\eta=0.001\), \(\gamma=10^{-6}\)), shock-dominated (\(\eta=0.02\), \(\gamma=10^{-6}\)), and dissipation-dominated (\(\eta=0.01\), \(\gamma=5\times10^{-4}\)) - and using Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) to showcase the solution. A sinusoidal activation function is used to capture the oscillatory behavior of the problem. The results of our study, with PDE residual converging to at least \(10^{-6}\), boundary condition loss to \(10^{-5}\), and the PINN loss converging to \(10^{-5}\) for each case at \(30,000\) epochs, show that \(\gamma\) scales the rate of amplitude decay, while \(\eta\) governs frequency-dependent phase speeds.

AI.tldr: The paper solves the one-dimensional nonlinear Westervelt equation for ultrasound propagation with physics-informed neural networks, using a sinusoidal activation, on linear, shock-dominated and dissipation-dominated synthetic cases.
AI.motivation: Modelling finite-amplitude ultrasound in biological tissue requires accuracy, and traditional solvers may struggle with the nonlinearity of the Westervelt equation.
AI.method: Physics-informed neural networks with a sinusoidal activation function are trained on three synthetic parameter cases, linear (eta = 0.001, gamma = 10^-6), shock-dominated (eta = 0.02, gamma = 10^-6) and dissipation-dominated (eta = 0.01, gamma = 5 x 10^-4), for 30,000 epochs.
AI.result: PDE residual converges to at least 10^-6, boundary-condition loss to 10^-5 and the total PINN loss to 10^-5 in each case; gamma scales the rate of amplitude decay, while eta governs frequency-dependent phase speeds.
AI.conclusion: PINNs can solve the Westervelt equation across linear, shock and dissipative regimes, and the roles of nonlinearity and attenuation parameters are identified from the solutions.

title: Physics-informed traditional and generative Mori-Zwanzig-reduced models for multiscale systems
summary: Model reduction via the Mori-Zwanzig (MZ) formalism is well understood for coarse-grained representations constructed from standard basis functions such as Fourier functions. We show that the same formalism can be used to build reduced-order models in bases discovered by physics-informed machine learning. The fluctuation-dissipation theorem (FDT) is used to close the resulting non-Markovian evolution equations for the expansion coefficients of the learned basis. We further introduce a complementary, generative closure model. Relative to the Markovian dynamics alone, both the MZ and generative closures substantially improve predictions of the filtered states.

AI.tldr: The paper extends Mori-Zwanzig reduction to bases discovered by physics-informed machine learning and closes the non-Markovian equations with the fluctuation-dissipation theorem plus a generative closure, improving predictions of filtered states over Markovian dynamics.
AI.motivation: Mori-Zwanzig reduction is well understood for standard basis functions such as Fourier modes, but it has not been applied to bases learned from physics-informed machine learning.
AI.method: The Mori-Zwanzig formalism is applied in learned bases, the resulting non-Markovian equations for expansion coefficients are closed with the fluctuation-dissipation theorem, and a complementary generative closure model is introduced.
AI.result: Relative to Markovian dynamics alone, both the Mori-Zwanzig and generative closures substantially improve predictions of the filtered states.
AI.conclusion: Mori-Zwanzig reduction can be carried out in physics-informed learned bases, and both closures are useful for multiscale reduced-order modelling.

title: Learning curves in natural and artificial systems
summary: A general mathematical model of experience formation is considered, in which the learning level is defined as the probability that the next value of the uncertainty factor has already been mastered and not forgotten. Within this model the shape of the learning curve is derived, and it turns out to be determined primarily by the distribution of situation occurrence: a uniform distribution yields an exponential curve, whereas a power-law distribution yields a power-law curve whose exponent equals the ratio of the distribution exponent to that same exponent increased by one. Both mechanisms generating power-law curves, established earlier in the analysis of debugging, assembly and repair activities, are shown to have been independently rediscovered in deep learning theory as the "frequency" and "spectral" mechanisms of scaling laws for artificial neural networks, while the exponential curves of machine learning (contraction operators, strongly convex optimization, stationary reinforcement) are generated by the same constancy of the contraction coefficient that was revealed half a century earlier in models of radioactive decay, the first-order lag element, and others. A solution is given for the problem of choosing a training distribution that differs from the deployment distribution. A methodological consequence is discussed: three distinct mechanisms generate curves indistinguishable in shape, so an observed learning curve does not allow one to judge the "internal" structure of the learning system.

AI.tldr: The paper models experience formation by defining learning level as the probability that the next uncertainty value has been mastered and not forgotten, showing that situation-occurrence distribution determines whether learning curves are exponential or power-law.
AI.motivation: Learning curves in natural and artificial systems are often described by separate mechanisms, and the link between scaling laws in deep learning and classical curve generators is unclear.
AI.method: Within a general model of experience formation, the learning curve shape is derived from the distribution of situation occurrence, giving an exponential curve for a uniform distribution and a power-law curve with exponent equal to the distribution exponent divided by that exponent plus one for a power-law distribution; a training distribution differing from the deployment distribution is also addressed.
AI.result: Two power-law mechanisms established earlier for debugging, assembly and repair activities correspond to the frequency and spectral mechanisms of deep-learning scaling laws, and exponential curves in machine learning arise from a constant contraction coefficient.
AI.conclusion: Three distinct mechanisms can produce curves indistinguishable in shape, so an observed learning curve cannot by itself reveal the internal structure of the learning system.

title: Regret-based Characterization, Information Limits, and the Sample Complexity of Auditing Adaptive Policies
summary:
A policy can earn its performance by where it locates on average or by reacting to information. For any Markov policy $\pi$ in a finite-horizon MDP, let $
u$ be its open-loop marginal, which plays $\pi$'s average action distribution at each step. We show that $J(\pi)-J(
u)$ equals $\sum_t tr Cov(Q^
u_t,\pi_t)$ under endogenous dynamics. Audits based on immediate costs alone can have the wrong sign. Writing the covariance as a joint-versus-product gap gives the bound $|J(\pi)-J(
u)|\le\sum_t span_t\sqrt{I(s_t;a_t)/2}$, with a sharp constant. Hence, an MDP's adaptivity gap is bounded by the information that its optimal policy uses. Estimating $J(\pi)-J(
u)$ from $\pi$'s own bandit-feedback logs takes $\Theta( ar\chi^2 \log(1/\eta)/\delta^2)$ rounds, where $ ar\chi^2$ is an average $\chi^2$-divergence. At the same time, deterministic non-constant policies cannot be audited at all. We also provide an importance-sampling auditor for episodic MDPs.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that the performance gap between an adaptive Markov policy and its open-loop marginal equals a sum of covariance terms, bounds it by the information the policy uses, and gives a bandit-feedback auditor with a sample-complexity result.
AI.motivation: Auditing whether a policy earns performance by reacting to information or by its average action location requires a principled decomposition, since immediate-cost audits can have the wrong sign.
AI.method: For a Markov policy in a finite-horizon MDP and its open-loop marginal, the gap is written as a sum of covariance traces under endogenous dynamics, bounded via a joint-versus-product information gap with a sharp constant, and estimated from the policy's own bandit-feedback logs with an importance-sampling auditor for episodic MDPs.
AI.result: The gap is bounded by a sum of span terms times the square root of half the mutual information between states and actions, so the adaptivity gap is bounded by the information the optimal policy uses; estimation takes Theta(chi-bar^2 log(1/eta)/delta^2) rounds, where chi-bar^2 is an average chi-squared divergence; deterministic non-constant policies cannot be audited.
AI.conclusion: Adaptivity can be audited from bandit feedback with a sample-complexity characterisation, but some deterministic policies cannot be audited at all.

title: Post-stratified importance sampling
summary: Importance sampling is a building block of modern statistical computing, but the weighted estimate is prone to high or infinite variance. Moreover, its empirical standard error is often unreliable, leaving importance sampling without practical uncertainty quantification. Motivated by multilevel regression and poststratification (MRP) in survey sampling, we propose post-stratified importance sampling (PIS) for estimating target expectations from proposal draws. PIS reformulates arbitrarily high-dimensional weighting into two one-dimensional probabilistic modeling problems: regression for the conditional mean given the importance ratio and marginal density estimation for the importance ratio. Different modeling choices yield a family of PIS estimators, encompassing ordinary importance sampling as a special case. We develop a model-based implementation that combines one-dimensional Gaussian process regression for the conditional mean and score-informed heavy-tailed density estimation for the marginal law, using both the observed weights and the available density evaluations. We study the oracle gains of PIS and establish consistency under general and model-specific conditions. Simulations and applications to cross-validation demonstrate improvements in estimation accuracy and uncertainty quantification.

AI.tldr: Post-stratified importance sampling reformulates high-dimensional importance weighting as two one-dimensional modelling problems, using Gaussian process regression and heavy-tailed density estimation to improve accuracy and uncertainty quantification.
AI.motivation: Importance sampling estimates are prone to high or infinite variance, and their empirical standard errors are often unreliable, so practical uncertainty quantification is lacking.
AI.method: Inspired by multilevel regression and poststratification, the method estimates the conditional mean of the target given the importance ratio and the marginal density of the ratio, with a model-based implementation that combines one-dimensional Gaussian process regression with score-informed heavy-tailed density estimation using observed weights and available density evaluations; ordinary importance sampling is a special case.
AI.result: The paper studies oracle gains and establishes consistency under general and model-specific conditions; simulations and cross-validation applications show improved estimation accuracy and uncertainty quantification.
AI.conclusion: Post-stratification of importance ratios is a general and practical route to better importance sampling estimates and their uncertainty.

title: Gaussian Partitioning for Reliable Learning of Multi-Index Models
comment: The abstract has been shortened for arXiv
summary: We introduce Gaussian partitioning, an algorithmic primitive for distributions smooth with respect to a Gaussian. It partitions space into polyhedral regions so that almost all mass lies in thin strips restricting a few orthogonal directions. Within each strip, the conditional distribution approximately matches low-degree Gaussian moments in the unrestricted directions. Our construction builds on logconcave partitioning of Diakonikolas, Kane, and Ma (FOCS 2026). Under input marginals smooth with respect to the standard Gaussian, we obtain agnostic learners with error $(1+c)\mathrm{opt}+\epsilon$ for broad classes of Boolean multi-index models, including functions of halfspaces, low-dimensional convex concepts, and low-dimensional polynomial threshold functions. For functions of $k$ halfspaces, both agnostic and testable agnostic learners achieve this error with dimension dependence $d^{\mathrm{poly}(k/c)}$, improving the previous exponential dependence on $k/c$ in the agnostic exponent. For learning from positive examples with imperfect unlabeled data (PUI), we give algorithms and Statistical Query (SQ) lower bounds that qualitatively characterize complexity through Gaussian moment matching. For fixed smoothness and positive-mass parameters, we learn intersections of $k$ halfspaces with dimension dependence $d^{O(\log(k/\epsilon))}$ and matching SQ lower bounds, improving the previous $d^{\mathrm{poly}(1/\epsilon)}$ upper bound even for one halfspace. A general reduction from agnostic reliable learning to PUI yields negative reliable learners for these intersections with the same dimension dependence, for fixed smoothness. Finally, for PQ learning and testable learning with distribution shift, we prove qualitatively optimal SQ lower bounds of $d^{\Omega(1/\epsilon^2)}$, even for intersections of two halfspaces with Gaussian training data and arbitrary test distributions.

AI.tldr: Gaussian partitioning partitions space into polyhedral regions for distributions smooth with respect to a Gaussian, yielding agnostic learners for Boolean multi-index models with improved dimension dependence and near-matching statistical query lower bounds.
AI.motivation: Learning Boolean multi-index models such as intersections of halfspaces had exponential dependence on the number of halfspaces in the agnostic exponent, and the complexity of reliable and PUI learning was not characterised for smooth input distributions.
AI.method: The construction builds on logconcave partitioning, producing thin strips with approximate low-degree Gaussian moment matching in unrestricted directions; it is used to design agnostic, testable agnostic and PUI learners and a general reduction from agnostic reliable learning to PUI, together with statistical query lower bounds.
AI.result: Agnostic learners reach error (1+c) opt + epsilon with dimension dependence d^poly(k/c) for functions of k halfspaces, improving the previous exponential dependence; intersections of k halfspaces are learned with d^O(log(k/epsilon)) dependence matching SQ lower bounds; PQ learning and testable learning under distribution shift have SQ lower bounds of d^Omega(1/epsilon^2).
AI.conclusion: Gaussian partitioning sharpens the complexity landscape for reliable and agnostic learning of multi-index models under smooth distributions, with several bounds shown to be qualitatively optimal.

title: Conformal Prediction at Performative Equilibrium: The Price of Performativity
summary: Conformal prediction gives finite-sample coverage when calibration and test points are exchangeable, but exchangeability can fail when deployment changes the data distribution. We study conformal prediction in performative settings, where the deployed predictor affects the data distribution, and seek prediction sets valid at performative equilibrium: coverage must hold under $D(f^\star)$ for a performatively stable predictor $f^\star$. Under total-variation $L$-sensitivity of the distribution map, we prove a phase transition at $L=1$. If $L \ge 1$, no finite-sample procedure can uniformly guarantee both equilibrium-valid coverage and nontrivial prediction sets. If $L<1$, the minimax excess miscoverage over informative procedures is $\widetilde{\Omega}(1/((1-L)\sqrt{n}))$, implying a sample-complexity inflation of order $1/(1-L)^2$ for fixed excess miscoverage. Our main technical tool is a transfer theorem: any procedure returning a predictor within $\varepsilon$ of equilibrium yields equilibrium-valid coverage up to an additive $L\varepsilon$ term after split-conformal calibration. We instantiate the theorem with two retraining algorithms: a model-free method for discretizable classes and a parametric tail-averaged method that matches the $n$- and $L$-dependence of this rate up to logarithmic factors. Experiments, including semi-synthetic credit scoring, demonstrate the predicted threshold behavior and scaling laws.

AI.tldr: The paper develops conformal prediction valid at performative equilibrium and proves a phase transition at total-variation sensitivity L = 1, below which informative, equilibrium-valid prediction sets exist at a sample-complexity inflation of order 1/(1-L)^2.
AI.motivation: Conformal coverage relies on exchangeability, which fails when deployment changes the data distribution through a performative predictor, so coverage must be guaranteed under the distribution induced by a performatively stable predictor.
AI.method: Under total-variation L-sensitivity of the distribution map, the authors prove a transfer theorem showing that any procedure returning a predictor within epsilon of equilibrium yields equilibrium-valid coverage up to an additive L epsilon term after split-conformal calibration, and instantiate it with a model-free method for discretisable classes and a parametric tail-averaged retraining method.
AI.result: For L >= 1 no finite-sample procedure can guarantee both equilibrium-valid coverage and nontrivial sets; for L < 1 the minimax excess miscoverage is of order 1/((1-L) sqrt(n)), implying sample-complexity inflation of order 1/(1-L)^2; experiments on semi-synthetic credit scoring confirm the threshold behaviour and scaling laws.
AI.conclusion: Performativity imposes a sharp price on conformal prediction, with a threshold at L = 1 and a quantified cost of sample complexity below it.

title: GSBR: Geometric Support Behavior Regularization for Online RL
summary: Regularizing online reinforcement learning (RL) toward a pretrained base policy can improve sample efficiency and learning stability, but regularization that is too restrictive limits how much the policy can improve. Base policies -- typically diffusion or flow-matching models trained by imitation learning on large, diverse datasets -- capture many behaviors that are reasonable but suboptimal. Existing regularizers using such base policies are too restrictive in one of two ways: behavioral cloning regularizers pull the actor toward the full base-policy distribution, penalizing it for discarding suboptimal modes, while hard support constraints forbid improvements that lie just outside the base policy's support. We propose Geometric Support Behavior Regularization (GSBR), which penalizes actions by their distance from the base policy's support. Actions within the support incur no penalty, so the actor can concentrate on high-value modes; outside the support, where value estimates are less reliable, the penalty grows smoothly with distance while still permitting improvement when the value gained outweighs the penalty. GSBR estimates this distance from a finite set of base-policy samples, so it requires only sample access to the base policy. Across 19 tasks on four robotic benchmarks, GSBR raises the average success rate from 33% for the base policy to 95%, achieving the highest average success rate and throughput among all compared methods, with about 23% higher normalized throughput than the next-best RL method. Project website and open-source code at this https URL .

AI.tldr: GSBR regularises online RL toward a pretrained base policy by penalising actions by their distance from the base policy's support rather than its full distribution, raising average success from 33% to 95% across 19 robotic tasks.
AI.motivation: Behaviour cloning regularisers pull the actor toward the full base-policy distribution, penalising useful improvements, while hard support constraints forbid improvements just outside the support.
AI.method: GSBR estimates the distance from each action to the base policy's support using a finite set of base-policy samples, applies no penalty within the support and a smoothly growing penalty outside it, so it needs only sample access to the base policy.
AI.result: Across 19 tasks on four robotic benchmarks, GSBR raises average success from 33% for the base policy to 95%, with the highest average success rate and throughput among compared methods and about 23% higher normalised throughput than the next-best RL method.
AI.conclusion: Geometric support regularisation is an effective and sample-access-only way to use a pretrained diffusion or flow-matching base policy in online RL.

title: GUILD: Guided Iterative Data Collection for Imitation Learning
summary: Imitation learning policies in robotics are trained on datasets collected through costly real-world teleoperation. Often, the data-collection process is unguided, relying on the teleoperator's intuition, resulting in data that contributes little to overall policy performance. Recent work has shown that curating such unguided datasets can substantially improve policy performance, but these approaches operate by filtering existing datasets after collection and therefore do not prevent the acquisition of uninformative data. In this work, we propose GUILD, a novel Guided Data Collection (GDC) method that actively reasons about which data should be collected to maximize downstream policy performance. We introduce an iterative framework that alternates between 1) task proposal and data collection and 2) data evaluation to close the loop. For task proposal, we leverage semantic priors from vision-language models to identify relevant environments, object configurations, and goals for data collection. However, since semantic relevance does not imply policy improvement, we perform data evaluation. By leveraging predictive data attribution we approximate how the collected trajectories influence policy performance on a target deployment setting. This signal is then used as feedback to guide subsequent data collection, closing the data collection loop. We evaluate our approach in simulation and real robot settings, demonstrating that guided data collection substantially improves sample efficiency and deployment performance compared to passive data collection strategies, multiple baselines and experienced roboticists. More information at this https URL

AI.tldr: GUILD is an iterative guided data collection method for imitation learning that uses vision-language model task proposals and predictive data attribution to choose which teleoperated data to collect, improving sample efficiency over passive collection.
AI.motivation: Teleoperated data collection for imitation learning is costly and often unguided, and curation after collection cannot prevent uninformative data from being acquired.
AI.method: GUILD alternates between task proposal and data collection, using semantic priors from vision-language models to identify environments, object configurations and goals, and data evaluation with predictive data attribution that estimates how collected trajectories influence policy performance on a target deployment setting, feeding this back to guide subsequent collection.
AI.result: In simulation and on real robots, guided data collection substantially improves sample efficiency and deployment performance compared with passive collection strategies, multiple baselines and experienced roboticists.
AI.conclusion: Closing the loop between task proposal and data attribution makes data collection for imitation learning more targeted and effective than passive approaches.

title: PolicyIK: High-Precision Inverse Kinematics for Robot Arms with Reinforcement Learning
summary: Inverse kinematics (IK) converts end-effector pose commands into joint motion, and many vision-language-action (VLA) policies rely on it to act on a given arm and to transfer across embodiments. Precise IK remains laborious: redundancy and singularities complicate the inverse mapping, execution depends on hand-tuned controllers, and training data on physical robots are costly to collect. We present PolicyIK, a goal-conditioned reinforcement learning policy for high-precision IK. It updates joint-position references from pose feedback and observes its accumulated reference relative to the measured joints, so it can retain the offset that the position controller needs at rest. Two-scale pose errors with an error-dependent action gain resolve millimeter residuals while preserving large motions. Progress and dwell rewards teach it to both reach the tolerance and stay within it. In simulation, a single attempt by the trained PPO policy keeps the mean errors over the final second within 1 mm and 0.2° on 93.5% of held-out tasks, and a deployment protocol raises success to 98.9%. When trained directly on a physical arm with an off-policy RL learner, PolicyIK achieves higher reaching and holding success than all four classical IK controllers under the same time budgets. In simulated pick-and-place, PolicyIK executes the end-effector commands of the $\pi_{0.5}$ VLA policy with 95.7% success. These results show that reinforcement learning can provide high-precision inverse kinematics for robot arms. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: PolicyIK is a reinforcement learning policy for high-precision inverse kinematics of robot arms that reaches millimetre and 0.2-degree accuracy in simulation and outperforms classical IK controllers on a physical arm.
AI.motivation: Precise inverse kinematics is laborious because of redundancy and singularities, hand-tuned controllers and costly physical training data, and VLA policies depend on it for embodiment transfer.
AI.method: PolicyIK updates joint-position references from pose feedback, observes its accumulated reference relative to measured joints, uses two-scale pose errors with an error-dependent action gain, and is trained with progress and dwell rewards; the physical arm is trained with an off-policy RL learner.
AI.result: In simulation a single PPO policy attempt keeps mean errors within 1 mm and 0.2 degrees over the final second on 93.5% of held-out tasks, raised to 98.9% with a deployment protocol; on a physical arm it achieves higher reaching and holding success than four classical IK controllers under the same time budgets; in simulated pick-and-place it executes pi_0.5 end-effector commands with 95.7% success.
AI.conclusion: Reinforcement learning can provide high-precision inverse kinematics for robot arms, supporting VLA policies across embodiments.
